# What a useful account must preserve

Second research cycle, 5 October 2026, Asia/Bangkok. Continuation of [Investigating the full picture](full-picture-synthesis.md).

**We now have a precise negative result, a positive theorem, and a consequence for model revision.** Equal total resources need not imply equal possibilities for correction—even when the available first actions are identical. Under explicit conditions, free immediate pooling restores that equivalence. A description adequate under one access regime can become inadequate when the permitted future changes.

This advances the larger investigation by identifying a distinction that sometimes must be retained, together with conditions under which it can safely be removed. It does not establish universal completeness. These are exact results about a constructed process, with independent computational checks; they are not measurements of human institutions.

## The question we actually tested

The earlier synthesis proposed testing whether a coarse description preserves attainable recovery. Here we isolated one omission: the location of funds. Everything else relevant to the existing process—productive stock, diagnostic readiness, fault belief, remaining time, and access regime—was retained.

Two accounts hold the resources: spendable cash and a treasury. The three access regimes are permanent exclusion from the treasury, free immediate access before each round, and access beginning in round two. We ask whether replacing the two balances by their sum preserves the outcomes available to an informed controller.

“Available” concerns admissible policies under the supplied information and payment rules. A controller cannot pay today's bill with tomorrow's income. We compare possibilities, rather than assuming that every controller chooses well or that a particular institution implements the calculated policy.

The protocol was frozen locally before the main numerical run. The two-round example below was derived before that run; it is an analytical witness, not held-out evidence. The full protocol, exact outputs, implementation, proofs, and audits are preserved in the [reproduction bundle](access-study-evidence.zip).

## Equal wealth and equal first actions, different futures

Consider a system with productive stock two, a fault known to be present, and an unready diagnostic. It has five total units of funds and two rounds remaining. Repair costs three. Compare these two allocations while treasury access is barred:

| Initial condition | Spendable cash | Treasury | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| B | 1 | 4 | 5 |

Neither can repair or rebuild the diagnostic immediately. Both have exactly the same sole first action: proceed without a test or repair.

Damage occurs in the first round with probability 0.8. On that branch, productive stock falls to one and earns two units of income. A now has two spendable units; B has three. The difference that could not change their first action now determines whether repair is affordable.

The fault remains present next round with probability 0.95. Without repair, second-round damage therefore has probability

\[
0.95(0.8)+0.05(0.1)=0.765.
\]

That damage collapses the stock-one system. A cannot afford to prevent it, so its minimum two-round collapse probability is

\[
0.8(0.765)=0.612.
\]

B can repair after the adverse first round. Repair clears the fault and adds productive capacity; even the remaining healthy-state damage cannot then reduce stock to zero. Its minimum collapse probability is zero. If the first round has no damage, both reach stock three and survive the remaining round without repair.

| Result under the selected collapse-minimizing policy | A | B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Collapse probability | 61.2% | 0% |
| Expected paid expenditure | 0 | 2.4 |
| Expected repairs when the fault target is absent | 0 | 0.04 |
| Probability terminal stock is below two | 61.2% | 8% |

The last row matters: preventing collapse does not guarantee the stronger, stipulated recovery condition. Equal initial wealth also does not mean equal spending or burden. B's additional possibility is used to fund repair, and the tradeoffs remain visible.

**An identical present action menu does not certify an identical future action process.** Income can move two apparently similar states to opposite sides of a later payment threshold. A model that merges them must either retain that distinction elsewhere or accept that it cannot answer this recovery question exactly.

## What the larger finite calculation adds

The main study used four rounds, three initial stock levels, three fault beliefs, six partitions of five units, and the three access regimes: 162 starting conditions. Each was optimized under seven declared linear combinations of four outcomes:

- probability of collapse;
- expected paid expenditure;
- a limited burden measure: repairs when their fault target is absent, plus 0.05 per paid test;
- probability terminal stock is below two.

The weights are probes of what is attainable, not an endorsed social objective. The burden measure is not total harm: a repair whose fault target is absent can still improve productive stock. No ethical ordering follows from choosing these coordinates.

All 1,134 main optimizations used exact rational arithmetic. For each stock, belief, and weighting, we checked whether changing the account partition changed the minimum weighted outcome. That gives 63 comparison groups per access regime.

| Access regime | Groups with unequal minima across same-total partitions |
|---|---:|
| Treasury permanently barred | 24 of 63 |
| Access begins in round two | 15 of 63 |
| Immediate free access | 0 of 63 |

These counts describe the constructed grid, not frequencies in the world. One unequal minimum proves that the two attainable outcome sets differ. Agreement on seven probes alone cannot prove equality of entire sets. The immediate-access equality has a separate structural proof below.

![Four-round minimum collapse probabilities across equal-total account partitions](access-outcomes.png)

*All curves hold initial total funds at five, the initial fault as known present, and diagnostic readiness at zero. Small positive risks near the horizontal axis should not be read as exactly zero.*

For initial stock two with a known fault and barred treasury, the four-round minimum collapse probability falls from **61.2%** at zero spendable cash to **1.36%** at one, **0.136%** at two, and **zero** at three or more. Immediate access and access from round two both attain zero for this particular stock-two slice.

Stock one exposes the deadline. With fewer than three spendable units, access beginning next round still leaves an 80% chance of collapse now. Immediate access reduces the four-round optimum to 0.017%, but does not eliminate all risk: rare adverse sequences can exhaust the available repair budget. Stock three buffers the difficulty sufficiently that all three regimes attain zero collapse on this slice. Access can therefore bind, arrive too late, or make no difference, depending on the physical state and horizon.

In all 378 matched comparisons, the minimum weighted outcome under immediate access was no worse than with delayed access, which was no worse than with permanent exclusion. Under the stated policy and transfer assumptions, this weak ordering follows from the ability to emulate a more restricted policy. It does not imply that every coordinate of the selected outcome improves. For example, a lower-risk policy can spend more.

## When total resources really are enough

Let cash be \(b\), treasury \(t\), total \(N=b+t\), and the cash cap \(C\). Free maximum transfer before acting produces the canonical allocation

\[
\nu_C(b,t)=\bigl(\min(C,N),\max(N-C,0)\bigr).
\]

Every same-total partition reaches the same allocation. After paying a total bill \(c\) and receiving income \(I\), total resources satisfy

\[
N'=N-c+I.
\]

This gives an exact operational reduction if the following conditions hold:

1. Transfers are guaranteed, free, immediate, and have no other effects on outcomes or observations.
2. Every complete round's bill, including every possible diagnostic branch, fits below the cash cap. Bills are nonnegative and precede income.
3. Overflow is retained without loss, and account location has no independent effect on physical dynamics, observations, or the outcome being assessed.
4. The retained state includes the information needed to predict the process. The omitted account split supplies no extra hidden-state information.
5. Controllers have enough allowed memory to implement the policy correspondence; here sufficient-belief memory is supplied freely.

The study has cap eight and maximum round bill six. Once normalized, same-total states have the same feasible operational prescriptions, the same observation and physical transition laws, and the same next-total rule. Induction gives the same attainable operational outcome laws at every finite horizon under these assumptions.

There is a stronger policy argument. Suppose transfers are optional and a controller deliberately leaves some money in treasury. A controller in the normalized system can keep a virtual record of those balances and make exactly the same operational choices. Its actual cash is sufficient for every bill the virtual controller could pay, and extra spendable funds do not force extra spending. Conversely, the optional-transfer controller can always choose maximum transfer. This establishes equality of attainable operational laws, including inefficient choices, rather than only equality of optimal scores.

The correspondence preserves physical outcomes, observations used for the operational task, spending, burden, and total funds. It does not preserve individual account histories or transfer events. A literal action such as “transfer five” may exist in one account allocation and not another. The result concerns an executable procedure—make funds spendable, then operate—with declared access to observed account balances.

Transfer fees, delays, account-specific obligations, signaling, losses, or insufficient controller memory can break the argument. The theorem identifies the work done by its assumptions; it does not assert that real resources are always interchangeable.

## Adequacy depends on what may change

The same process admits different sufficient financial descriptions:

| Admitted access process | A sufficient financial description for these operational outcomes |
|---|---|
| Treasury remains barred forever | Spendable cash |
| Free immediate pooling every round | Total funds |
| Barred now, pooling from next round | Spendable cash and total funds |

These are sufficient descriptions, not claims of global minimality. A bookkeeping question still needs the treasury balance even when it can never finance repair. A very short horizon or a restricted outcome can allow further simplification.

The most consequential result concerns changing the model's admitted future. Take two systems with stock two, a known fault, zero spendable cash, and two rounds remaining. Give one treasury zero and the other treasury three. Under permanent exclusion, both have minimum collapse probability 61.2%; the treasury can safely be omitted from this operational model.

Now allow access beginning next round. Their current cash and first actions remain identical. After an adverse first round, the system without treasury has only two spendable units and cannot repair. The other can pool its resources and pay three. Their minimum collapse probabilities become 61.2% and zero.

**The recovery question stayed fixed; the admitted future mechanism changed. A previously sufficient description stopped being sufficient.** This is a concrete instance of the earlier claim that sufficiency is relative to a model family. It does not imply that every detail must always be retained. It says that a claim of irrelevance needs a scope: irrelevant to which questions, under which possible changes?

This also keeps two changes distinct. Releasing access during a modeled trajectory is a world event. Extending a model that assumed permanent exclusion to include later release is a revision of the model family. Our two-model comparison is not yet a model of an agent discovering or negotiating a new access rule.

## Controls, verification, and a useful negative result

Removing earned income eliminates the two low-cash states' distinction: with barred treasury, both cash-zero and cash-one cases then have four-round minimum collapse probability **79.18345%**. This verifies the role of the production-to-payment bridge in that contrast. It does not eliminate every access effect; greater initial liquidity or immediate access can still help.

The known-safe control starts healthy, with fault onset and healthy-state damage both removed. No repair is needed, and the selected failure-minimizing policies have zero failure, expenditure, and burden. The four operational outcome coordinates also agree across permission regimes in the initially all-liquid base cases in this tested horizon; individual terminal account balances can differ. That agreement is a checked result, not a general theorem: later income can overflow into treasury and become inaccessible.

The study also ran initially ready and uninformative-diagnostic controls. **None of the 1,134 selected main optima uses a paid diagnostic test.** The current result is therefore about access to direct repair. It does not show that inquiry is useless, establish the value of maintained diagnostic capacity, or reproduce the inherited simulator's different objective. A later test of inquiry must make discrimination matter under an explicitly justified scenario, rather than relabeling these repair results.

An independent implementation enumerated hidden faults, signals, damage, and public observations, then solved the small decision problems without reusing the main transition helpers. It matched 4,536 one- and two-round optima, reevaluated their selected policy vectors, and matched 18 targeted four-round optima. Additional checks covered kernels for all control configurations across 5,184 audited states, 1,134 saved main score and ledger identities, the reported group counts, and 378 access-order comparisons. No discrepancy was found. Separate algebra checks covered 53,228 banking identities and 73,130 payment-prefix cases.

All eight numerical and audit scripts also ran successfully from the packaged copies; the four main deterministic result files reproduced byte for byte. These are useful error checks, not external replication. The independent solver did not rerun every four-round optimum. No longer-horizon result, demonstrated transfer to a different physical or institutional implementation, or field result is claimed.

## Relation to established work

Hard resource feasibility under partial observation already has a substantial mathematical treatment. Brázdil and colleagues distinguish a resource constraint along an execution from an expected-cost objective and explicitly represent observable resource levels. Our particular account-access example does not invent resource-constrained planning. [Primary paper, sections 3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.07565).

Controller abstraction also has established implementation requirements. Reissig, Weber, and Rungger's feedback refinement work makes explicit that a transferred controller must use information actually available at its interface. That motivates the observed-balance adapter here; it does not by itself prove equality of our stochastic outcome laws. [Primary paper, sections IV–VI](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.03715).

No priority claim is made. The contribution to this investigation is the explicit connection between a failed resource summary, its repair conditions, and the revision of what counts as relevant state.

## What this lets us say next

The larger account can now make a sharper claim: **a useful description preserves the distinctions required by the future processes and questions it undertakes to explain. Its boundary of adequacy can itself change.** Here that statement has a specified example and a conditional positive theorem, rather than only an analogy.

There may be indefinitely many further consequences and applications to uncover. The pooling proof already covers infinitely many model instances through its parameters and every finite horizon satisfying its assumptions. That is mathematical generality within a declared class; it is not evidence that one account already explains every phenomenon, nor a proof of infinite-horizon control under additional criteria.

The next major evidential gap remains the [transport test](next-test.md): freeze the mechanism and measurement rules, then test whether independently measured properties of a second implementation predict its recovery outcomes. The later recognition-and-feedback stage also remains unrun. More elaboration within this simulator cannot substitute for that test.

# When total funds suffice: a finite access theorem and its boundaries

Formal research appendix, 5 October 2026. Companion to [the access study](access-and-correction.md). The frozen protocol, local inherited-model snapshot, verification scripts, and exact results are in [the reproduction bundle](access-study-evidence.zip). No source-workspace or root experiment files were changed. This memo proves a stronger positive result than the observation that inaccessible money may be unusable. The result is conditional and not claimed novel.

## 1. Precise result

**With guaranteed free, immediate transfers, a sufficiently large cash cap, lossless overflow storage, and no other effects of account location, replacing separate accounts by total funds preserves all attainable operational outcome laws under an explicit normalization interface.** It need not preserve literal transfer/payment actions or account-specific outcomes.

The distinction is important. The negative example refutes a raw total-money projection under restricted access. The positive theorem identifies conditions under which that projection can be repaired by changing the action interface to “make the available money spendable, then act.” This is a proved transformation of a declared model, not evidence that real accounts are interchangeable.

The frozen experiment has cash cap 8 and maximum full-round bill 6. Its immediate-access mode already performs the required normalization automatically before each round. The main positive numerical check therefore verifies an algebraically warranted contract; it is not an independent discovery of financial fungibility.

## 2. Objects and assumptions

Write the financial state as \((b,t,p)\), where \(b\) is accessible cash, \(t\) treasury funds, and \(p\) the access mode. Use \(\pi\), rather than \(p\), for the hidden-fault posterior. Let \(z\) retain remaining horizon, productive stock, readiness, posterior, and all other nonfinancial variables needed for the declared process. Total funds are \(N=b+t\).

For the positive result assume:

1. \(0\le b\le C\), \(t\ge0\), with a fixed cash cap \(C\). The horizon is finite.
2. Access is guaranteed whenever normalization is required. Treasury-to-cash transfers take zero time, cost nothing, and preserve total funds. They have no effects on production, observation, risk, authority, or the protected outcome vector.
3. Operational/infrastructure payments are nonnegative and occur before new income. Every complete round, including every diagnostic-contingent branch, has total bill at most \(L\le C\).
4. Income \(I\ge0\) is credited after the round's payments: fill cash to \(C\), retain every remaining unit in treasury. There is no inaccessible external overflow sink in the immediate-access model.
5. Conditional on the retained physical/belief state and the chosen nonfinancial actions, the environment and primitive observation laws do not depend on the partition between the accounts. The split supplies no additional hidden-state information omitted from the retained posterior.
6. There are no holding costs, distinct account yields, seizure risks, transfer fees, transfer-dependent rewards, signaling effects, or terminal preferences over the partition. Criteria may depend on physical outcomes, latent target absence, expenditures, action counts, total funds, and time; the same environment realization will be coupled below.
7. The comparison allows admissible observation-history policies with private randomization and memory sufficient to emulate a virtual financial ledger. No policy is allowed to spend funds it lacks or treat future income as current cash. The maximum-transfer procedure itself is implementable from observed account balances or by a declared authorized bank operation.

The original model gives sufficient-belief memory freely. This memo retains that idealization explicitly. If controller memory and computation are priced, one must also price and verify the virtual-ledger implementation; equality of ideal attainable sets would then not establish equality of physically affordable controller sets.

All finite-horizon reachable totals are bounded: in the primary H4 grid, initial total is 5 and each round earns at most 6, so \(N\le29\). An unbounded treasury type therefore does not create an infinite reachable financial state set for this experiment.

## 3. The banking identity

Define the canonical split of a nonnegative total by \(\kappa_C(N)=(\min(C,N),(N-C)_+)\), and normalization of valid accounts by

\[
\nu_C(b,t)=\bigl(\min(C,N),(N-C)_+\bigr),\qquad N=b+t.
\]

It moves \(\min(t,C-b)\) into cash. It preserves \(N\), is idempotent, and makes every same-total partition identical at the start of the operational round.

After a feasible total payment \(c\le\min(C,N)\), then income \(I\), cash and treasury become

\[
b'=\min\{C,\min(C,N)-c+I\},
\]
\[
t'=(N-C)_++[\min(C,N)-c+I-C]_+.
\]

Consequently

\[
b'+t'=N-c+I,
\qquad
\nu_C(b',t')=\kappa_C(N-c+I).
\tag{1}
\]

Because all payments are nonnegative and no income arrives between them, an affordable full realized bill makes every earlier prefix affordable. A contingent prescription must still be feasible on every possible diagnostic branch. Since \(L\le C\), normalization once before the round is sufficient for every financially feasible branch; no hidden within-round transfer is required.

The operational state \((z,N)\) therefore has closed finance dynamics \(N'=N-c+I\). This is a genuine exact macro transition, provided the nonfinancial kernel and observation assumptions also hold.

## 4. Proposition 1: exact quotient of the normalized operational model

Consider the frozen immediate-access model at living, nonterminal decision points, and use as its action a complete operational prescription: infrastructure choice, test/no test, and diagnostic-contingent repair rule. Let

\[
q(z,b,t,0)=(z,b+t,0).
\]

For same-total states, normalization produces the same cash and treasury before the prescription is selected. Thus:

- The feasible operational prescriptions are the same, including every prefix constraint.
- The conditional laws of diagnostic observations, physical transitions, expenditure, target-absence burden, and output are the same for a common prescription.
- The next total satisfies (1); the posterior and readiness updates are the same.

Therefore \(q\) is an exact action-conditioned stochastic quotient **for this normalized macro interface**. The primary outcome vector \((F,E,B,U)\) is preserved. So are action counts and earned output. Terminal total funds are preserved. Terminal cash and treasury separately need not be preserved by an arbitrary total projection; in the particular living H4 comparison, the first normalization makes the full subsequent state laws identical under common prescriptions, which is stronger.

**Proof.** Equality of the normalized financial states gives equality of prescription availability. By assumption 5, the same prescription has the same primitive observation and physical-outcome law. The finance update's pushforward depends only on total funds, the realized cost, and income by (1). The retained posterior, readiness, and time updates agree. Induction over the finite horizon yields equal operational trajectory laws for every common operational policy and hence equal declared outcome vectors. At terminal or collapsed states the operational criteria depend only on the retained terminal physical state, and no further payment is available. ∎

This proposition does not claim equality of arbitrary policies that deliberately choose different actions in the two systems. It pairs each policy with its counterpart through the specified interface. An identical deterministic tie rule will choose matching optimal metrics when it sees identical normalized states and action orderings.

## 5. Proposition 2: normalization does not remove attainable operational outcomes from arbitrary lawful transfer policies

Now enlarge the concrete comparison class: the controller may choose any lawful partial transfer, or no transfer, before operating. The round's other assumptions remain unchanged. Transfer decisions may depend on its legitimate history and private randomness. Let \(\mathcal A_{\rm raw}(z,b,t)\) be the set of attainable laws of retained operational/environment traces, excluding transfer amounts, account-specific signals, and individual account paths. Let \(\mathcal A_{\rm norm}(z,N)\) be the corresponding set under compulsory maximum normalization and operational policies with the same history/random-memory allowance.

Then

\[
\boxed{\mathcal A_{\rm raw}(z,b,t)=\mathcal A_{\rm norm}(z,b+t).}
\tag{2}
\]

This includes the joint latent physical path for assessing target-absence burden; it does not grant either controller observation of that hidden path. In particular, all attainable primary expected vectors are equal, not merely one scalar optimum or the efficient frontier.

**Proof, normalization to raw.** A raw controller can choose the maximum lawful transfer each round and then execute any normalized controller. All actions, observations, physical outcomes, and costs can be coupled identically.

**Proof, raw to normalization.** Fix any admissible raw controller and initial split. A normalized controller stores a virtual copy of that raw controller's ledger, action history, and private random state. It executes the raw controller virtually, including its partial-transfer decisions, and takes the same nonfinancial actions in the actual normalized system. Couple the systems using the same diagnostic and physical random outcomes. At the start of a round, normalized cash is \(\min(C,N)\). The virtual raw controller can have at most that much cash. Any complete raw feasible branch costs at most \(N\), at most \(L\le C\), and therefore fits in normalized cash. Every nonnegative payment prefix also fits. By the account-independent environment assumption, the same nonfinancial choices give identical physical signals, costs, burden, and income. Both total accounts change by \(-c+I\). The virtual ledger can be updated exactly from its earlier balances, chosen transfer, payments, and observed income. Continue inductively. Thus every raw operational law is achieved in the normalized system. ∎

The policy can intentionally refrain from an action that has become affordable. Extra liquidity does not compel extra treatment, testing, or spending. This fact is needed for equality, rather than only an ability to achieve “better” outcomes.

The theorem concerns **lawful** policies. If the raw model admits deliberate invalid-payment attempts that trigger a special failure sink, that behavior is outside the stated feasible-policy class. Equality would require adding the same failure-producing action to the macro model or restricting attention to admissible policies. Similarly, a resource-oblivious controller class or a fixed installed program might not contain the virtual-ledger implementation.

For the exact finite belief MDP, scalar optimization can use deterministic Markov policies. The policy-emulation proof permits more history because it compares arbitrary transfer strategies. Equality of attainable expected vectors can alternatively be stated for randomized history policies; restricting both sides to a smaller stationary or memoryless class needs a separate argument and is not assumed here.

## 6. Raw labeled actions still fail to commute

Take \(C=8\), \((b,t)=(0,5)\) and \((5,0)\). Both have total 5 and granted permission.

- The literal action “pay 3 now, without preceding transfer” is feasible only from the second state.
- The literal action “transfer 5 into cash” is feasible only from the first state.

Thus the original same-label transition quotient fails. The operational prescription “make funds spendable, then pay 3” has an implementation in both states. Its cash transfer amount depends on the observed balance, but does not require hidden fault information.

This is a controller refinement with zero-time, zero-cost internal transfer steps. It is not a proof that transfer events, observers of those events, or raw microstep trace lengths are identical. If the original question concerns payment timing at microstep resolution, signaling, legal process, or a transfer's legitimacy, those discarded details may be precisely what matters.

## 7. A sufficient financial representation depends on the access regime

The protocol has three observed modes: \(-1\) is permanently barred, 0 is immediate, and 1 is barred this round then immediate. A useful sufficient representation is a typed union:

\[
\psi(z,b,t,p)=
\begin{cases}
(z,-1,b), &p=-1,\\
(z,0,N), &p=0,\\
(z,1,b,N), &p=1.
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]

For permanently barred funds, the treasury never affects operational feasibility or any primary metric. Cash evolves as \(b'=\min(C,b-c+I)\), and treasury can be omitted from this particular operational model. Its amount still matters for the bookkeeping identity, which is a different query.

For immediate access, Proposition 1 applies. For delayed access, current cash controls today's bills while total funds determine next round's normalized resources; keeping both suffices. There can be further horizon- or query-specific reductions, so (3) is sufficient rather than a globally minimal state representation.

**Adding permission to total is not enough in barred mode.** Both barred states can have the same total and still have different access. Conversely, retaining every account forever is unnecessarily detailed if a treasury is permanently irrelevant to every retained question. This is the positive structural result: the appropriate state depends on the intervention/permission contract.

If permissions can change later, the permanently barred reduction no longer applies. Two states with equal current cash but different treasury holdings can become operationally different when permission is granted. A current permission bit alone does not summarize the future permission process.

### Exact corollary: an institution change can invalidate an old sufficient state

Consider H2, stock2, readiness0, known current fault, accessible cash0, and treasury either0 or3. Under permanent exclusion, both states have minimum failure .612: both must do nothing in round one, and neither can repair after the adverse first-round stock transition. Thus treasury can legitimately be omitted within the permanently barred model.

Now enlarge the institutional transition family to permit a known unlock at the start of round two. At the current decision point both treasuries are still inaccessible, and every current accessible variable and action is identical. First-round damage has probability .8 and yields stock1 with income2. On this branch, next-round normalization gives the treasury0 state only2 and the treasury3 state5. The former cannot repair; the latter can pay3 and avoid collapse. The exact minimum failure probabilities are therefore .612 and0. The treasury3 witness again has expected expense2.4 and absent-target burden .04. Without first-round damage, both survive the one remaining round regardless.

The predictive question—attainable two-round survival—has stayed fixed. What changed is the admitted future permission mechanism. A summary sufficient under permanent exclusion is no longer sufficient in the expanded family. This is a structural analogue of inherited claim U20's model-relative sufficiency, not a demonstration of discovery of unconceived institutions or a general claim that all historical details should be retained.

## 8. A two-round failure that cannot be detected from the first action menu

Use the frozen process with horizon 2, stock 2, readiness 0, known initial fault \(\pi=1\), total funds 5, and permanently barred treasury. Compare accessible cash 0 and 1. Both have the same sole first operational action: drop readiness, no test, no repair.

First-round damage has probability .8. Damage leaves stock 1 and produces income 2. The two cash balances become 2 and 3. If damage does not occur, stock becomes 3, and collapse is impossible in the one remaining round even without repair.

After the first damage observation, the next-round fault posterior is .95: the fault has clearance probability .05. Without repair, second-round damage has probability

\[
.95(.8)+.05(.1)=.765.
\]

The cash-0 initial state now has only 2 and cannot pay the repair cost 3. Its minimum two-round collapse probability is therefore

\[
.8(.765)=.612=153/250.
\]

The cash-1 initial state now has 3 and can repair when stock fell to 1. Repair clears the fault and gives stock increment 2 before any damage, so even damage leaves stock 1 rather than zero. Its minimum collapse probability is exactly zero. This witness policy spends expected \(.8\times3=2.4\), and its expected absent-target repair burden is \(.8\times.05=.04\). It buys no test.

The distinction is generated by a later payment threshold after endogenous income. Equal current total funds and equal current action menus do not suffice for a closed dynamic abstraction. The analytic witness was known before the main H4 run; it is not held-out evidence.

## 9. Boundaries: delay, fees, capacity, observations, and terminal preferences

**Delay.** With one round remaining, stock 1, known fault, readiness 0, and total 5, a transfer available only next round cannot finance the present repair. Cash 0 has minimum collapse probability .8; cash 3 can repair and achieve zero. Delayed funds are not made current by having the same eventual total.

**Transfer fees.** Suppose a repair costs 1, total funds are 1, and transferring from treasury incurs a separate fee 1. State \((1,0)\) can repair, while \((0,1)\) cannot cover both transfer and repair. Even when both could repair, unequal transfer fees can change the expense coordinate. Maximum normalization may then itself be wasteful relative to a just-enough transfer.

**A cap below the round's total bill.** With cash cap 1 and total 2, two mandatory payments of 1 cannot both be funded by one start-of-round normalization if no transfer is allowed between them. A rule looking only at total bill \(2\le N\) would be false. Allowing another transfer between payments repairs that different model. The frozen model avoids the problem by maximum bill \(6\le8\).

**Account-dependent losses.** Distinct interest, holding costs, seizure risk, overflow destruction, or production effects of the balance can make normalization change the future total or physical process. Equation (1) and the coupling must then be rederived.

**Information or signaling.** If the initial split is correlated with the hidden fault and its information is omitted from the retained posterior, merging splits loses information. If observed transfers change another actor's actions, omitting transfer behavior changes the causal process. Neither case satisfies the common-kernel assumption.

**Account-specific terminal obligations.** “Leave one unit in treasury” and “leave one unit in immediately accessible cash” are different predicates. Total funds alone cannot preserve them. The primary protocol explicitly excludes terminal partition preference while retaining both balances for audit; the distinction must remain visible in reporting.

**No free controller implementation.** A finite memory budget can prevent simulation of an arbitrary virtual ledger. A fixed policy might automatically spend any accessible amount, so greater liquidity changes its behavior. Proposition 2 compares selectable policies in a declared class, not every installed controller's response to a transfer.

## 10. Entire attainable sets, frontiers, and seven support probes

Propositions 1–2 establish equality of all attainable primary expected vectors under their contracts. This is stronger than the equality of efficient frontiers. For example, attainable sets \(\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\) and \(\{(0,0)\}\), with both coordinates minimized, have the same efficient point but differ as sets. Their convexifications still have that distinction.

Conversely, checking finitely many scalar support directions cannot prove equality of entire frontiers or attainable sets. In two dimensions, the convex hull of \((0,2),(2,0)\) and that hull enlarged with \((.9,.9)\) have identical minima in each coordinate separately, but different minima of their sum. A finite probe set can miss a difference in an unprobed direction.

For a finite experiment with arbitrary ex ante lotteries, attainable expected-vector sets are compact and convex. Equality of their support functions in **all** real directions characterizes equality of the sets. The frozen seven directions are a useful, declared subset. A difference in any one proves inequality; agreement in all seven is inconclusive unless an independent structural theorem applies. No sampled lottery is needed to optimize a single linear support direction: at least one deterministic finite-horizon policy attains its optimum.

A lexicographic tie rule selects one point among policies with the same primary scalar value. Equal support values by themselves do not imply equal selected metric vectors if the policy spaces or tie rules differ. Under immediate normalization the full normalized state, operational action set, dynamics, and tie rule coincide, which supplies the stronger equality used by the protocol.

## 11. Access monotonicity and its limits

For the same initial accounts and environment, allowing immediate free access permits emulation of a delayed or permanently barred policy by maintaining its virtual ledger and taking the same nonfinancial actions. Likewise, delayed access can emulate permanently barred use. Under the same history/random-memory and account-neutral criteria assumptions,

\[
\mathcal V_{\rm barred}\subseteq
\mathcal V_{\rm delayed}\subseteq
\mathcal V_{\rm immediate},
\]

where \(\mathcal V\) denotes attainable operational expected vectors. Hence the minimum of each fixed scalar support direction under immediate access is no worse than under delayed/barred access.

This does not say every coordinate of the selected policy improves, that every installed controller improves, or that equality is impossible. A failure-minimizing policy may spend more or impose more target-absence burden. The institutional validity of the access rule remains an external question.

An initially all-liquid state is not automatically an all-horizon equality control: later production can create treasury overflow, and later bills can make it useful. The protocol correctly records that proposed control expectation as something to check, not as a theorem. Known-safe controls likewise need their stated damage/onset assumptions; “fault absent now” does not alone remove later need.

## 12. Verification and status

`formal_access_verify.py` independently enumerates 53,228 canonical payment/income identities over caps 1–8, totals 0–30, incomes 0–6, and all admissible partitions and payments. It also checks 73,130 two-payment prefix-dominance cases, and exactly recomputes the H2 .612 versus 0 witness, its 2.4/.04 expense/burden, the H1 delayed-access boundary, and the delayed-unlock model-expansion corollary. Results are saved in `formal_access_checks.json`.

Those checks support the formulas and analytic examples. They do not independently solve the main H4 support-probe grid, demonstrate empirical adequacy, or discover a universal access law. The general preservation claims follow from the stated proofs and require each assumption to be checked when transported to another setting.

The useful conclusion is conditional: a resource sum becomes an adequate operational state only when the access, timing, observation, cost, and outcome contracts make the different partitions interchangeable for the permitted procedures. The present model supplies one exact positive case and several exact ways it can fail.

# What makes protected generation possible

Investigation for Ren, 5 October 2026.

**We can now give a necessary-and-sufficient answer for indefinite protected continuation and recurring specified progress in finite controlled systems, including incomplete observation.** The answer is constructive: it supplies a controller and a finite certificate when the objective is achievable, and rejects it when no such strategy exists under the declared model.

This establishes a precise mathematical foundation for part of the proposed theory. It does not establish a completed fundamental theory of all existence. The mathematics still receives the system's mechanisms, observation rules, feasible actions, and protection/progress criteria as inputs. It also distinguishes recurring accomplishment from endlessly distinct novelty. Those distinctions determine what the result actually answers.

## The operational root we can prove

The central condition is the existence of **one compatible strategy that keeps the required conditions intact while repeatedly making progress**. Separate opportunities to repair, investigate, replenish, or revise are insufficient if they cannot be combined within the available information, resources, permissions, and time.

For a finite system, this condition has a finite structural certificate. Include the controller's memory in the description and identify a set of reachable situations with these properties:

1. Every situation satisfies the declared protection requirements.
2. The controller chooses an executable action using only information actually available to it.
3. Every allowed consequence of that action stays inside the certified set.
4. Between completed progress rounds, a positive integer rank strictly decreases. Completing a round permits the rank to reset while remaining inside the set.

A positive integer cannot decrease forever. Therefore the controller must repeatedly complete progress rounds, and its closure inside the certified set preserves protection throughout. Conversely, in the finite game class studied here, whenever protected recurring progress is achievable, a certificate of this kind can be constructed. This is the necessity direction that a list of useful ingredients would lack.

Under hidden conditions, the rank belongs to an information-and-memory state, not to a hidden state that the controller magically knows. An additional memory component tracks outstanding possible histories that have not yet made progress in the current round. A round completes only when every still-compatible history has done so. This avoids requiring all possible hidden states to be at the progress target simultaneously.

This is established safety and infinite-visit game mathematics applied to our question, with proofs and checked implementations supplied here. It is not claimed as a newly discovered law. The relevant lineage includes knowledge-based synthesis and fixed-point methods for imperfect-information games. [Chatterjee, Doyen, Henzinger, and Raskin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0706.2619).

## The exact safety theorem

Let \(K\) be the protected states. An information state \(B\) is the nonempty set of physical states still compatible with the actor's observations and earlier actions. For a proposed family \(W\) of protected information states, define

\[
\Phi(W)=\left\{B\subseteq K:
\text{some common executable action sends every possible observation update into }W
\right\}.
\]

Start with all protected information states and repeatedly remove any state that has no such action. In a finite system, this procedure stops. Call the remaining family \(W^*\).

The theorem is

\[
\boxed{B_0\in W^*
\iff
\text{one observation-based finite-memory controller can preserve protection forever}.}
\]

The family is computed from local transitions and observations, without first assuming the desired infinite outcome. A surviving information state supplies a witnessing action. A removed state supplies a finite obstruction: for every policy, some compatible physical path violates protection within its removal rank. The obstruction does not imply every hidden initial state is individually hopeless.

This also resolves the earlier finite-horizon quantifier gap inside this class. There are finitely many relevant information states. If some policy can survive every requested finite horizon, then one finite-memory controller can survive indefinitely. We no longer need to leave that implication as an unexamined assumption.

The result is a **sure guarantee against every modeled possibility**. It is different from positive survival probability, probability-one survival, or a high expected lifetime. The earlier financial experiments optimized probabilities and costs; their four-round results alone do not certify this stronger indefinite guarantee.

## Which assumptions we have actually removed

The existence characterization does not fundamentally require a finite state space. On arbitrary sets, the greatest family closed under feasible observation updates still characterizes indefinite sure safety, using ordinary set-theoretic choice to select actions. Finiteness is required for the finite algorithm and finite-memory guarantee given above, not for the bare existence equivalence.

Even with infinitely many states and observations, finitely many available controller choices at each information state suffice to interchange the two horizon quantifiers. For each horizon, collect the first actions that can succeed; these form nested nonempty subsets of a finite set, so at least one action works across every horizon. Its successors satisfy the same condition.

There are exact boundaries. If the initial choice can be any finite reserve \(n\), followed by unavoidable consumption without replenishment, every finite horizon is achievable but no one choice lasts forever. Infinite-state systems can also require unbounded controller memory even when only two actions are available. Removing finiteness therefore strengthens existence while losing certain implementation guarantees.

The proof does not grant an actor free physical memory or computation. The finite controller must still be affordable and authorized in an application. If computing its decisions consumes time or resources, those costs must be included. Likewise, an abstract infinite selector is not automatically a computable or physically realizable controller.

## Recurring progress adds a second condition

Safety alone permits an idle self-loop. To represent continued productive response, let \(P\subseteq K\) mark an independently specified progress event and require infinitely many visits to \(P\).

In a fully observed finite system, define \(\operatorname{CPre}(T)\) as the states **in \(K\)** with an executable action whose nonempty set of possible successors lies entirely inside \(T\). The exact winning region is

\[
W=\nu_{Z\subseteq K}\,\mu_{Y\subseteq K}\,
\bigl[(P\cap\operatorname{CPre}(Z))\cup\operatorname{CPre}(Y)\bigr].
\]

The inner calculation finds states that can force progress and then return to the outer candidate set. The outer calculation removes candidates that cannot keep repeating that achievement. Its final ranks and selected actions provide the certificate described above. Unsafe successors and deadlocks are losing; they are never deleted merely to make an action appear safe. This is a standard Büchi-game construction. [Grädel, Lücking, and Naaf, sections 2 and 5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.08327).

For incomplete observation, replace the hidden physical state by a pair \((B,O)\): current possibilities \(B\), and outstanding possibilities \(O\) that still owe a progress visit during this round. The pair is updated from the public observation and chosen action. Apply the same finite-game calculation with target \(O=\varnothing\). The construction is exact for the declared finite sure-winning model and produces a finite-memory controller. A full proof, including why infinitely persistent obligations imply a real progress-avoiding path, is included in the evidence.

The extra memory matters. In a hidden two-state alternation, every actual path repeatedly visits the first state, although the observer never knows which state is current. Requiring certainty that the current state lies in \(P\) would reject this valid recurrence. Tracking obligations handles it correctly. The underlying acceptance construction has established automata-theoretic precedents. [Boker, Kupferman, and Rosenberg, sections 1 and 3](https://faculty.runi.ac.il/udiboker/files/AlternationRemoval.pdf).

These results concern infinite sequences of modeled events. A claim about indefinite elapsed physical time additionally needs timing rules that cannot compress infinitely many events into a finite duration. Resource and timing requirements remain part of the application contract.

## A second implementation gives a concrete situational test

We also completed a separate finite service-queue challenge. It has jobs with deadlines, a hidden persistent fault, paid diagnosis, restart that consumes a service slot, and completion income. These mechanisms differ from the earlier stock-and-repair simulator.

The target exposed isolated service, diagnostic, and restart distributions. A separately written predictor composed those component laws with the declared queue and payment chronology. Its 864 outcome vectors were frozen before the integrated target policies were run. A separate evaluator then enumerated every reachable branch of the registered policies with exact arithmetic.

**All 864 cells and 6,048 registered coordinates matched exactly.** These are synthetic component and implementation checks. The component laws were stipulated, not measured in a real service, and no advantage over a conventional model with the same full information was demonstrated. This does not complete the earlier strict two-gate transport protocol, whose assumptions differ.

The more informative result is an exact reversal. Fix a known fault, one job, cash three, a restart that clears the fault with probability \(3/4\), and the same evaluation: probability of missing the deadline. Only the deadline changes.

| Time available | Always serve | Restart first then serve | Lower failure risk |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| One slot | Failure \(3/4\) | Failure \(1\) | Serve |
| Three slots | Failure \(27/64\) | Failure \(9/64\) | Restart first |

Restarting the urgent job consumes its only service opportunity. With more time, the same restart can clear the fault and leave two service attempts. Thus the same affordable intervention is harmful to the stated objective in one situation and beneficial in another. This gives a precise sense in which a theory can identify an unreasonable choice relative to a declared objective and situation.

A coarse description retaining job count, fault belief, accounts, regime, and time but omitting deadlines fails this test. Among the three policies that do not themselves read deadlines, 132 of 144 same-description/policy groups have different outcomes across the omitted deadlines. The deadline-aware fourth policy is excluded from those common-policy counts. The coarse model was deliberately expected to fail; this is an explicit abstraction challenge, not a surprise discovery or a refutation of every formulation of the wider theory.

## What this decides about the proposed full root

There is an affirmative answer to the operational question: **we have an exact characterization of indefinite protected recurrence in the declared finite class, together with a broader set-based existence theorem for safety.** It unifies information, resource access, timing, and action feasibility when their mechanisms are represented correctly. It can explain failure and success through one structure.

There is not yet an affirmative answer to the stronger claim that the distinctive philosophical root determines all generative phenomena. The current transition schema admits arbitrary supplied dynamics. Writing continuation as \(J(x)=\{x\oplus i:i\in I(x)\}\) can represent any transition relation by letting \(I(x)\) be its successors and defining \(x\oplus y=y\). Without additional restrictions, this form admits static, terminating, productive, and destructive processes alike. Its expressive generality does not choose which mechanism occurs in the world.

This does not disqualify a general constraint theory or require it to predict every detail. It identifies the missing stronger content: a restrictive common law, or a justified interpretation bridge, that supplies more than the mechanism already entered into the model. The queue comparison supplies a correct representation requirement, but the conventional fully specified queue model makes the same predictions.

Distinction alone is insufficient for ongoing generation: distinct terminal states supply a countermodel. Conversely, alternative branches are not necessary for endlessly distinct change: the fixed rule \(n\mapsto n+1\) has a single successor and never repeats a state. Any richer meaning of 間 must therefore be stated and connected to continuation explicitly rather than equated with branching or mere describability.

## What remains open about inexhaustibility

Recurring progress is not automatically recurring novelty. A fixed finite repertoire of novelty labels admits only finitely many first occurrences. This is a restriction on the repertoire, not on every finite controller: a finite controller can write words of increasing length into an unbounded output medium. Whether those outputs count as meaningful novelty depends on the declared equivalence and evaluation criteria.

A substantive inexhaustibility claim therefore needs a growing object space, a criterion for what counts as new, a mechanism that keeps producing qualifying objects, and an account of its continuing physical and evaluative requirements. Our recurrence theorem does not supply those premises. Nor does it prove that the actual universe eventually exhausts its possibilities.

The wider theory's later formulation offers a more distinctive testable proposal than the bare transition schema: success may buy power over future rules while consequences escape effective feedback and independent alternatives lose the ability to reproduce. The source also states conditions for withdrawing that diagnosis. Testing those independently specified causal links would examine a substantive claim of the theory. Their universality does not follow from the safety or recurrence proofs.

## Evidence and verification

The [continuation proof](continuation-proof.md) gives the safety theorem, assumption removals, countermodels, and partial-observation recurrence construction. The [progress proof](progress-proof.md) gives the nested fixed point and rank certificate. The [evidence bundle](continuation-root-evidence.zip) contains the independently written solvers and oracles, target protocol and frozen predictions, component calibration, outcomes, comparisons, and reviews.

The safety implementation was checked across 12,005 finite games with 100,842 explicit policy-tree comparisons. The fully observed progress implementation was checked across two exhaustive small classes and 500 additional seeded cases, plus edge cases. The hidden-progress construction was checked across 4,608 plant/observation/protection/progress cases, including verification of extracted controllers against actual plant-and-memory cycles. These computations support the implementations; the general statements rest on the written proofs. They are not empirical observations, proof-assistant certification, or independent human replication.

Reference repositories and earlier frozen studies remain unchanged. The new queue challenge has its own local protocol and prediction freeze; the anticipated deadline effect and chosen component laws were already known when it was designed.
