## Decision rules

Reject an exact projection claim after one verified counterexample within its registered domain. Reject the registered transport model for the target when its exact predictions fail beyond numerical tolerance, or its sampled primary differences exclude zero under the prespecified simultaneous procedure. A systematic reversal of the predicted interaction is particularly diagnostic.

Report a narrower success if the shared model transports only after an independently identified boundary restriction. Label changes suggested by target outcomes as a new exploratory model and evaluate them on a new held-out target. Do not redefine the original success criterion.

If a conventional control model matches the transported model using the same assumptions, conclude that the common formulation organizes established mechanisms; do not infer a new law. If the shared model predicts equally well with fewer independently calibrated mechanisms across implementations, that supports explanatory compression and scoped integration. Neither outcome settles universal ontology or ethical adequacy.

Real empirical application remains a separate stage requiring independently observed mechanisms and outcomes, appropriate permissions, and no reliance on simulator labels as evidence about people. No external study or publication is authorized or performed by this protocol.

# Exact conditions for protected recurring progress

Prepared 2026-10-05. This is a mathematical characterization for a specified finite game, with an independent small-class implementation check for full observation and a proved obligation-monitor extension for partial observation. It does not establish that any physical or social domain satisfies that game model. It extends indefinite safety by requiring recurrent registered progress; it does not establish unbounded semantic novelty.

## A precise attainable answer

Let S be a finite state set, K ⊆ S the safe states, and P ⊆ K the states registered as progress. At each state s, the fully informed controller chooses an available action a, and an adversarial environment chooses the next state in F(s,a). Available actions have nonempty successor sets. The controller acts before the environment chooses the successor; there is no fairness restriction on that choice. The action sets are finite for the implementation below. A deadlock loses the infinite-continuation objective, even if its state lies in K or P.

Define, for T ⊆ K,

    CPre_K(T) = {s ∈ K : some available a has ∅ ≠ F(s,a) ⊆ T}.

An action with an unsafe possible successor does not satisfy this predecessor. Neither does an empty successor set. Thus restricting to the safe subgame must not mean silently deleting unsafe successors while retaining the original action.

The desired objective is: every resulting run is infinite, stays in K, and visits P infinitely often. Its exact winning region is

    W = νZ ⊆ K . μY ⊆ K . ((P ∩ CPre_K(Z)) ∪ CPre_K(Y)).       (1)

Here μ is the least fixed point and ν the greatest fixed point on subsets of K. In particular, s₀ ∈ W if and only if a causal strategy can guarantee this objective against every allowed environmental choice. A deterministic strategy depending only on the present state is sufficient. The theorem is conditional on the specified dynamics, observations, action order, safety predicate, and progress predicate, but it is an exact characterization within that class.

This is an instance of established Büchi-game theory. Section 2 provides our direct proof in this controlled-transition notation; source capsule A records the primary text and the slightly different displayed formula there. No novelty claim is made for the fixed-point method.

## Direct proof and a checkable controller certificate

Write Φ(Z) for the inner least fixed point in (1). All operators are monotone. Compute Z₀ = K, Zₙ₊₁ = Φ(Zₙ). This sequence decreases and stabilizes in the finite subset lattice. Each evaluation of Φ starts Y₀ = ∅ and iterates

    Yᵢ₊₁ = (P ∩ CPre_K(Z)) ∪ CPre_K(Yᵢ).

**Sufficiency.** At the final outer fixed point W, let r(s) be the first positive index i at which s enters the inner iteration. Rank-one states belong to P and have an available action into W. Every higher-rank state has an available action whose successors all have strictly smaller rank. Choose one such action at every state of W. Every successor stays in W. From any state, a rank-one progress state is reached after at most r(s)−1 transitions. From a rank-one state the next transition returns to some state of W, and the same descent repeats. All resulting runs are infinite and safe and visit P infinitely often.

Every W state consequently has an action into W. Hence P ∩ W = P ∩ CPre_K(W), so all progress states in W are rank one. The maximum rank is at most |W|. The extracted controller reaches the first progress state within at most |W|−1 transitions and has at most |W| transitions between successive progress visits. These are event-step bounds; a bound on elapsed physical time additionally requires bounds on event duration.

**Necessity.** Let V be the true winning region, allowing arbitrary causal history-dependent strategies. After any reachable history of a winning strategy, its residual strategy wins from the current state. Every successor permitted by its chosen action is therefore in V. In particular, any progress state reached by the strategy lies in T = P ∩ CPre_K(V).

The least fixed point Φ(V) is the finite sure-reachability attractor to T within K. To see the relevant direction without assuming memoryless winning strategies, consider a safe state outside this attractor. Every available action has either an unsafe successor or a successor still outside the attractor; otherwise that state would have entered the next attractor layer. The environment can select such a successor at each step. A deadlock already loses. Otherwise the controller either leaves K or avoids T forever. But a safety-and-Büchi winning strategy must eventually reach a progress state, and every such state lies in T. Contradiction. Thus V ⊆ Φ(V).

For a monotone operator, every postfixed set lies in its greatest fixed point. Therefore V ⊆ W. The rank construction proves W ⊆ V, establishing equality and the stated memoryless controller.

**Certificate form.** A finite set U ⊆ K containing the initial state, a selected nonempty-successor action at every s ∈ U, and positive integer ranks bounded by m suffice if: (i) actions at progress states stay in U; (ii) actions at non-progress states strictly decrease rank; and (iii) rank one occurs only at progress states. The fixed point constructs such a certificate whenever the objective is achievable. Conversely, such a certificate proves safety and recurrence directly. This is a concrete answer, not merely a request to test indefinitely.

Formal-core peer review: the independent formal agent checked the sufficiency/completeness argument on 2026-10-05 and confirmed the reachability-complement argument and rank bounds. This is a mathematical review, not a proof-assistant verification.

## Independent implementation check

`progress-check.py` implements (1). Its comparison oracle does not use a fixed point: it enumerates deterministic state-based policies, forms the induced successor graph, and rejects an initial state if an unsafe or deadlocked state is reachable or if a reachable directed cycle can remain entirely outside P. In a finite nondeadlocking graph, such a cycle exists exactly when an adversarial infinite run can eventually avoid P. The oracle therefore checks every environment path for each enumerated policy.

The verifier also checks the ranks/actions extracted from (1), and compares (1) with the standard variant whose second disjunct is guarded by ¬P. Their final winning sets agree in all checked cases. The primary source displays that guarded variant; our direct proof above establishes the unguarded variant independently.

| Class | Plant/safety/progress cases | Initial-state verdicts | Policy enumerations |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| All 256 two-state, two-action plants; each successor set may be empty; all 9 pairs P ⊆ K ⊆ S | 2,304 | 4,608 | 9,216 |

All comparisons and certificates passed. Four explicit edge examples below also passed. A policy enumeration means one positional choice tuple considered by the oracle; already-established winning initial states can skip redundant policy evaluation. The counts do not represent empirical observations or distinct mathematical theorems. These checks cover complete small classes plus a reproducible sample, and support the implementation; the general result rests on the proof.

## Controls that separate the requirements

1. **One success then stasis:** s → p → d → d, all states safe, P = {p}. Infinite safety is possible and progress is reached once, but W is empty. Reachability is insufficient for recurrence.
2. **Recovery and reset:** at s choose either s or p; from p return to s; P = {p}. Choosing recovery each time gives W = {s,p} and progress every two steps. This proves a maintained cycle of registered success, with no new states required.
3. **Unfair indefinite postponement:** s has an action with successors {s,p}, and p returns to s. The environment may always select s, so W is empty for P = {p}. A separate probabilistic model could yield an almost-sure result; possibility of success is insufficient for this adversarial guarantee.
4. **Progress deadlock:** P = K = {p}, with no available nonempty-successor action. The state is losing. The nonemptiness condition prevents a vacuous universal-successor test from labeling it winning.

## Exact extension under partial observation

Equation (1) is proved here for full observation. A concrete state-based controller cannot be deployed when two indistinguishable states require different choices. The companion safety result computes a greatest fixed point over information sets and requires one action to work for every state currently possible.

For recurrence there is a second issue: progress itself may be hidden. Consider two states a and b, one observation, forced transitions a → b → a, initial information set {a,b}, and P = {a}. Every actual path visits P infinitely often. The current information set nevertheless remains {a,b} forever and is never contained in P. Therefore applying a Büchi target of “current information set is contained in P” would reject a winning hidden-progress system. It certifies repeated *knowledge that progress holds now*, which is stronger in this example.

The missing memory can be supplied exactly in the finite, sure-winning setting. Maintain a pair (B,O): B is the nonempty current information set, and O ⊆ B ∖ P contains endpoints of compatible histories still owing a visit to P during the current progress round. Initially O₀ = B₀ ∖ P. For an action a and next observation class o, write

    Post(D,a) = ⋃{F(s,a) : s ∈ D},
    B' = Post(B,a) ∩ o,
    O' = B' ∖ P                         if O = ∅,
         (Post(O,a) ∩ o) ∖ P            otherwise.                 (2)

The controller may choose a only if it is available with nonempty successors at every s ∈ B. The environment chooses any observation class with B' nonempty. The safe product states satisfy B ⊆ K; product transitions into a B' containing an unsafe state remain possible and therefore disqualify an action from a safe predecessor. The product progress set is Q = {(B,O) : O = ∅}. This differs from B ⊆ P: histories can discharge their obligations at different times.

**Pathwise equivalence.** Fix any infinite observation/action branch. Between resets, O contains exactly the endpoints of its compatible concrete histories that have avoided P since the round began. This invariant follows inductively from (2). If O becomes empty infinitely often, each actual concrete run visits P in each completed round. Conversely, if O is nonempty forever after some time, take the tree of outstanding concrete histories from that round. It has nodes at every later depth. Finiteness of S makes it finitely branching, so König's lemma gives an infinite concrete suffix that avoids P; a compatible finite prefix exists because its initial endpoint was in B. Thus some actual run on the branch violates recurrence. Therefore all compatible concrete runs satisfy GF P exactly when the monitor visits O = ∅ infinitely often.

There is no hidden choice of an impossible observation branch in this proof. Every infinite branch with successive nonempty B has finite compatible prefixes of every length. The same finite-branching argument supplies a compatible infinite concrete run. Controller choices are fixed by the common observation/action history, so the witness respects the same causal controller.

The finite pair arena has at most 3^|S| states, before removing empty or observation-inconsistent beliefs: each concrete state is outside B, in B without obligation, or in O. Apply (1) to this arena with safety B ⊆ K and progress O = ∅. The resulting initial pair is winning **if and only if** an observation-based causal controller can ensure concrete safety and GF P from every state in B₀. A positional strategy in the pair arena implements a finite-memory controller in the original plant. Conversely, every original observation-based strategy induces the same branch choices in the product, and the pathwise equivalence preserves its winning condition. No probability or fairness assumption is used.

For the hidden a ↔ b example, B stays {a,b} while O starts {b} and becomes empty after the next transition. The monitor accepts correctly although B never lies in P. A monitor that resets because only *some* compatible history made progress would be unsound.

This is a specialization of the established breakpoint construction (source D), with our explicit safety, action availability, and game-quantifier proof. `progress-check.py` above checks the fully observed solver, not the product-building code. If the product is implemented separately, meaningful verification checks its synthesized controller in the **concrete state × controller memory graph** for unsafe/deadlocked vertices and P-free cycles. Enumerating only observation-memoryless controllers is insufficient as an exact oracle: the synthesized controller may need obligation memory.

## Recurrence does not imply unbounded distinct novelty

Fix a finite set L of distinguishable novelty labels, and let each candidate achievement receive a label in L under an unchanged interpretation. Across any execution there can be at most |L| first occurrences of labels. This is the pigeonhole principle, independent of control policy, survival, recurrence, or randomness. Repeating registered progress infinitely often cannot overcome the bound.

The restriction is the **fixed finite label repertoire**, not merely a finite controller. A finite controller can produce output words of arbitrarily increasing length, and a finite nondeterministic graph can generate nonperiodic infinite output. All finite words over even a finite alphabet form an infinite repertoire. Histories, an external tape, growing artifacts, or an unbounded counter can therefore carry infinitely many distinct objects while controller memory remains finite. Counting every longer prefix as a new object makes even repetition “novel”; the scientific or semantic significance then lies in the chosen novelty criterion.

For a substantive unbounded-novelty claim, specify: what objects can grow; the equivalence relation defining sameness; what counts as improvement or useful novelty; what resources the distinction and validation require; and which environmental behaviors are quantified over. An unbounded artifact space defeats the finite-label impossibility theorem but does not itself guarantee production, value, or indefinite resources. A growing schema can be modeled inside a larger ambient language; this does not by itself show that the system anticipates every possible future conceptual distinction.

The strongest warranted present claim is consequently: **within the specified finite controlled model, safe repeated registered progress has an exact winning-region characterization and a finite controller certificate; under partial observation the controller also tracks outstanding progress obligations.** Whether P tracks worthwhile progress, whether the model keeps matching the world, and whether genuinely unbounded novelty is possible remain additional questions. They are not refuted by this theorem, and they are not answered by relabeling a recurrent cycle “generation.”

# Removing assumptions and proving a general theory of generation

Investigation for Ren, 5 October 2026.

**Removing assumptions, deriving them from deeper principles, and proving invariance are legitimate ways to strengthen this theory. Describing a result as conditional identifies its current proof obligations; it does not set a ceiling on its eventual importance.** The right objective is a compact, nontrivial account of when continued generation is possible, what prevents it, and which changes preserve those possibilities.

This investigation makes one concrete advance: financial feasibility can be characterized beyond the earlier restriction on total spending per round. A stronger characterization accommodates transfers with limited capacity, delayed opportunities, and income between payments. This broader result does not preserve the earlier conclusion that total funds alone suffice under every access regime. It illustrates how to pursue the wider claim without treating every special condition as a universal fact.

## What a proof of the central claim would establish

Let a system description include its possible changes, observations, feasible actions, resource flows, and the capabilities to be protected. Let \(G(M,z)\) mean that the specified form of continued generation is attainable from state \(z\) in system \(M\). The strongest useful central target has the form

\[
\forall M\in\mathcal C\;\forall z,\qquad
G(M,z)\iff C(M,z),
\]

where \(\mathcal C\) is the declared system class and \(C\) is an independently specified structural condition. The two directions do different work. Sufficiency proves that the conditions guarantee the possibility. Necessity proves that every successful case must satisfy the conditions.

The condition must have content beyond “whatever allows generation.” It should be stated through independently identifiable features, yield forbidden cases, and ideally be easier to check than solving the original continuation problem. A characterization that simply renames the desired outcome is correct by definition but supplies no explanatory gain. No claim is made here that the displayed equivalence has already been proved for the whole theory.

There are several possible meanings of \(G\). Remaining active, retaining the capacity to recover, producing recurring novelty, and protecting the future capabilities of multiple affected parties are different properties. A repeating process can remain active without generating anything new. A process can maintain itself while reducing another process's options. The theory can address all these properties, but each needs its own criterion and the bridges between them need arguments.

This respects situationality. A universal characterization need not say that every system continues, or that one intervention is always reasonable. It can explain both continuation and failure under one law. It also need not determine every microscopic detail: a fundamental constraint can leave many mechanisms possible while ruling out a significant class of outcomes.

## How to discharge an assumption

Suppose the present argument is \(A\land H\Rightarrow T\), where \(H\) is the assumption under examination.

| Result of the audit | What must be shown | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| The assumption is dispensable | \(A\Rightarrow T\) | Remove it and enlarge the theorem's scope |
| It follows from the remaining basis | \(A\Rightarrow H\) | It is no longer an independent premise |
| It is an overly strong special case | Find a weaker condition that still implies the conclusion | Replace it with the broader condition |
| Its variation changes the answer | Construct a case satisfying the other premises where the conclusion fails | Retain the distinction or generalize the law to explain both cases |
| It is proposed as a law of the intended world | Give an independent interpretation and restrictive consequences | Establish applicability through argument and evidence appropriate to that claim |

Deriving several assumptions from a deeper principle can be a major unification. The deeper principle's consistency, content, and applicability still matter. Making an assumption true by defining the admitted class around it proves a result for that class; coverage of the intended phenomena remains a separate obligation.

The strongest possible theory may therefore retain some foundational commitments and turn many former assumptions into variables. “Transfers are immediate” can become a value of a timing parameter. “Repair is effective” can become a measured response law. A unified theory then predicts how those variations change attainable outcomes.

## An assumption we can now remove

The earlier pooling proof required enough cash capacity to cover the entire round's bill before any income arrived. That is sufficient but unnecessarily restrictive when payments, income, and transfer opportunities occur within a round.

For the stronger theorem, an event consists of income arriving, an opportunity to transfer funds from treasury into cash, and a bill falling due. Arbitrary finite sequences of income arrivals, opportunities, and bills can be represented by inserting events with zero values for unused components. Cash capacity is \(C\), initial cash is \(b_0\), and total initial funds are \(N_0\). Event \(j\) has income \(i_j\geq0\), transfer limit \(r_j\geq0\), and bill \(c_j\geq0\).

Income is credited to cash up to capacity, with excess retained in treasury. Transfers are free, can be chosen anywhere from zero to the permitted amount, and have no other effects. The per-event opportunities do not consume an omitted shared transfer quota. Borrowing is excluded, and an indivisible bill cannot be split artificially to evade the cash cap. Define

\[
N_j=N_{j-1}+i_j-c_j,
\qquad
B_j=\min\{C,N_{j-1}+i_j,B_{j-1}+i_j+r_j\}-c_j,
\quad B_0=b_0.
\]

**All bills in the sequence can be paid if and only if this greedy recurrence remains nonnegative at every payment.** At any fixed total balance, putting more funds into cash cannot reduce the next attainable cash balance under these rules. The recurrence therefore gives the greatest cash balance reachable after every successfully funded prefix. If it fails, every other admissible transfer schedule fails at that prefix. If it succeeds, it constructs a funding schedule.

With unrestricted refill immediately before each payment, the characterization reduces to two requirements: each individual bill fits the cash capacity, and cumulative spending never exceeds initial total funds plus income already received. Total spending over a round may exceed the capacity many times. For example, a wallet holding at most one unit can pay two separate one-unit bills from a two-unit treasury if it can refill between them.

The general recurrence also explains why total funds alone sometimes fail to predict feasibility. One unit locked in treasury until after a payment deadline cannot pay the one-unit bill due now. The same total available before the deadline can. A universal theory should retain that causal difference; proving that delays never matter would contradict the example.

The written argument applies to nonnegative real-valued amounts and every finite event sequence under its premises. An exact finite checker compared the recurrence, exhaustive transfer choices, and an equivalent set of funding inequalities across **504,840 schedules and 1,032,816 examined prefixes**, with no disagreement. These constructed checks support the derivation; they are not empirical observations or the proof of the wider theory. The [general access proof](general-access-theorem.md) records the theorem, its full conditions, and its relation to policy transfer.

## What invariance would mean here

An invariance claim needs a specified change and something preserved by it. Changing coordinates, changing the controller, changing the available information, changing a physical mechanism, and extending a model are different changes. A useful proposal is that implementations related by a stated correspondence preserve the same attainable continuation possibilities, even though their material details differ.

That proposal needs an executable correspondence: the translated actor must have the information, access, time, and resources required to perform its translated actions. A correspondence that uses unavailable future information does not establish attainable continuation. Controller-refinement theory provides precedents for proving both sufficient conditions and converses under explicit interfaces. [Reissig, Weber, and Rungger, sections V–VI](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.03715).

Unrestricted preservation under arbitrary changes would be much stronger and often empty. If permitted changes can carry any state to any other, every scalar quantity invariant under all those changes must be constant. This follows immediately by taking any two states and applying a permitted transformation between them. Meaningful universality usually concerns all changes of a specified relevant kind, or a law whose form applies across varying mechanisms.

The physics comparison supports this discipline. Noether's theorem starts with a specified variational structure and a specified continuous symmetry; its conservation conclusions follow within that structure. It does not establish that every property survives every alteration. [Noether, section 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0503066). Our access model is not claimed to have a Noether conservation law.

## A more general structural result to build on

A simple characterization already connects information, action, and continuation. Consider a finite action set, and let \(B\) be the nonempty collection of states compatible with what an actor knows. Assume all these current states lie in the declared protected set. Let \(S(z)\) contain the actions that the actor can execute from state \(z\), within the resource and timing rules, and whose allowed successors all remain in that protected set.

An action guaranteeing one-step continuation despite this uncertainty exists exactly when

\[
\bigcap_{z\in B}S(z)\neq\varnothing.
\]

Necessity follows because one action chosen from the same information must work in every compatible state. Sufficiency follows by choosing an action in the intersection. This assumes that the actor can implement that choice; computational, memory, or authorization limits must be included if relevant. It is a robust guarantee, not an expected-risk optimum.

This result explains two apparently different situations through the same relation. Information can help when compatible states require conflicting actions. Information is unnecessary for this guarantee when one available action already works across them. Resource access, timing, and efficacy affect the feasible safe-action sets. More information changes which states remain compatible.

The characterization is elementary and is not claimed as a new discovery. It is a useful basis for deriving longer-horizon conditions, identifying failure witnesses, and proving which descriptions preserve those conditions. Those extensions must retain the actor's information and implementation limits. Merely listing information, resources, and action as important does not establish the required equivalences.

## The additional obligation for indefinite generation

“For every finite duration, some policy can continue that long” is not automatically the same as “one policy can continue indefinitely.” The order of the quantifiers matters:

\[
\forall H\;\exists\pi_H
\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad
\exists\pi\;\forall H.
\]

For example, from one fixed initial decision state, a system can permit a choice of any finite reserve \(n\), then consume one unit at each step with no replenishment. Every finite horizon can be met by choosing a sufficiently large reserve. No permitted initial choice yields an infinite run. The example uses unbounded initial branching; additional compactness or finite-branching conditions can support an infinite-path argument, with further care for policies, uncertainty, and implementability.

Consequently, an indefinite-generation theorem must specify what persists, under which disturbances, by which admissible policy, and whether its guarantee is sure, probabilistic, or an expectation. Recurring novelty needs a progress condition beyond staying inside a safe set. These are precise obligations rather than a claim that such a theorem is impossible.

## How to establish the full intended reach

The proof program has four connected obligations. First, state the central properties and a small basis with enough precision to construct models and countermodels. Second, prove the strongest necessary-and-sufficient structural results and identify which assumptions are redundant, derived, or essential for the advertised conclusion. Third, prove preservation under explicit changes of representation and implementation. Fourth, establish that the intended real cases satisfy the interpretation and admission conditions without defining membership by whether the prediction succeeds.

The last obligation requires more than reproducing a supplied model. Our proposed second implementation remains untested: independently measure a task-processing service's local failure, monitoring, repair, payment, and scheduling behavior; freeze its mapping and integrated predictions; then compare against outcomes not used to fit those predictions and against a serious alternative with comparable information. This can challenge whether the supposedly sufficient state omits something such as deadlines. It would provide evidence about that transfer, not a deductive proof covering every possible future application.

Where the theory judges an outcome unreasonable, specify whether it violates a feasibility bound, defeats a stated goal, rests on a false expectation, or conflicts with an ethical commitment. Those judgments can be related, but continued operation alone does not settle whose future possibilities ought to count. Normative premises need their own justification.

**The productive route is to prove an increasingly general characterization of the conditions for continued generation.** This investigation has replaced a restrictive financial-feasibility premise with a broader exact characterization. The whole-theory equivalence, its coverage of the intended world, and its claims about indefinite novelty or justified conduct remain distinct proof obligations.

## Decisions and rejected formulations

1. **Retain the unification ambition, but do not substitute a catalog for its achievement.** A family of models must share checked interfaces and transfer a useful result. The final conjecture was strengthened after review from “may predict some cases” to a frozen target prediction that can fail.
2. **Do not collapse world change, model revision, and abstraction.** Their different preservation questions are central, including when a representation's carrier is itself an object in the world.
3. **Reject unrestricted invariance.** If arbitrary replacement is allowed, a nontrivial property can be replaced by its violation. Declare the transformation class.
4. **Reject one scalar resource ontology.** Money, energy, information, access, authority, and burdens have different units and operations. Shared notation is not a conservation law.
5. **Reject necessary-bounds-as-sufficiency.** The two-observation diagnostic counterexample demonstrates the gap exactly.
6. **Reject self-inclusion-as-omniscience.** The construction can represent fallible model-making. Its actual premises, interpretations, and controller resources still need assessment.
7. **Reject persistence-as-ethics.** Coercive stability, manipulative evaluation, and unequal options remain possible under viable dynamics.
8. **Reject cultural sameness and priority claims.** Only limited interpretations are defended; Chinese wording has a provisional own gloss and a specialist translation comparison remains open.
9. **Reject replay with future information.** A target run's own future feedback cannot be used to select its supposedly ex ante comparison schedule. Equal nominal allocation and equal realized spending are different.
10. **Keep failed claims visible.** The inherited failed frame-escape prediction, corrected nonhyperbolic case, signaling correction, and limited S06 trace remain in the audit rather than being presented as uninterrupted progress.

# A wrong dynamics anchor can stabilize the wrong physical zero

Post-evaluation analytic explanation, 5 October 2026. No frozen algorithm, parameter or result was changed. The exact calculations below explain a possible mechanism; they are not a new fitted model or a proof of finite-horizon convergence of every filter run.

## Exact change of coordinates and the required signs

Let the true system be

\[
x_{t+1}=a x_t+u_t+g+w_t,\qquad
y_t=x_t+b_t+\epsilon_t,\qquad z_t=x_t+d+\eta_t,
\]

where g is constant and a!=1. Define r=g/(1-a), and write

\[
\widetilde x=x-r,\qquad \widetilde b=b+r,\qquad
\widetilde d=d+r.
\]

The bias signs are **plus**: y=(x-r)+(b+r)+epsilon. Using minus r for both transformed state and transformed bias would not preserve the observation.

In these coordinates,

\[
\widetilde x_{t+1}=a\widetilde x_t+u_t+w_t,\qquad
y_t=\widetilde x_t+\widetilde b_t+\epsilon_t,\qquad
z_t=\widetilde x_t+\widetilde d+\eta_t.
\]

These are exactly the transition and observation equations of the filter that assumes g=0 while allowing both sensor biases to vary in its state space. This is the previous shift transformation with c=-r. If b changes, adding the same constant r preserves its change increments, although its transformed sign-reversal values are no longer centered on zero.

The relative bias is preserved:

\[
\widetilde b-\widetilde d=b-d.
\]

Thus an estimator can represent relative sensor discrepancy correctly while representing the absolute physical state with the wrong origin.

## Conditional control equilibrium

Suppose the estimator tracks this transformed coordinate exactly, and clipping is inactive. With the study's common controller u=-k*x_hat, taking x_hat=tilde x gives

\[
\widetilde x_{t+1}=(a-k)\widetilde x_t+w_t.
\]

In the noiseless case, |a-k|<1 implies tilde x tends to zero. Hence

\[
x^*=r=\frac{g}{1-a},\qquad u^*=0.
\]

For a=.8, k=.5 and g=+/-.15, the physical equilibrium is x*=+/-.75, even though the estimated coordinate approaches zero. The estimator need not openly revise its zero-forcing assumption: it can absorb the discrepancy into both inferred sensor biases.

This equilibrium is also the true system's passive equilibrium under u=0. The controller stabilizes deviations around that location; it need not create the entire displacement. The precise failure is regulating a shifted coordinate instead of the supplied absolute target x=0.

At this equilibrium, squared-state loss is .75^2=.5625 per step. Sixty steps *already at equilibrium* give 33.75. This is a scale comparison, not the exact expected loss of an episode starting with the study's initial prior. Under the idealized noiseless perfect-coordinate controller,

\[
x_t=r+(a-k)^t(x_0-r).
\]

For x_0 with mean zero and variance one, the exact expected state loss over t=1,...,60 is

\[
60r^2-2r^2\sum_{t=1}^{60}(a-k)^t
+(r^2+1)\sum_{t=1}^{60}(a-k)^{2t}.
\]

At these parameters it is approximately 33.4224, before process noise, imperfect filtering or clipping. The evaluated filter's observed state losses around 30 need not equal either figure: its estimate begins at the declared prior and acquires the coordinate shift over time.

## Contrast with retained scalar reference correction

For constant b and d, a noiseless converged scalar update based on y-z learns h=b-d. Its state estimate becomes

\[
x_{hat}=y-h=x+d.
\]

The same unsaturated proportional controller then gives

\[
x_{t+1}=(a-k)x_t+g-kd,
\qquad x^*=\frac{g-kd}{1-a+k}.
\]

With a=.8 and k=.5, the denominator is .7. If d=0 and g=+/-.15, the equilibrium is +/-.214286. With g=.15 and d=.25 it is .035714; with g=.15 and d=-.25 it is .392857. Reference bias and forcing can partially cancel or reinforce one another. A lower state cost in a particular sign combination does not establish more accurate understanding.

These are converged constant-regime formulas. Six noisy references, a changing bias, adaptive gains and finite time need not produce a fully converged h. They explain a baseline mechanism rather than predict every scalar-policy result.

## What the finite priors allow—and what they do not

The simulation has a fixed x_0~N(0,1) generating prior. The transformed initial state instead has distribution N(-r,1). Also, the filter's supplied zero-centered priors for b and d are not the generating priors shifted by r. Therefore the full finite-episode probability model is **not** exactly invariant under this transformation while keeping those priors fixed.

The code uses soft Gaussian priors with positive variance, not exact constraints fixing x_0 or a sensor bias. Shifted latent values remain possible under its assumed model, with different prior weights. Its transition/measurement equations can consequently fit data in the shifted coordinate, but the prior affects the transient and finite-horizon result. No claim that its posterior must converge to that coordinate is proved here; proving that for this time-varying filter would require a separate analysis.

The actual three-state filter also supplies a random-walk bias variance and observation/process noise, while g is omitted entirely. Its posterior covariance is conditional on those assumptions. A small reported covariance does not account for uncertainty about an excluded forcing term. Observational consistency inside that model can coexist with a large error against the evaluator's absolute state.

An exactly known initial state, a truly known unbiased reference, or a correct model for g can supply information against the shifted interpretation. A fixed known initial distribution can provide a statistical anchor across episodes, but does not give the exact initial state from one noisy run. The stochastic factorial experiment is not the unrestricted shift-closed class used in the earlier impossibility argument.

## Connection to the saved results

In the saved constant-bias worlds with nonzero forcing, the anchor filter's mean squared-state episode losses are 30.0827 for d=0 and 30.1372 for nonzero d. Their nominal 90% coverage rates are approximately 2.57% and 2.47%. The g=0 counterparts have state losses .5240 and .5892 and coverage approximately 91.10% and 90.24%. These figures are read from the existing evaluation summary; they are descriptive benchmark results, not new primary contrasts.

The exact shifted-coordinate construction explains why allowing the reference bias to be inferred does not guarantee a better physical anchor when the dynamics are fixed incorrectly. Protected references can all arrive, and relative sensor calibration can remain useful, while the model and controller agree on the wrong absolute zero. The evidence supports this mechanism as an interpretation of the observed failure; exact per-run convergence or exclusive causal attribution would require further testing.

# Maintaining access to correction under a confidently wrong model

Formal research note, 5 October 2026. This develops the earlier identification argument. Its claims concern specified observation, acquisition, detection and control rules; they are not empirical claims about introspection or consciousness. No earlier deliverable or frozen evaluation was changed.

## 1. Three distinct achievements

An opportunity for correction can fail at several separate points:

1. **Access:** a post-change observation is actually acquired within some delay and budget.
2. **Discrimination:** the acquired data distinguish the changed condition from an unchanged one, with stated false-alarm and miss rates.
3. **Effective revision:** the system uses the evidence to revise a relevant estimate or policy, and the resulting behavior meets a stated criterion.

A sampling schedule can guarantee the first without guaranteeing the second or third. A correct alarm is not necessarily an accurate state estimate. An accurate estimate is not necessarily used, and its use is not necessarily stabilizing. The criterion being protected—accuracy, control, revisability or something else—must also be specified.

“Detection” cannot mean merely emitting an alarm: a policy that always alarms has zero apparent delay. Every meaningful detection guarantee must also constrain false alarms or require a correctly distinguishing observation.

## 2. An exact failure of confidence-dependent access

Let a latent condition be q_t=0 before a persistent change and q_t=1 afterward. The ordinary stream is y_t=0 in both conditions. A purchased reference is z_t=q_t exactly. This intentionally simple example has an uninformative ordinary sensor and an informative reference; it is not a neural or physical architecture claim.

A model begins with estimate q_hat=0 and modeled uncertainty V=0. Its acquisition rule buys only when V exceeds a positive threshold; its update rule cannot increase V from the unchanged ordinary stream. It therefore buys no further references, remains wrong after the change, and remains certain according to its own calculation. The reference would have corrected it if obtained.

The same obstacle is broader than a variance threshold. Consider any acquisition rule based on ordinary observations, past purchased references and internal randomness. Until a new reference is purchased, the no-change and changed worlds above give it identical histories. Couple the same internal randomness. Its purchases, internal updates and alarms must then follow the same paths in those two worlds. A correctly distinguishing zero-false-alarm detector cannot recognize the change before a reference reveals it.

Consequently, a gate that can stop purchasing indefinitely on the no-change history cannot promise finite detection delay in this example. An ordinary-innovation trigger also fails because its available ordinary history does not differ. Additional computation of that history does not create the missing distinction.

This does **not** say that every history-based gate fails. A gate can contain a clock or enforce a maximum gap. “Protected” and “history-dependent” are not mutually exclusive algorithm classes. Protection is a constraint on what the rule must continue to permit, even when its current estimate or uncertainty gives no reason to ask for evidence.

## 3. Exact finite-budget bound for protected sampling

Fix the timing convention before using a numerical bound. There are N equal opportunity intervals after an initial boundary at time 0, and potential acquisitions at integer times 1,...,N. A persistent change may occur immediately after any boundary j in {0,...,N-1}. An acquisition at time s>j can reveal the change. We measure the wait as s-j. No acquisition at time 0 is included in the following budget B.

Assume 1<=B<=N and that a reference is perfectly discriminating after the change. Let selected sample times be

\[
0=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_B=N.
\]

The terminal sample is required to cover changes late in the interval. The maximum wait is exactly

\[
D(S)=\max_{1\le i\le B}(s_i-s_{i-1}).
\]

Since these B positive integer gaps sum to N,

\[
D(S)\ge \lceil N/B\rceil.
\]

Balanced gaps differing by at most one attain this bound. Thus the minimax maximum wait is exactly ceil(N/B). With opportunity spacing Delta, multiply the bound by Delta. For continuous-time changes between opportunities the same quantity bounds the supremum waiting time, provided the start and terminal coverage boundaries are stated.

This is also a lower bound for deterministic adaptive gates in the example of Section 2. Follow the gate's no-change path. Before the first revealing sample, a change produces the same observations and therefore the same acquisition choices. Placing the change just after the start of that path's largest gap realizes the same delay. Adaptivity cannot improve the worst case merely by conditioning on an uninformative ordinary stream. This argument assumes correct discrimination without false alarms; an unsupported premature alarm is not a way around it.

For randomized gates, the gap bound applies to every realized schedule required to satisfy a hard pathwise guarantee. Randomization may alter expected delay against a change time chosen independently of the random seed; that is a different objective. Do not silently substitute an expected guarantee for a hard one, or assume an adversary sees randomness unless that model is intended.

### Boundary conditions that matter

- **No terminal sample:** a change after the last purchase has no detection guarantee by the stated horizon.
- **Initial calibration costs money:** if the initial boundary itself uses a purchased reference, charge it separately. With total budget B_total and one mandatory initial purchase, only B_total-1 purchases remain to cover later intervals.
- **Finite horizon:** original opportunities 0,5,...,55 cannot reveal a change occurring after 55 within a 60-step episode, regardless of unused budget. A promised bound must restrict eligible change times or extend follow-up.
- **Finite lifetime budget, unlimited runtime:** after the last of at most B purchases, an unchanged-history gate leaves an unbounded uncovered tail. No uniform finite detection bound is possible for arbitrary later changes in the uninformative-ordinary-stream example.
- **Persistence:** a transient condition can appear and disappear entirely between samples. Even perfect references then reveal no change. Require persistence through a revealing sample, a sufficient dwell-time condition, or explicitly accept missed transients.
- **Availability:** a scheduled opportunity that is cancelled or unavailable is not an acquired measurement. The theorem assumes those opportunities can actually be used.

## 4. Protected and discretionary purchases can coexist

Split a finite budget into B_p protected purchases and B_r discretionary purchases, with B_p+B_r<=B. Reserve the B_p purchases for a schedule that covers the declared interval and ends at the terminal boundary. The discretionary gate may add observations but may not exhaust the protected reserve or remove its coverage.

For an arbitrary protected schedule S_p, the guaranteed maximum acquisition wait is its actual largest gap D(S_p), including the initial and terminal coverage boundaries. If the protected dates are chosen with balanced integer gaps as in Section 3, that maximum equals ceil(N/B_p). Reserving B_p purchases alone does not establish the balanced bound. Extra discretionary purchases can shorten waits and cannot increase D(S_p) if the protected purchases remain intact. Protection has an explicit opportunity cost: fewer purchases are available for reacting to the model's current priorities.

A more flexible implementation can move scheduled checks, but must maintain a verifiable coverage constraint. After a protected sample at opportunity s, covering the remaining N-s intervals with maximum gap D requires at least ceil((N-s)/D) future purchases, including the terminal one. Spending below that reserve invalidates the guarantee. This formula applies immediately after an anchor sample; at other times the already elapsed gap must also be accounted for.

There is no need to treat a reactive observation at a protected date as two purchases. Conversely, counting an early reactive purchase as a replacement for a later protected one is valid only if the resulting maximum-gap and terminal conditions are still satisfied.

This is a mechanism design condition, not a claim that any particular budget split is morally required. Added observations have costs, and an unnecessary update based on them can add noise. A protected purchase need not force the estimator to accept its content as correct.

## 5. Acquisition guarantees become detection guarantees only with extra assumptions

### Perfect or bounded-noise informative reference

Suppose a known baseline is q_0, a persistent change is delta, and a reference is z=q+eta with |eta|<=sigma. Under no change, |z-q_0|<=sigma. Under change, |z-q_0|>=|delta|-sigma. Therefore, if |delta|>2 sigma, the test

\[
|z-q_0|>\sigma
\]

has no false alarms and detects at the next sample. Protected sampling supplies its acquisition-delay bound. If the baseline estimate itself can err by beta, a sufficient uniform separation condition is |delta|>2(sigma+beta), with threshold sigma+beta.

These are sufficient conditions under stated bounds. At overlapping observation supports, an adversary can choose noise that makes an unchanged and changed reading identical; certainty no longer follows from one sample.

### Gaussian noise: high probability, not certainty

For independent Gaussian reference errors with nonzero variance, the unchanged and changed distributions of any fixed finite number of observations have positive densities everywhere. A test with false-alarm probability exactly zero therefore also has zero detection probability against a finite mean shift. Certain finite-sample detection and zero false alarms cannot both be claimed.

A conditional high-probability statement is possible. Suppose q_0 is known, reference errors are independent N(0,sigma^2), and a persistent mean shift has magnitude at least delta_min. Average m post-change references. For at most M tested windows, allocate alpha/M false-alarm probability to each two-sided test. With Phi the standard normal cumulative distribution, use

\[
h=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt m}\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/(2M)).
\]

The union bound gives at most alpha probability of any false alarm under the unchanged model. Overlapping windows need not be independent for that union bound. A sufficient condition for detection probability at least 1-beta on an entirely post-change window is

\[
\delta_{min}\ge\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt m}
\left[\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/(2M))+\Phi^{-1}(1-\beta)\right].
\]

The miss probability is bounded by the appropriate one-sided Gaussian tail. This statement requires a genuinely post-change window; averages mixing old and new regimes may dilute the signal. With a maximum sample gap D, the mth post-change protected sample arrives within mD intervals **if those m future samples exist**. Changes too near the endpoint require additional follow-up or must remain unresolved.

The error model, known baseline and number of tests are substantive assumptions. Correlated reference noise, an estimated baseline, selective sampling dependent on current reference noise, or an unbounded sequence of repeated tests needs a different calculation. A small reported posterior variance does not establish these assumptions.

## 6. Protected evidence can still be uninformative

The earlier model has

\[
x_{t+1}=a x_t+u_t+g+w_t,\quad y_t=x_t+b+\epsilon_t,
\quad z_t=x_t+d+\eta_t.
\]

When unknown constant g,b,d and the initial-state class admit the shift

\[
(x,b,d,g)\mapsto(x+c,b-c,d-c,g+(1-a)c),
\]

both sensor histories remain identical under the same observation-based controls, even when every possible reference is purchased. Protected access alone cannot distinguish the absolute latent states. A known initial prior, known forcing or unbiased reference can supply an anchor, but must be established rather than assumed by the word “reference.”

There is also an exact estimation lower bound. If two observationally equivalent states are separated by c, any estimate based on that same history has identical distribution in both worlds. For any realized estimate h,

\[
(h-x)^2+(h-x-c)^2=2(h-x-c/2)^2+c^2/2.
\]

Thus at least one world's expected squared error is at least c^2/4. For a trajectory pair separated by c for T steps, at least one world's expected cumulative squared estimation error is at least T c^2/4. This bound concerns the unanchored model class, not the original anchored simulation.

The broader lesson is that sampling and identification are different achievements. Even “independent” sensor hardware need not provide an independent absolute anchor if its error structure shares the same unresolved symmetry.

## 7. Informative evidence can still fail to produce useful correction

An implementation can acquire and correctly flag a discrepancy while its bias estimate remains frozen. For instance, logging z-y but enforcing h_next=h leaves a prior wrong correction unchanged. This is failure of the revision path, rather than failure of observation.

Even a perfect state estimate does not guarantee good control. In the noiseless system x_next=.8x+u, take u=clip(-2x,-2,2). Starting at x=10/9 gives x_next=-10/9, and the next state is 10/9 again. Perfect observations coexist with a persistent two-cycle. Without clipping, the same gain gives x_next=-1.2x and is unstable.

A limited positive guarantee can be stated explicitly. Suppose the revised estimate obeys x_hat=x+nu with |nu|<=epsilon; process disturbance satisfies |w|<=W; control is u=-k*x_hat without active clipping; and rho=|a-k|<1. Then

\[
|x_{t+n}|\le\rho^n|x_t|+
(|k|\epsilon+W)\frac{1-\rho^n}{1-\rho}.
\]

This follows by iterating |x_next|<=rho|x|+|k|epsilon+W. It supplies convergence to a bounded region, not exact convergence to zero in persistent noise. For a clipped implementation, a sufficient invariant-region check is to choose M with

\[
M\ge (|k|\epsilon+W)/(1-\rho),\qquad
|k|(M+\epsilon)\le u_{max},\qquad |x_t|\le M.
\]

Then the command remains unclipped and the bound applies inductively. If an unknown forcing remains, the state-error bound or controller must account for it. Detection alone does not establish any of these conditions.

## 8. A precise combined claim

For a persistent change within a covered interval, protected sampling supplies a maximum acquisition delay **if** budget, opportunity and terminal conditions hold. An informative reference and valid detector convert that into a discrimination guarantee. A revision rule with proved estimation and control properties then supplies a behavioral guarantee. Each implication has separate premises.

Failure at one stage cannot be repaired merely by calling the next stage more reflective. Nor does a protected schedule solve the unknown-reference problem. The useful structural proposal is to preserve a specified route by which evidence can still arrive and alter an estimate when its current confidence would otherwise stop the process. Whether to preserve that route, at what cost, and for whose purposes remains an additional design and normative question.

## 9. Criteria for this synthetic study and later extensions

- Declare the change-time support, end-of-horizon follow-up and minimum persistence before claiming a delay bound.
- Report acquisitions after change, informative residuals, alarms, parameter revision and useful state recovery separately.
- Include a confidently wrong gate that never opens, a confidence gate with protected opportunities, and an ordinary-innovation gate. Do not presume the ordinary innovation is informative in every world.
- Include reference bias or drift and unknown forcing. A protected but misspecified reference should not be advertised as a valid anchor.
- Count initial calibration, protected and discretionary purchases against the same budget; verify reserve invariants directly.
- Report no-change purchases and false alarms, late or undetected changes, capped delays and total sensing cost. Exclude undetected cases from neither denominators nor summaries without disclosure.
- Distinguish fixed finite-horizon bounds from expected performance over a chosen distribution of change times.
- Compare the update path itself: acquiring a warning, accepting a change and restoring useful behavior need not coincide.

The accompanying standard-library check script exhaustively verifies the finite scheduling bound for small N and checks the exact algebraic counterexamples. Its finite examples corroborate the arguments; the proofs state the general claims.

## 10. Review of the proposed continuation protocol

The protocol read at `work/correction-access/protocol.json` uses a 60-step horizon, opportunities at 0,5,...,55, six paid observations, and an integer bias-change time tau uniform on 8,...,47. The change applies before the observation at tau. Thus a purchase at tau has arrival delay zero; a gap of G integer steps can have maximum arrival delay G-1. This convention differs from the “immediately after boundary” convention in Section 3 and explains the numerical one-step difference.

The fixed schedule 0,10,20,35,45,55 guarantees arrival within 14 steps over the declared support; tau=21 attains it. The hybrid's protected dates 0,25,55 guarantee arrival within 29 steps; tau=26 attains it. Up to three extra observations cannot weaken that bound if protected purchases remain reserved. Exhaustive enumeration of all 130 possible optional subsets confirms it. These bounds are for reference arrival, not correct detection, and rely on the restricted change-time support. Neither schedule is asserted to be minimax over that restricted support.

The factorial worlds use fixed forcing g and fixed reference bias d, with the ordinary bias b either constant or changing sign once. Since y-z=b-d+epsilon-eta, fixed forcing does not enter this residual and fixed d does not change its jump magnitude. Every such reference remains informative about a persistent reversal of b under the supplied noise model. Reference bias can still contaminate absolute-state interpretation, and unknown forcing can confound the ordinary-innovation gate. This study should not be described as demonstrating reference observations that are intrinsically uninformative about the change itself.

The proposed standardization of ordinary innovations is explicitly a heuristic, not an exact conditional variance. This is appropriate: the retained bias estimate can share noise with the previous ordinary observation, and adaptation creates further dependencies. Its threshold exceedances in constant-bias worlds are reasonably labeled model-discrepancy alarms; they are not automatically statistically defined false discoveries, because the initial estimate, forcing or reference model may still be wrong.

The descriptive three-state filter's d prior variance .0625 is a supplied assumption matching the nonzero +/- .25 regime. The equally weighted mixture of zero and nonzero-reference factorial worlds instead has d variance .03125. Calling the algorithm a Gaussian moment filter is reasonable, but describing that particular prior as the exact pooled-world moment match would be inaccurate.

The proposed six primary comparisons correctly retain the paired seed as the independent unit and average worlds within seed before comparing losses. Equal sensing caps do not ensure equal actual expense; separate purchase counts and costs remain necessary. The protocol appropriately reports missing arrivals, recovered fractions and costs, and excludes computation, energy and memory pricing from its causal claims.

No material mathematical defect was found in these declared access bounds or statistical comparison definitions. This pre-evaluation protocol review did not certify the implementation. Reserve bookkeeping, update chronology, actual clipped actions in the innovation, absence of unpurchased-reference leakage, and independence of all exogenous draws from policy decisions are obligations for the separate implementation checks.

# Independent method review: correction access

5 October 2026. Design recommendations prepared before development or evaluation of this continuation. This file distinguishes proposed design choices from later observed results. It does not modify the earlier frozen experiment.

## Adopted protocol review, before development results

The coordinating researcher subsequently supplied `protocol.json`. The adopted protocol is coherent and has no blocking design issue. It uses development seeds 20000–20199, evaluation seeds 30000–31999, test seeds 40000 onward, eight factorial worlds plus a descriptive no-bias world, and hidden uniformly sampled integer change times 8–47. The scalar audit update is shared and fixed; only innovation and hybrid thresholds are selected on development. Primary inference concerns six gate-minus-confidence contrasts: three alternatives, each averaged within seed over the four change worlds or the four constant worlds. Estimate uncertainty across the 2000 seed averages, not 8000 world trajectories.

Protected periodic times are 0,10,20,35,45,55. Hybrid protects 0,25,55 and permits at most three other purchases, so its reserve cannot be consumed early. Innovation is evaluated before the current reference update and records the maximum score between opportunities; clearing at each opportunity is explicitly declared. The residual standardization is a heuristic, not an exact conditional innovation test. The no-change alarm count is correctly described without assuming each alarm is a false statistical discovery.

One deliberate revision from the initial recommendation below is that computation has no price in this continuation. The primary score is control plus sensing loss only. Monitoring workload is counted separately. Therefore interpret results as gate performance under free computation, not total resource efficiency or empirical cognitive efficiency, and do not directly compare its loss scale with the earlier compute-priced study without adjustment.

Policies assume g=0 while challenge worlds contain constant hidden forcing ±.15; scalar correction also assumes reference offset d=0 while challenge worlds contain ±.25. This is explicit model misspecification. The stochastic factorial has supplied priors and does not itself instantiate every world in the unrestricted shift-symmetry class. For the correction h, distinguish relative calibration target b−d from absolute sensor bias b. A three-state anchor estimator is a descriptive benchmark, because it changes inference as well as access.

The six primary tests describe a supplied equal-weight mixture of four factorial settings in each change group. Every world-specific result should still be shown, so an average gain cannot conceal harm under forcing or a biased reference. The adopted practical margin .02 and Bonferroni family of six are declared before evaluation. Secondary recovery/delay/coverage remain descriptive. These adopted choices supersede conflicting conditional suggestions below.

## Question and intervention

The preceding experiment identified a specific failure: an audit could assess a calibration discrepancy only after a variance gate allowed access to calibration. This continuation should test whether another route to buying evidence helps under randomized change times, without simultaneously changing the underlying estimator and attributing everything to access.

Hold fixed the correction estimator, its update rule, control gain, observation opportunities, cost accounting, and simulator dynamics across the main confidence, innovation, periodic, and hybrid policies. Vary only the acquisition decision and the state required to implement it. A different estimator may be a separately named benchmark but should not enter the primary claim as if it isolated acquisition. The retained bias estimate itself remains a kind of model of the observation process; policy names do not establish representational depth.

Suggested primary estimand: the within-world paired mean full-horizon total-loss difference for each alternative access policy minus confidence access. Use identical exogenous draws and true-change timing within seed. Full-horizon loss includes pre-change operation, false triggers, observation cost, computation overhead, and post-change control. Do not replace it with recovery speed after seeing outcomes. The estimand is a policy effect inside the specified simulator, not the benefit of an additional semantic meta-level.

## Fresh samples and freezing

Previously used ranges include development 0–99, evaluation 1000–1999, and tests 7000–7010. One suitable new allocation is development 20000–20199, evaluation 30000–31999, and tests starting at 40000, but any recorded disjoint allocation is acceptable. Pre-generate every possible sensor/process draw and a hidden change time for each seed before running policies. Do not consume reference noise only on purchases. Save exact seed ranges, simulation and policy parameters, candidate grids, development scores, selection rules, price weights, practical margin, and code hashes before evaluation.

Randomize the hidden change time uniformly over a declared interior range that includes all offsets modulo the five-step opportunity spacing. The exact range is a research choice. It should leave adequate pre-change calibration and post-change follow-up, and should not be chosen from evaluation performance. Generate a latent time even in no-change controls to support a comparable descriptive observation window. Do not pass true change time or true forcing/reference bias to the policy. The gate may know the fixed horizon and its own prespecified schedule.

Tune each alternative globally on the same development objective and equally weighted worlds, rather than selecting a favorable threshold per evaluation world. If the estimator has parameters, fix or tune them globally before the acquisition-policy comparison. A separate exploration of estimator-policy co-design changes the estimand and should be labeled separately.

## Worlds and anchors

Use separate factors for sensor change versus no change, constant forcing zero versus an unknown nonzero forcing, and clean versus biased reference. A full factorial is interpretable if computationally affordable; otherwise name each chosen contrast and its confounding factors. At minimum retain a clean no-change control, a clean sensor-change world, a forcing-misspecification world, a biased-reference world, and a joint challenge. Keep initial sensor-bias distributions comparable in change and no-change worlds. If initial bias can be zero, report the actual nonzero-change subset for detection/recovery metrics rather than treating a sign reversal of zero as an event.

Unknown forcing can mean that its realized value is hidden but its family is correctly modeled, or that the estimator wrongly fixes it at zero. These are different tests. Likewise distinguish an unknown reference bias from incorrectly assumed perfect reference calibration. A four-variable unanchored state/bias/reference/forcing model has the previously derived shift symmetry, but a supplied initial-state prior or known population distributions can still be statistical anchors. Do not describe failure of a misspecified filter as a proof of absolute non-identifiability for the actual sampled model.

An ordinary innovation can reveal mismatch without identifying which assumption failed. In particular, a change or error in physical forcing can create an innovation even when the ordinary sensor's bias is unchanged. Acquiring the reference can then be useful, useless, or harmful depending on its credibility. A successful gate is not a causal diagnosis of the origin of error.

## Acquisition policies and fairness

1. **Confidence gate:** retain the prior modeled-variance gate as a frozen comparator, including its cost assumptions and limitations. It does not by itself establish a globally rational value of information.
2. **Ordinary innovation gate:** compute a prediction residual before conditioning on current ordinary observation. Evaluate at every declared monitoring time, and charge that overhead. When opportunities occur only every five steps, latch a threshold crossing until the next opportunity or a declared expiration/reset; otherwise a step-32 discrepancy may vanish before inspection at step 35. State whether the latch resets on a successful purchase, on any eligible attempt, or only on an explicit rule.
3. **Protected periodic checks:** guarantee a declared schedule within the common acquisition cap. Its protected checks must not be consumed by earlier optional access. Schedule timing should not use the realized change time. Specify whether initial calibration is a protected purchase shared by all policies.
4. **Hybrid:** combine a fixed protected reserve with innovation-triggered optional acquisitions. Deduct protected future purchases before allowing discretionary ones, so it really preserves the guarantee. Report reserved, discretionary, attempted, successful, and denied counts separately. If the chosen hybrid is simply a union that can exhaust its cap early, call it a union gate rather than claiming guaranteed checks.

The cap is a sensing cap unless computation has its own enforced cap. Charge monitor and budget checks even when no purchase occurs. A common cap does not establish equal actual expenditure. Do not force a frugal policy to waste remaining allowance; show expenditure alongside loss. A cheap periodic method and a more expensive monitor should retain their actual execution counts under the disclosed abstract price model.

For a scalar correction implementation using previous ordinary y and bias estimate h, a possible ordinary residual is

`r_t = y_t - a*y_(t-1) - u_(t-1) - (1-a)*h_(t-1)`.

Under the extended dynamics its exact decomposition is

`r_t = g + b_t - a*b_(t-1) - (1-a)*h_(t-1) + w_(t-1) + eps_t - a*eps_(t-1)`.

This explains why an abrupt bias switch may trigger it and why unknown forcing can also do so. Its nominal standardization is generally approximate: h is itself estimated from past observations and residuals are serially correlated. A joint filter may instead expose its conventional pre-update innovation. Do not label a residual normalized by an approximate variance as a calibrated z-test without checking the conditional assumptions.

## Outcomes and inference

Keep the prior declared loss form unless there is a documented reason to change it: sum of next-state squared error and .05 action effort, plus .02 per acquired reference and .0001 per disclosed weighted work block. Report these components separately. Include state-estimate error, action-conditioned forecast error, Brier score, interval coverage and width, normalized forecast error, maximum excursion, acquisition counts/timing, and operation counts. Supplied prices are research preferences, not psychological measurements.

Report delay to the first acquired reference after a true switch and confirmed recovery delay as secondary outcomes. Right-censor episodes with no post-change reference or no confirmed recovery; state the horizon-dependent cap and non-event fraction separately. Acquisition delay and detection delay differ if the gate does not diagnose or record a change. Recovery under a biased reference can remain misleading as evidence of knowledge; the hidden physical state is available here only to the scorer.

Report no-change alarm/purchase cost without calling every no-change acquisition pointless: initial calibration or reducing uncertainty about constant bias can still help. If using a false-alarm rate, define its ground-truth target and timing convention beforehand. An innovation caused by a real forcing error is not a false alarm for generic model mismatch, although it may be a false sensor-change diagnosis. Disaggregate triggered, protected, and initial purchases.

For inference use a complete seed trajectory as the independent unit. Retain its paired observations across policies and worlds. For K prespecified primary contrasts, use two-sided normal or t intervals with per-interval coverage 1-.05/K for Bonferroni family coverage of at least .95, subject to the approximation. Alternatively give explicitly descriptive 95% intervals without family-wide claims. State whether the family covers three alternatives across every world or a smaller focused subset. The practical margin must be frozen, with a favorable difference required to clear its bound. Secondary endpoints and post-observation subgroup analyses remain exploratory.

If stratifying by switch-time offsets or late versus early changes, fix bins in advance or label them exploratory; never select the strongest bin as the overall result. Equal-weight averages across chosen worlds answer an explicitly supplied mixture objective. Show world-specific effects so an average benefit cannot hide failure under an inaccurate reference or physical model. Monte Carlo uncertainty covers this data-generating procedure, not uncertainty that it describes cognition.

## Primary-source context already verified

- [Friedland 1969](https://researchwith.njit.edu/en/publications/treatment-of-bias-in-recursive-filtering/) provides established precedent for state and constant-bias estimation under linear assumptions. This review previously inspected the author-institution abstract, not the full article. It does not validate the new thresholds or unknown-forcing assumptions.
- [Hay et al. 2012](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~russell/papers/uai12-meta.pdf) formulates metalevel computation choices and demonstrates limitations of myopic evaluation. Its results do not prove the acquisition gates optimal.
- [Tzoumas et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.08376) evaluates sensing through control objectives with fixed sensor-set selection and declared costs. Its guarantees do not transfer automatically to online, observation-triggered purchases, clipped actions, or misspecified models.
- [Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf) supports proper forecast scoring and separating calibration from sharpness. Brier differences across intervention policies also reflect their induced event distributions; interval coverage and state error remain useful complementary diagnostics.
- [Banerjee and Veeravalli 2012](https://vvv.ece.illinois.edu/papers/journal/bane-veer-sqa-2012.pdf), checked during the later audit, studies quickest detection with a geometric change-time prior, known pre/post-change observation laws, and observation control. Equation 2.3 updates the change posterior to `p+(1-p)rho` even without a new sample. The paper also gives cases where a simple two-threshold policy is not exactly optimal. Its asymptotic results do not transfer to our uniform timing, control objective, or misspecified physical/reference model. It supports treating absence of sampling separately from absence of possible change.

No new empirical consciousness claim or universally optimal reflection policy follows from this design. Its useful possible result is narrower: whether a specific affordable route to fresh evidence improves judgment/control when the current model can otherwise suppress that evidence.

### Mechanism checks and interpretation

The constant-bias control is not initially calibrated: h starts at zero while b is ±1. With noiseless clean calibration and no fast update, the residual bias after n slow updates is .8^n times its initial error. Postponing early observations can therefore prolong initial error even without a later change. This is a mechanism explanation under the shared rule, not a randomized mediation estimate.
