# How a decision rule adopts or loses sustainable repair

This experiment adds an actual, repeatedly executed selection rule to the [third-cycle repair process](../cycle-3/scale-and-renewal.md). It explains infrastructure adoption **conditional on that rule**, its horizon, the known process, and available funds. It does not explain the origin of the rule or horizon. No infinite-viability test is used by the implemented planner.

The main finding is stronger than a short-horizon planner eventually running out of money. Its first successful repair can move the process outside the set from which **any** permitted policy can continue indefinitely. The same short-horizon rule can nevertheless maintain a sustainable apparatus if it inherits that apparatus already installed.

## The physical process and what changes

Retain eight modules, perfect paid diagnosis, and the strict diagnose–authorize–execute pipeline. Each required stage takes one slot and costs one unit per module. The selected channel count `k` limits simultaneous diagnoses. All production stops until all modules are repaired. Per-slot operating cost is one per module, healthy surplus before channel upkeep is four per module, and every installed channel costs two per slot to maintain. Repair must finish in six slots.

For this experiment, fault waves occur exactly eight slots apart. This is a specified deterministic timing law, and one of the histories admitted by the previous robust model. Fresh hidden fault bits remain arbitrary; the diagnostic pipeline corrects each assignment. Its within-episode report registers remain supplied infrastructure. The separate paid-learning model studies a different information problem and is not silently inserted into this pipeline.

There is now a design decision at every fault boundary. If `k` channels are installed, choosing `j>k` costs `30(j−k)` before repair. Removing channels costs zero and yields no resale proceeds. Removed channels must be bought again if needed later. Installation has zero modeled latency. These are new physical intervention rules; the earlier fixed-infrastructure theorem did not permit them.

The model starts with 240 cash units, no diagnostic channels, and carried-cash cap 240. Production modules and other apparatus are supplied assets. At each boundary the sequence is:

1. Choose the channel count and prepay any additions.
2. Execute the repair pipeline, prepaying every slot. No income arrives during repair, including its completion slot.
3. Receive healthy gross production before paying each healthy slot's operating and channel expenses; cap carried cash afterward.
4. Begin the next scheduled fault wave eight slots after the preceding onset.

The fixed model, planning program, public clock, and computation are supplied without a further price here. The existing costs cover installation, operating support, and diagnosis; this is not a claim that deliberation is free in the world.

## The boundary transition and its physical implementation

For a chosen design `j`, define

\[
T_j=\lceil8/j\rceil+2,
\quad C_j=24+(8+2j)T_j,
\quad q_j=32-2j,
\quad g_j=(8-T_j)q_j-C_j.
\]

Only designs finishing by the six-slot deadline are admitted. From current state `(b,k)`, let `I(k,j)=30\max(j-k,0)`. The next complete cycle is payable precisely when

\[
b-I(k,j)\ge C_j.
\]

The healthy increments in this parameter regime are nonnegative. Thus every paid pipeline and healthy-slot prefix is safe exactly when the displayed first-episode guard holds. The boundary transition is

\[
(b,k)\longmapsto
\left(\min\{240,b-I(k,j)+g_j\},j\right).
\]

The program independently expands this transition into installation, diagnostic stages, operating payments, gross receipts, and overflow. It checks the compressed transition against that physical sequence rather than assuming that endpoint solvency proves the prefixes.

| Channels | Repair slots | Episode expense | Net cash change per cycle before new installation |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 10 | 124 | Inadmissible: misses deadline |
| 2 | 6 | 96 | −40 |
| 3 | 5 | 94 | −16 |
| 4 | 4 | 88 | +8 |
| 5 | 4 | 96 | −8 |
| 6 | 4 | 104 | −24 |
| 7 | 4 | 112 | −40 |
| 8 | 3 | 96 | −16 |

Four channels are the only design with nonnegative recurrent net cash change in this supplied regime. That fact is used in the analyst's capacity proof below. It is **not** an admissibility filter in the actual planner.

## The implemented selection rule

For an integer planning horizon `h≥1`, the rule enumerates every sequence of design choices that can complete the next `h` cycles without missing a payment or repair deadline. It chooses the sequence with the greatest terminal carried cash. Ties use the lexicographically smaller sequence of channel counts. It executes only the first choice, observes the new cash and installed apparatus, and replans with horizon `h` at the next boundary.

Write the finite forecast recursively as

\[
V_0(b,k)=b,
\qquad
V_h(b,k)=\max_{j\text{ with payable cycle}}
V_{h-1}(F_j(b,k)),
\]

where branches that cannot complete all remaining cycles are excluded. This is an implemented finite cash objective, not an invocation of indefinite viability. Terminal cash is counted once; receipts and expenses enter through the transition. There is no terminal salvage value or extra continuation bonus.

If no complete `h`-cycle plan exists, the rule uses the greatest smaller positive depth that is feasible. It fails the continuing-duty test when no complete next repair can be implemented. This fallback matters: an empty two-cycle forecast does not mean that the current physical system cannot complete one more cycle.

The role of the horizon is therefore precise. It is the period over which the rule credits future financial consequences. It is not automatically a person's lifespan, institutional tenure, time preference, or competence. Those interpretations would require a measured mechanism mapping them to this rule.

## A short horizon loses capacity before reserves are exhausted

Starting from `(240,0)`, the feasible first designs are two, three, and four channels. Their one-cycle final cash values are 140, 134, and 128. A one-cycle planner therefore installs two channels.

| Boundary or completed cycle | One-cycle planner | Two-cycle planner |
|---|---|---|
| Initial state | Cash 240, channels 0 | Cash 240, channels 0 |
| First installed design | 2 | 4 |
| After first complete repair and replenishment | Cash 140, channels 2 | Cash 128, channels 4 |
| After second cycle | Cash 100, channels 2 | Cash 136, channels 4 |
| After third cycle | Cash 60, channels 2 | Cash 144, channels 4 |
| Fourth fault | No payable complete repair | Continues with four channels |

The two-cycle forecast chooses four channels immediately: completing two cycles leaves 136, compared with at most 118 after first choosing three and at most 100 after first choosing two. The one-cycle rule replans repeatedly and still chooses two. With adequate cash, upgrading from two to four costs 60 and improves one cycle's return by only 48. In the displayed run there is an additional obstruction: after the first cycle, its 140 cash cannot pay the 60 upgrade **and** the 88-unit first repair with four channels.

### Exact continuation capacity with movable infrastructure

In this deterministic periodic model, the set of states from which some admissible policy can complete every future cycle is exactly

\[
\boxed{b\ge88+30\max(4-k,0),\qquad b\le240.}
\]

**Sufficiency.** Install enough channels to reach four, or discard any excess. The displayed cash pays the additions and the 88-unit repair. Retaining four then maps cash to `min(240,b+8)` at every boundary, preserving the 88-unit repair reserve.

**Necessity.** If `k≥4` and `b<88`, no design has an affordable first complete episode: 88 is the smallest episode expense and additional installation is nonnegative. For `k<4`, consider capital-adjusted support `P=b+30k` until four channels are first reached. A transition among smaller admissible designs either preserves installed capital through purchase or discards it without refund; both designs two and three have strictly negative cycle cash changes. Hence such complete cycles cannot increase `P`. An attempted first transition to design `j≥4` requires

`P ≥ 30j+C_j ≥ 208`.

If initially `b+30k<208`, no detour among smaller designs can make that transition payable. Remaining among them forever is also impossible with finite cash because every cycle has a strictly negative change. Designs above four likewise have negative changes, and reaching them from below four requires at least as much initial support as reaching four. Thus the threshold is necessary.

The program also computes the exact greatest fixed point over all 2,169 cash/design states and confirms this entire threshold, independently of which planning rule is used. A separate descending-set implementation agrees on the full winning set; both implementations use the declared boundary transition.

Initially `(240,0)` is viable because 240 exceeds 208. After the one-cycle planner's first successful cycle, `(140,2)` is **not** viable because it needs at least 148. After the two-cycle choice, `(128,4)` is viable because it needs only 88.

Changing the horizon after the first short-horizon choice cannot rescue the displayed state under the admitted physical rules. Its problem is no longer only which policy is selected. No policy can produce indefinite continuation from that state without a new resource, a cheaper route, or a changed physical mechanism.

More generally, if the cap accommodates the initial cash, initial wealth between 208 and 247 inclusive permits direct sustainable installation but the one-cycle rule's first choice loses that possibility. It installs two and leaves `b=W−100<148`. Larger finite starting wealth can postpone the trap; it does not make this repeatedly applied one-cycle preference sustainable.

## Adoption and inheritance have different thresholds

Once four channels are installed, both the one-cycle and two-cycle planners retain them for every cash state from 88 through 240. The checker verifies all 153 states for each rule; the transition `b'=min(240,b+8)` proves continuation indefinitely.

Consequently a successor using the short horizon can continue successfully if it inherits four channels and sufficient reserve. Inheriting a longer planning horizon is not necessary in this particular regime. Starting from no channels with the same short-horizon rule produces the failure above.

This separates **constructing an apparatus**, **maintaining an inherited apparatus**, and **transmitting a decision rule**. We hold physical assets fixed when replacing the horizon. Resetting the channel count to zero would destroy real capital and define a different succession intervention. Changing the decision rule at a boundary has no extra modeled handoff fee in this comparison; the companion transmission model explicitly charges its own succession process.

No general preference for inherited institutions follows. An inherited apparatus can become unnecessary, costly, or harmful in another regime. The claim is about the supplied financial process and continuing-duty test.

## A conditional horizon threshold

Consider the two-design restriction `{L,R}` with constant cycle returns `g_R>g_L`, added initial installation expense `A` for `R`, ample prefix finance, no binding cash cap, no resale, and the same terminal-cash criterion. Suppose `R` is physically available immediately. Over a horizon `h`, selecting it rather than retaining `L` improves terminal cash exactly when

\[
\boxed{h(g_R-g_L)>A.}
\]

Equality retains `L` under the supplied tie rule. Any profitable eventual switch to `R` is weakly improved by making it immediately: the installation expense is the same and more high-return cycles follow. Reverting to `L` saves no already-paid installation expense and reduces the return. These assumptions justify comparing the constant-design plans; they do not hold for arbitrary lumpy finance, changing returns, or reversible resale.

For designs two and four here, `g_R−g_L=48` and `A=60`, so one cycle rejects the investment and two cycles favor it when both can be financed. A longer horizon cannot override a missing first payment. With initial cash 207 and no channels, indefinite continuation is impossible regardless of horizon; the exact initial requirement is 208.

This is an infrastructure-adoption mechanism under a supplied objective. It does not require an infinite optimizer, but it does use correct forecasts. Learning those forecasts, paying for the information, and passing it to successors are additional causal tasks.

## Controls where continuation is not the selected duty

**No fault.** Remove the fault mechanism and allow zero diagnostic channels. The same terminal-cash rule selects zero channels: no repair interface is required and maintaining one reduces healthy income. For this check the cap is raised to 2,000 to prevent early saturation from hiding the financial differences. This is a declared no-hazard control, not a causal claim that every existing institution should disappear when one task is removed.

**Permitted ending after one cycle.** Keep the fault and start at `(240,0)`, but declare the duty complete after one successful cycle and permit a costless, harmless exit then. Two channels meet that finite duty and leave the largest cash balance, 140. The fact that the same action would later lose indefinite capacity is not a violation of this different duty. Real closure obligations or harms would need their own costs and tests.

**Insufficient initial finance.** Correct knowledge and a longer forecast do not create support. The wealth/horizon grid separately records the number of completed cycles and entry into the independently certified viable region. It never calls a merely long simulated survival trace an infinite proof.

## What transfers under physical replication

Replicate modules, cash, installed channels, and the cash cap by a positive integer factor `a`. Keep the price per added channel and the per-module production parameters fixed. Crucially, the new admissible design menu is the **scaled image** `{aj:j in the original menu}`. This excludes additional intermediate designs from an alleged exact comparison.

Repair duration is unchanged, and installation, repair expenses, healthy inflows, and carried cash scale by `a`. Therefore every feasible design sequence maps to a feasible replicated sequence and conversely. Every terminal cash objective scales by the same positive factor; feasibility depth and tie order agree. The actual rolling selector, including its fallback, chooses correspondingly scaled designs. Hence both the short-horizon failure and the longer-horizon continuation transfer to the replicated process.

Allowing every intermediate channel count after replication changes the action menu. That may be a useful larger system, but exact selector equivalence then requires a new argument. Likewise, different forecasting, copying, or environmental probabilities cannot be dismissed as a change of scale.

## Verification and remaining limits

The [checker](verification/check_adoption_dynamics.py) and [results](verification/adoption-dynamics-results.json) preserve:

- 120 horizon-planning comparisons against exhaustive design-word enumeration using expanded slot ledgers;
- 17,352 compressed-transition comparisons with explicit installation, stage, receipt, and payment steps;
- the full 2,169-state continuation kernel and 153-state invariant for both actual horizons;
- a [1,446-row wealth/horizon frontier](verification/adoption-frontier.csv), with minimum viable initial cash 208 for the tested horizons two through six;
- 180 exact replication checks and 120 two-design horizon-threshold checks, including exact ties.

All assertions passed. The horizon-one planner never enters the viable invariant in that wealth grid. The horizon-two continuation claim comes from the invariant and proof, not from its forty-cycle trace.

The experiment remains conditional on periodic faults, correct model knowledge, free planning computation, fixed objectives, zero installation delay, and the specified channel purchase/removal rules. It establishes actual infrastructure adoption under an explicit mechanism and demonstrates a loss of future capacity. It does not establish that longer horizons always improve behavior, explain the evolutionary origin of the horizon, or provide empirical evidence about a real institution.

# Paid learning that changes an implemented selector

5 October 2026. The earlier studies distinguished feasible correction from what an actual selector chooses. This module supplies a concrete learning mechanism: a finite controller pays for observations, retains a specified statistic in a physical register, updates its posterior over an unknown regime, and uses that posterior to decide whether to maintain a corrective apparatus. The observations change the implemented decision; the analyst does not substitute the true regime for them.

This is a finite Bayesian study with exact rational calculations. It does not claim that expected-score optimization supplies a sure-safety guarantee. A low-reserve example makes that distinction consequential rather than merely verbal.

## 1. The physical episode and the unknown object

A persistent hidden regime `Θ∈{H,L}` determines the frequency of a fault. The supplied prior is `P(H)=π`. Conditional on that single regime, the probe observations `Y₁,…,Y_N` and the later deployment fault `Z` are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter `p_Θ`.

The learner does not know `Θ`. It does know the prior, the two likelihoods, the candidate actions, and their costs. What is learned is **which supplied regime is more plausible**, not the likelihood family, a new concept, an objective, or a new repair procedure.

Before deployment it can choose between:

- **Maintain:** pay `m` to keep local diagnostic readiness. If the deployment fault occurs, the known diagnose–authorize–implement protocol restores the function for a further cash bill `C` within its deadline.
- **Do not maintain:** pay no readiness fee. On a fault, a substitute provider can perform timely repair for cash bill `A`. If that bill cannot be prepaid, repair fails and the declared evaluation assigns consequence `L`.

The local route has the same simple physical interpretation as the earlier recurrent-repair model: ready diagnosis, authorization, and indicated implementation can restore production, with their support expense included in `C`. The substitute is explicitly retained; maintenance is not made valuable by deleting every alternative. Both service routes meet the declared three-slot repair deadline when funded. Fault occurrence is visible, and the specified repair services supply any fault-specific diagnosis their execution needs.

The model assesses one deployment duty after learning. It is not silently identified with the third cycle's eight-module model or its recurring finance. There is no cash income between the episode's payments. Later restored production is not used to pay an earlier test or repair bill.

**Actual cash and imputed consequence differ.** Failure loss `L` enters the stated objective but is never deducted as an imaginary cash payment. Every actual branch keeps cash nonnegative. If a repair bill is unaffordable, the program records failure instead of granting credit that the process does not possess.

The objective for this supplied selector is

`expected money spent + L × probability of failed repair`.

This is a declared valuation, not a derived ethical ranking of money and harm. A protected requirement to repair every possible fault would be a different test.

## 2. Paid observations and actual controller memory

The institution chooses a fixed probe count `N` and a register architecture before observing any data. A probe takes one lead-time slot and costs `s`; this is the supplied all-in charge for its comparable diagnostic exposure, measurement, and current write operation. The later deployment can begin after the chosen cohort completes, and `N` must fit the public lead-time bound. There is no hidden delay utility beyond that bound and the declared prices.

A retained data bit costs `μ` per holding interval. The final interval between the last report and the selection action also requires retention. The physical alternatives are:

| Register protocol | Final retained information | Paid retention |
|---|---|---|
| OR accumulator | Whether any probe was positive | One bit over `N` intervals |
| Counter | Exact positive count from zero to `N` | `ceil(log₂(N+1))` bits over `N` intervals |
| Last report only | The last probe result | One bit for the final interval only; earlier reports discarded |
| Erased | Empty register | No retained payload |
| Paid OR, then lost | Empty register after final loss | Same expenditure as the OR accumulator |

The zero-probe case uses no data storage. Register validity and the public program phase are supplied payload-independent metadata; the counter's charged data cells encode the `N+1` possible counts. The program and public clock are fixed operating infrastructure, not claimed to be physically free in every implementation.

The actual update rules are `R←R OR Y_t`, `R←R+Y_t`, overwrite by `Y_t`, or erase to `⊥`, according to the selected architecture. The final selector receives **only** this physical register, the public `N`, its known architecture, and the resulting cash. No observation history is passed to it.

The planned probe and storage fees are paid before their outcomes become available. With no intervening income, affordability of their total is sufficient for all those payment prefixes. Fees, cohort size, and timing are independent of the payload, so remaining cash and stopping time do not secretly encode discarded observations. Adaptive stopping and its informative public traces are outside this fixed-cohort class.

After learning, paying for maintenance deliberately converts evidence into a physical action. Its cost and later effects are included. That visible choice is an intended output of the selector, not an uncharged route by which earlier data circumvent its register restriction.

## 3. The actual selection rule

For each possible final register value `r`, the program computes

`P(H|r)=πP(r|H)/[πP(r|H)+(1−π)P(r|L)]`,

then predicts `p(r)=P(H|r)p_H+[1−P(H|r)]p_L`.

Crucially, the likelihood is that of the **final register**, not the full history that the analyst enumerates. After erasure, `P(r|H)=P(r|L)=1`, so the selector returns to the prior. A last-report controller conditions on one report rather than on the earlier discarded reports.

When both routes can be fully financed after learning, the rule chooses maintenance precisely when

`p(r)(A−C)>m`.

Ties choose no maintenance. If the substitute is unfunded but the local route is affordable, the same rule replaces `A` by the stated failure consequence `L`. If local repair also cannot be afforded, its score includes failure rather than an unfunded successful repair. The checker uses actual remaining cash in every comparison.

**Why the rule is optimal for its supplied criterion.** At each register value, the two expected continuation scores are affine functions of its posterior fault probability. Selecting the smaller gives the minimum conditional expected score. Summing over register values gives the minimum for that fixed architecture; independent randomization cannot improve a minimum of two available scores. This is ordinary finite Bayesian decision theory, not a new learning theorem.

The outer comparison enumerates all public `N` and register choices in the declared finite menu. It is a supplied architecture optimizer, not a claim that the learner invents its own memory representation or discovers the model family.

## 4. Base result: evidence induces selective maintenance

Take

`π=1/5`, `p_H=1/2`, `p_L=0`,

`s=0.08`, `μ=0.02`, `m=1`, `C=6`, `A=L=14`.

Initially the predicted fault probability is `0.1`. Maintenance would cost `1+0.1×6=1.6`, while the substitute route has expected expense `0.1×14=1.4`; the actual prior-based selector therefore does not maintain.

Any positive probe rules out the supplied no-hazard regime. With no positives in `N` probes,

`P(H|0,…,0)=1/(1+4·2^N)`.

Maintenance requires posterior high-regime probability above `1/4`. Thus the implemented policy is:

- maintain after a retained positive;
- do not maintain after all retained negatives.

An OR bit plus the public fixed `N` is sufficient for the entire relevant posterior in this special family. Counting every positive supplies no additional decision information here and can cost more to retain. This sufficiency is model-relative; the overlapping-regime control below removes it.

The adoption probabilities are exact:

`P(maintain|H)=1−2^(−N)`, `P(maintain|L)=0`.

At initial cash fifteen, the selected two-probe protocol pays `0.20` for probes and retention, leaving `14.80`, enough for either subsequent route. It maintains in 75% of high-regime episodes and zero low-regime episodes. The substitute repairs faults in the remaining cases. Every actual deployment fault is therefore repairable under this selected protocol.

### Exact learning-size threshold

For the tested base OR cohorts (`0≤N≤8`), and more generally while the relevant response bills remain funded, the total expected score is

`J_N=0.8+0.6·2^(−N)+0.1N`.

**Derivation.** In regime H, maintenance is chosen with probability `1−2^(−N)` and costs `1+(1/2)6=4` on average; the unmaintained route costs seven on average. Regime L incurs no deployment expense. Weighting by prior `1/5` gives `0.8+0.6·2^(−N)`, then add `0.1N` learning expense.

| Probes `N` | Expected score |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1.4 |
| 1 | 1.2 |
| 2 | **1.15** |
| 3 | 1.175 |

The next probe's gross expected benefit is `0.3·2^(−N)`. It exceeds its `0.1` expense for the first two probes and falls below it thereafter. The minimum is `N=2`. Even if the lead-time limit were relaxed, no larger OR cohort could beat it: knowing the regime for free already has minimum expected deployment expense `0.8`, so any `N≥4` costs at least `0.8+0.1N≥1.2`; `N=3` is checked explicitly. Insufficient remaining cash cannot lower that bound because the stated failure consequence is at least the successful repair fee. The finite menu also includes last-only, erased, counter, and paid-but-lost memory; none beats the two-probe OR protocol at these prices.

Knowing the regime without learning expense would yield expected deployment cost `0.2×4+0.8×0=0.8`. The difference is not presumed recoverable: information costs, finite evidence, and the supplied memory interface limit the implemented learner.

## 5. Capacity and actual adoption can diverge

Now keep the same statistical family and selector but provide only eight initial cash units. Two-probe learning still costs `0.20`, and the maintained route still fits (`1+6≤7.80`). The substitute's fourteen-unit bill does not.

The selector nevertheless has the same expected score and chooses the same policy, because the model deliberately assigns an unfunded fault the numerical failure consequence `L=A=14`. That equality is a supplied valuation, not a statement that failure and purchased repair are materially equivalent.

The failure event is exactly: high regime, no positive in the two probes, and a later deployment fault. Its probability is

`(1/5)·(1/2)^2·(1/2)=1/40=0.025`.

Under the same initial eight units, **unconditional maintenance without inquiry** costs at most seven and repairs every admitted fault. The protected robust capacity therefore exists, while this expectation-minimizing implemented selector does not use it. The failure is not a theorem that learning or Bayes updating is inherently harmful; the actual selector optimizes a criterion that permits this risk.

For any finite `N`, all-negative evidence remains possible in regime H. Its posterior never reaches zero. If the protected duty demands repair for every event in the model's support and the substitute is unaffordable, such evidence cannot certify that maintenance may safely be dropped. A robustly constrained selector in this example must retain the local route even after negative evidence; no probing is needed for that decision.

The same formula quantifies finite rather than absolute assurance. Under the OR rule and sufficient residual cash for local repair, high-regime maintenance adoption reaches `1−δ` only if `2^(−N)≤δ`. Greater confidence needs more paid probes and memory. No finite such threshold turns the all-negative event into impossibility.

### Learning itself can consume an enabling margin

With initial cash `7.1`, unconditional maintenance is initially feasible. One probe with retention spends `0.1`, leaving exactly seven. Two probes spend `0.2`, leaving `6.9`: now neither the seven-unit maintained route nor the fourteen-unit substitute can be fully prepaid on a fault. At that point the register may contain stronger evidence while the physical guarantee is gone.

The specified architecture optimizer responds to this constraint by choosing one probe, score `1.2`, rather than two. If the two-probe architecture is imposed anyway, its modeled fault-failure probability is `0.1`, the unconditional deployment hazard. Thus spending on discovery can change later feasible actions; accurate information does not itself finance implementation.

## 6. Reversals and controls

### Maintenance is unnecessary when the relevant hazard is absent

If both supplied regimes have fault probability zero, every probe is negative and no deployment fault can occur. No maintenance and no inquiry achieve score zero. Any positive probe/storage expense is wasted for this objective, and maintenance adds `m` without benefit. This is a direct proof in the no-hazard model, not a simulation frequency claim.

When the base regime is known to be H, the controller instead maintains immediately and needs no inquiry; its expected expense is four. When L is known, it chooses neither inquiry nor maintenance. Information is useful only when it can change a relevant choice enough to repay its cost.

### High learning or memory prices remove the incentive to learn

Raising probe price to `0.4` or retained-cell price to `0.3` makes the best checked protocol use no probes and retain the prior-based policy, score `1.4`. In the base OR family, the first observation's maximum gross improvement is `0.3` and later improvements decrease; these prices defeat that improvement. Last-report, count, erased, and lost-memory alternatives are also enumerated.

If only one lead-time slot is available, the best protocol takes one probe and scores `1.2`; it cannot realize the two-probe optimum before deployment. Giving storage a zero price improves the two-probe score to `1.11`, while the probe expense remains real.

### A cheap substitute can make local maintenance and learning unnecessary

Reducing the substitute's fault bill from fourteen to seven means even the high regime has expected incremental saving `p_H(A−C)=0.5`, below the one-unit readiness fee. No regime warrants maintenance under the supplied score. The optimum is no inquiry and the substitute route, expected expense `0.7`. This control keeps a concrete replacement mechanism rather than treating incumbent preservation as the objective.

### The memory sufficient for one model can become insufficient in another

Set `p_L=0.1`, retain `p_H=0.5` and prior `0.2`, set maintenance fee two, and reduce probe and retained-cell prices to `0.005` each. Now a positive may come from either regime, and positive counts carry distinctions that the OR flag merges.

At a matched cohort of three:

| Register | Total expected score | Implemented response |
|---|---:|---|
| OR | 2.46016 | Maintain after any positive |
| Counter | **2.39188** | Do not maintain after one positive; maintain after two or three |

The counter pays for its additional physical data cell. Its better evidence changes the actual selector enough to cover that price. Across the full declared menu up to eight probes, the optimum is five probes with a three-bit counter, score **2.3732016**. It maintains with probability `0.8125` in H and `0.08146` in L. Some unnecessary maintenance remains possible because the regimes have overlapping evidence laws.

This does not show that larger records are always preferable. In the base family, the OR bit is sufficient and the extra count storage merely costs more. Appropriate memory depends on the admitted model and decision test.

### Losing paid memory actually changes behavior

Forcing loss of the final OR register after two paid probes gives the selector the empty symbol, so its posterior is the prior and it never adopts maintenance. At base cash fifteen its expected score is `1.6`: the original `1.4` deployment expense plus `0.2` of spent learning support. The corresponding intact register scored `1.15`. No hidden transcript allows the lost-memory controller to use the observations anyway.

## 7. Exact verification and scope

The [standard-library checker](verification/check_paid_learning.py) writes [complete rational results](verification/paid-learning-results.json) and a [protocol frontier](verification/paid-learning-frontier.csv). It enumerates every binary probe history for each public cohort and register architecture, aggregates likelihoods by the physical final register, and separately evaluates every positive-probability regime/fault/payment branch.

The current record covers **505 protocols**, **28,120 enumerated probe histories**, and **2,426 positive cash/outcome branches** in twelve parameter cases. Nine base cohort sizes agree exactly with the closed-form posterior, adoption, and score expressions. Every cash branch satisfies

`cash_remaining + actual_learning_expense + actual_deployment_expense = initial_cash`,

with nonnegative remaining cash. A second register-conditioned score calculation agrees with the explicit branch calculation. The overlap example and limited-cash risk have additional exact assertions. All checks passed.

These checks establish the implemented finite calculations, not a general convergence theorem or empirical institutional claim. The probes are conditionally independent under the supplied regime; model drift, strategic reporting, correlated probes, changing interventions, and selection of the probe grammar would require different likelihoods and mechanisms. The final fault does not finance the preceding research, and the episode is not restarted with free inherited cash inside the code.

The mechanism is now more than a capacity assertion: an actual specified selector learns from paid retained evidence and changes action. Its remaining supplied components—prior, models, actions, prices, valuation, and architecture optimizer—are explicit. Explaining how those components are formed and transmitted remains separate from learning the hidden regime within them.

# Selection, transmission, and actual behavior across scale

Cycle 4 mathematical memo, 5 October 2026. This extends the [cycle-3 transport result](../cycle-3/constraint-transport.md) from available control to the controller actually implemented. It provides finite-state proofs, an exact counterexample, and executable checks. The mathematics specializes established simulation and Markov aggregation reasoning; no mathematical originality or empirical universality is claimed.

## 1. A capacity correspondence does not select its implementation

The previous result has the form

`an abstract winning controller π exists ⇒ a compiled concrete winning controller κπ exists`.

It does not say that the actual concrete selector is `κπ`, learns it, adopts it, or transmits it intact. Equal capacity profiles can coexist with different actual behavior. Conversely, two particular selectors can have the same outcome even when their systems possess different unused capacities. These are distinct comparison questions.

Write the actual augmented configuration as `z=(q,c)`, where `q` contains the plant, accessible resources, access relations, and clocks, while `c=(g,m)` contains the current rule/program `g` and its physically retained working memory `m`. The separation is bookkeeping: controller memory and program carriers are physical components, with whatever costs and access constraints the model supplies.

An implemented mechanism specifies:

1. an action rule using only its permitted information and memory;
2. a plant/environment transition with its event order and actual payments;
3. an update rule for the program, memory, or parameters;
4. any succession or transmission channel that constructs a later controller.

These stages can be represented as separate phase states. When a stage learns, searches, interprets, communicates, or installs a new program, its duration and expense belong to that mechanism. A declared optimizer is not automatically a physically available operation. An initial program, supplied model, or fixed interpreter can instead be an endowed component, but this must be stated. Representing an update rule as state does not explain its origin or require an infinite hierarchy of unexplained optimizers; a model may explicitly take a finite update mechanism as its starting assumption.

Once the actual mechanism is fixed, the resulting closed loop has no analyst-controlled choice of a better policy. Denote its possible labeled transitions by

`z —e→ z'`.

The label `e` can report action, output, payments, elapsed time, or a rule-transfer event. Hidden state and retained memory remain in `z`; labels need not reveal them. Failure is an explicit absorbing state. Environmental restrictions and persistent random seeds must be represented in the augmented state or admitted histories. A missing transition or forgotten random seed is not an unmodeled source of success.

## 2. Exact example: same financial capacity, different selectors

The plant has three mandatory one-tick phases per cycle and a carried-cash cap of two. A cycle begins with two units of cash.

| Phase | Available operation | Payment and result |
|---|---|---|
| Operation | `RESERVE` or `CONSUME` | `RESERVE` costs zero and produces visible output one. `CONSUME` spends one reserve unit and produces visible output two. Neither output is a cash receipt. |
| Service | Pay one | A one-unit service bill must be paid before proceeding. |
| Succession | Pay one | A one-unit transmission/renewal bill must be paid. Only afterward does an external two-unit receipt arrive; surplus above the cap is discarded. |

The external receipt is a supplied renewal input, conditional on completing the succession stage. It cannot finance that stage's earlier fee. The model does not claim to explain the source of the receipt or equate visible output with money. Program execution between these events is supplied infrastructure. Copying the rule costs the same one unit regardless of its payload, so bills do not secretly signal the program bit.

The general controller class may choose either operation from the observed plant state. For the test of indefinite payment and cycle completion, the plant has a winning controller: always choose `RESERVE`. Its cash path within each cycle is `2→2→1→0→2`, where the final arrow is the post-payment receipt. The same test fails under an actual selector that always chooses `CONSUME`: its path begins `2→1→0`, so the succession fee cannot be paid. It produces more visible output before failing.

The complete controlled safe set, with phase labels `O,S,T`, is

`{(O,2),(S,2),(T,1),(T,2)}`.

This is obtained by the greatest safety fixed point in the checker. Starting plant state, menus, financial capacity, available observations, and disturbance conditions are identical in the two comparisons. Only the implemented selection rule differs. The capacity statement is relative to the declared financial test and general controller class; it is not equality for every imaginable test about program identity.

### An initially correct selector can fail through transmission

Let the actual controller carry a rule bit `g∈{R,C}`. At the operation phase it uses `RESERVE` when `g=R` and `CONSUME` when `g=C`; at other phases it attempts the mandatory bill. Its action rule is fixed and uses the visible rule register. There is no hidden optimizer.

An identity transmission channel preserves `g=R`, so the actual system continues. Another channel has the same fee, receipt, initial rule, and first two actions, but changes `R` into `C` at the first handoff. The first cycle succeeds; the second fails at succession. A correspondence that matches the initial selector and plant transition while omitting the controller update is therefore insufficient.

More generally, let each successful handoff independently change `R→C` with probability `μ`, and let `C` remain `C`. From initial rule `R`, survival through `N≥1` complete cycles is

`P(survive N cycles)=(1−μ)^(N−1)`.

**Proof.** A cycle entered with `R` completes. A cycle entered with `C` fails. The first `N−1` handoffs must therefore retain `R`; the final handoff's outcome cannot cause a payment failure until the following cycle. Multiply the independent retention probabilities. ∎

For `μ>0`, infinite survival has probability zero; the expected failed-cycle index is `1+1/μ`. These are statements under the supplied independent channel law, not consequences of merely allowing a corruption transition. At any two rates strictly between zero and one, the supported finite paths are identical, but their probabilities differ. For example, survival through four cycles is `27/64` at `μ=1/4` and `1/8` at `μ=1/2`.

The controlled plant still admits an always-`RESERVE` controller independent of the mutable program bit. This compares controllers at the plant's input interface; it does not claim that the already installed bit-driven program can replace itself for free. That particular mechanism does not implement the winning input sequence after corruption. This is precisely the gap between an available strategy in the declared comparison class and an actual transmitted one.

## 3. S4.1 — Robust transfer of a fixed actual closed loop

Consider augmented closed loops `L` and `H` with finite state and event sets, and nonempty successor sets including explicit failure. Let `R⊆Z_L×Z_H` relate their boundary configurations and let `χ` translate event labels. Suppose:

- each admitted concrete initial state has a related admitted abstract initial state;
- for every related pair and every **actual** concrete transition `z_L —e_L→ z'_L`, there is an actual abstract transition `z_H —χ(e_L)→ z'_H` with `z'_L R z'_H`;
- the tested observations, protected states, and target conditions translate in the required direction.

Then every actual concrete path has a matching actual abstract path after label translation. Hence every all-path property of the abstract closed loop that is preserved by the stated translation holds for the concrete loop.

**Proof.** Extend the matching path one actual transition at a time. The successor clause supplies a matching abstract edge from the already selected abstract state and reestablishes the relation. Induction gives every finite prefix. For an infinite concrete path, the finite, finitely branching tree of matching abstract prefixes has an infinite branch, yielding a matching path. Property transfer follows from the hypothesis on the test and labels. ∎

This theorem checks the system that runs; it does not replace the implemented concrete action with a better action that merely exists. In particular, the concrete update and transmission outcomes must be covered by the abstract **actual** update and transmission process. An identity relation on plant states cannot conceal a future difference caused by an omitted rule register.

For different time resolutions, an actual abstract step may correspond to a concrete adaptive protocol. Then all the cycle-3 conditions remain necessary for this sufficient certificate: recognizable stopping, admitted information and memory, every-prefix affordability and safety, and bounded completion. The actual lower-level selector must execute the certified local protocol. Controller amendments during it are included. A matching endpoint does not certify internal solvency. Stuttering or compression does not preserve an arbitrary deadline or liveness test without the appropriate progress and clock conditions.

S4.1 is sufficient, not necessary for equality of one selected performance score. Programs may have different internal representations while producing the same relevant behavior. What must correspond is the behavior needed for the specified transfer, not literal source code.

## 4. S4.2 — Exact transfer of path probabilities

For stochastic claims, matching supports is weaker than matching laws. Consider Markov closed loops with finite augmented state and event sets, whose states contain all retained controller and environment memory. S4.2–S4.4 use this finite setting; continuous event labels would instead require kernel equality or approximation on measurable sets. Let

`K_s(z; e,z')`

be the joint probability of the next event and state. This kernel includes the actual selector's randomization, environmental law, controller update, and transmission channel in their declared order. It includes their correlations; separate one-variable marginals are insufficient.

Let `φ:Z_L→Z_H` be a state projection and `χ:E_L→E_H` an event translation. Assume corresponding initial distributions and, for every concrete state and every abstract event/next-state pair, the equality

`Σ_{χ(e_L)=e_H, φ(z'_L)=z'_H} K_L(z_L;e_L,z'_L)`

`= K_H(φ(z_L);e_H,z'_H).`  **(K)**

Then the translated concrete labeled-state process has exactly the abstract path law. In particular, corresponding measurable path tests have equal probabilities, and corresponding integrable path costs have equal expectations after their stated unit conversion.

**Proof.** The initial pushforward distributions agree. Conditional on any concrete past, the next projected event/state distribution is the right side of (K); it depends on that past only through the current projected state. Multiplication and summation therefore give equality of every finite cylinder probability by induction. On the finite-state infinite product space, the cylinder probabilities determine the path measure, giving the infinite-path statement as well. ∎

This is a labeled strong aggregation condition. It must hold for every concrete state in each relevant fiber, not just for a favorable hidden representative or one average distribution. An implementation-specific restriction to an invariant reachable subset is allowed when that subset and its initial coverage are established. Standard finite Markov aggregation and stochastic bisimulation provide the mathematical precedent. [Givan, Dean, and Greig (2003), *Equivalence notions and model minimization in Markov decision processes*](https://cs.brown.edu/people/tdean/publications/archive/GivanetalAIJ-03.pdf).

One practical way to establish (K) is phase-by-phase correspondence of the actual action kernel, plant/environment kernel, observation delivery, memory update, and transmission kernel, with paid operations included. These sufficient local equalities compose into the whole-step equality by summing over the internal phase states. Accidental cancellation can also produce the same overall kernel; literal equality of every internal procedure is not logically necessary for every observable equivalence.

A proof for one environmental law does not establish transfer under another law or under every adaptive adversary. For a robust family of laws, the appropriate correspondence must hold uniformly for that family. If the environment has history-dependent behavior, its required state or history must be included. A hidden persistent coin and a newly sampled coin at every tick both have fair one-time marginals, but the probability that two consecutive outputs agree is respectively one and one-half.

The theorem is about the declared observation process. It does not assert preservation of information deliberately omitted from `φ`, arbitrary future tests, or physical internal safety erased by temporal sampling.

### A positive implementation in the checker

The checker builds three descriptions of the same actual mechanism. Their currency units scale as `1,2,6`; their rule registers encode `R` as respectively `0,1,7`; and their irrelevant phase tags cycle modulo `1,2,6`. Action interpretation and transmission are adapted to each encoding. Cash fees, receipts, and caps scale consistently. The maps divide currency units, decode the rule, and project the phase tag.

For each `μ∈{0,1/4,1/2,1}`, condition (K) holds in all three comparisons `L→M`, `M→H`, and `L→H`. Their translated finite path laws agree. Leaving the transmission law at a different `μ` breaks (K), even though action menus and supported paths can remain unchanged. These are unit and representation transformations with redundant state, not a general proof about physically enlarging an organization.

## 5. S4.3 — Correspondences compose

For robust relations, if `L→M` and `M→H` satisfy S4.1 with compatible tests, their relational composition and composed event translation satisfy S4.1. A concrete edge first obtains its matching middle edge, and that edge obtains its matching abstract edge. The paired successors remain in the composed relation. Actual local protocols can be nested under the additional cycle-3 interface, timing, and memory obligations.

For exact kernels, if `(φ_LM,χ_LM)` and `(φ_MH,χ_MH)` satisfy (K), then

`φ_LH=φ_MH∘φ_LM`, `χ_LH=χ_MH∘χ_LM`

satisfy (K). **Proof.** Sum the lower-level kernel first over each middle event/state fiber, replacing that sum with `K_M` using the first equality; then sum over the middle fibers belonging to the abstract event/state pair and apply the second equality. Initial distributions push forward by the same composition. ∎

Thus an actual process can be transported through several descriptions. This does not follow from a sequence of capacity inequalities if each intermediate system implements an unrelated selector.

### S4.4 — A finite-horizon approximation bound

Suppose initial projected distributions differ by total variation at most `δ`, and the two sides of (K) differ by total variation at most `ε` uniformly over relevant concrete states. Then the translated path laws through `N` transitions differ by total variation at most

`min(1,δ+Nε)`.

**Proof.** Couple the initial projected states with mismatch probability at most `δ`. Whenever the projected states still agree, couple the next joint event/state pairs with mismatch probability at most `ε`; the uniform bound applies whatever concrete state and past remain. A union bound gives `δ+Nε` for any mismatch. Differences in any path-event probability are bounded by that coupling's mismatch probability. ∎

The approximation controls a finite horizon. It may become vacuous as `N` increases, and does not by itself preserve an infinite sure guarantee, a strict threshold, or a narrow quality margin. Additional contraction, recurrence, or stability structure is needed for a sharper long-run assertion. The checker verifies this bound for the two mutation rates; it does not establish its universal proof mechanically.

## 6. S4.5 — When a supplied planning selector itself transports

The preceding conditions apply to optimizers as well as fixed rule bits, provided an optimizer is the actual declared mechanism. A useful special case concerns a finite planning selector that examines a tree of feasible candidate schedules, chooses the schedule with best terminal value, and executes its first action.

Suppose a scale map supplies:

1. a depth-preserving bijection between the two feasible planning trees, including all internal payment and access guards;
2. corresponding first actions and future observations;
3. terminal values related by `J_L=a J_H+b`, with `a>0` and `b` independent of the candidate at the current root;
4. a deterministic tie order that is preserved by the mapping;
5. corresponding controller updates, memory, and replanning events after each executed step.

Then the actual selected first actions correspond. If the same conditions persist at later states, the rolling selectors remain in correspondence.

**Proof.** Positive affine transformation preserves every strict value comparison and equality. The tree bijection preserves feasibility and the tie order selects corresponding maximizers. The first actions therefore match. The update condition reestablishes the hypotheses at the next planning root, so induction gives the closed-loop correspondence. ∎

A fallback that first maximizes feasible planning depth and then terminal value also transports under the same depth-preserving bijection and tie rule. If a physical replication introduces extra intermediate designs, the tree is no longer bijective; one must restrict menus to the scaled image or separately prove those new alternatives cannot change the decision. Merely scaling the optimum value of one candidate is insufficient.

This explains the scope of the companion rolling-horizon model. A supplied finite-horizon planner can explain how infrastructure choice changes with the current reserve and horizon. It does not explain why that horizon, objective, model, or algorithm was adopted. Supplying an explicit update and transmission rule for those quantities advances that causal explanation. It is not supplied by an abstract existence proof or by calling the planner rational.

## 7. What the extension establishes

The theory now distinguishes three implications:

- **Capacity transfer:** a response implementable at one level has an implementable counterpart.
- **Actual robust transfer:** every admitted trajectory of the implemented concrete mechanism has a corresponding trajectory of the implemented abstract mechanism.
- **Actual probabilistic transfer:** corresponding joint kernels and initial laws give corresponding trajectory probabilities.

These results require progressively different evidence. Capacity is not realized selection; robust support is not a probability law; and an individual rule's initial match is not a certificate for its learning or succession dynamics. Feedback-refinement work likewise emphasizes implementation architecture rather than arbitrary state-informed controller matches. [Reissig, Weber, and Rungger (2017), *Feedback Refinement Relations for the Synthesis of Symbolic Controllers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03715).

None of these results chooses a legitimate objective, establishes that a real organization has the declared channels, or guarantees that future unmodeled concepts fit the same representation. Their contribution is a checkable route from a proposed mechanism to a prediction, and a clear location for failure when scale changes selection, memory, updates, or environmental dependence.

# Selection audit: adoption, continuation, and succession

Research audit, 5 October 2026. This cycle connects the existing feasibility models to specified selectors and transmission mechanisms. It does not derive inevitable improvement, inevitable preservation of repair capacity, moral authority from persistence, or a universal empirical theory. The earlier [universality audit](../cycle-3/universality-audit.md) explains the larger scope.

## What this cycle can genuinely explain

A fixed finite-horizon decision rule can genuinely model **endogenous adoption of infrastructure**: installation, retention, or abandonment becomes an outcome of the current state and the rule. Calling the rule an optimizer does not invalidate it as a behavioral mechanism. The model should state that the objective, horizon, information, and computational implementation are supplied assumptions.

That is different from explaining why the decision rule itself was adopted. Four levels should remain distinct:

| Level | Explicit modeled object | Claim justified |
|---|---|---|
| Feasible capacity | Existentially quantified admitted controller | A successful policy exists |
| Actual choice | A specified selector `σ` acting on its permitted information | This system chooses these actions under the supplied rule |
| Learning or institutional amendment | An update mechanism for estimates, objectives, horizon, or selector code | These aspects of the rule change through specified feedback |
| Population selection and transmission | Contributions, copying/influence, mutation or transformation, and a population update | Some variants become more or less represented through this specified process |

There is no requirement to endogenize every assumption before making useful predictions. Every model has an outer semantics. The improvement is to identify which formerly unexplained choice has become an outcome and which rule remains a boundary assumption. A perfect externally calculated policy can be a declared benchmark. It becomes the actual system's behavior only if access to that decision procedure is assumed or modeled.

## A common semantic contract for selector comparisons

Hold the physical process, starting configuration, disturbance realization or declared distribution, action menu, observation interface, and payment order fixed when comparing selectors. Include clocks and existing apparatus in that starting configuration. Changing the horizon and quietly changing initial cash, free information, or installation state would compare different systems.

An actual selector can choose an attempted action that fails. It must not receive only the actions lying inside the infinite viability kernel unless that protective filter is explicitly part of its implementation. Otherwise long-run solvency has already been imposed on the selector being tested for short-term failure.

For each decision rule, specify:

- what is scored: output, withdrawals, terminal cash, welfare, survival, or another quantity;
- which outcomes and costs enter the score, including costs borne after turnover;
- horizon, discounting, terminal value, and terminal constraints;
- whether the plan is committed to or recomputed after each observation;
- how exact ties are resolved, using the same rule across the comparison;
- which model and observations the selector possesses, and whether computation or search is charged or supplied as a boundary assumption.

These are mechanism parameters, not inconvenient qualifications. They determine the predicted choice.

## Finite horizons: the discriminating issue is the omitted continuation

A short planning horizon does not by itself imply bad maintenance decisions. Immediate effects may justify maintenance; a good terminal value can summarize distant consequences; and a certified terminal region can keep later choices feasible. Conversely, a longer horizon does not automatically optimize the external evaluator's objective or correct a wrong environment model.

An elementary benchmark makes the distinction precise. In a discounted stationary finite decision process, let `V*` be the infinite-horizon optimal value for the same reward and admissible controls. A finite-horizon calculation with terminal value `V*` returns `V*` at every backward step because `V*` is a Bellman fixed point. Thus even one-step planning with that exact continuation value selects an infinite-horizon optimal action. This is a mathematical benchmark, not a claim that an actual system knows or can afford to calculate `V*`.

The useful intervention therefore separates **horizon length**, **terminal continuation treatment**, and **available model information**. If only the zero-terminal-value short-horizon selector fails, the result supports that specified truncation mechanism. It does not establish a universal disadvantage of every short-horizon implementation.

Model predictive control already supplies precise examples where finite optimization is combined with terminal conditions to guarantee a continuing property. Chen and Allgöwer use a terminal cost and region in a particular nonlinear control scheme. Its restricted stability result motivates the terminal-condition control here; it does not establish solvency or institutional stability for our renewal process. [Chen and Allgöwer, 1998](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0005109898000739).

### Accounting and horizon traps

1. **Count flows and terminal assets consistently.** If the reward already includes the net change in cash, adding all final cash can count the same gain twice. If the reward is withdrawals or delivered output instead, retained cash can be a distinct terminal asset. State the intended objective rather than calling every expression “profit.”
2. **Retain prefix feasibility.** A positive projected terminal balance cannot finance an earlier installation fee. Receipts, expenses, capacity limits, and overflow must have the same order in the selector's forecast and actual execution.
3. **Expose cash-cap effects.** Spilled surplus can make extra earning valueless under a terminal-cash objective. This may create broad ties or make costly maintenance appear free at the cap. That is a property of this supplied financial objective, not necessarily a physical benefit.
4. **Specify the horizon boundary.** A failure at the first excluded step, a cost payable just after turnover, and a completed duty followed by safe retirement are distinct events. An indexing convention should not decide the substantive result accidentally.
5. **Distinguish commitment from replanning.** A planned delayed installation may be postponed again whenever the horizon moves. Verify the realized trajectory, not only the initial optimal plan.
6. **Check all tied optimal actions.** If the reported collapse depends on an arbitrary tie-breaking convention, show that dependence. A strict ranking or an all-ties conclusion is stronger evidence for the proposed mechanism.

## Learning is an update process with a survival problem

Changing an action because a known model and state changed is adaptive control in a broad sense, but it is not necessarily learning. A learning claim needs an estimated object, an observation/update rule, retained state, and a relationship between acquired evidence and later actions. Perfectly solving the true model afresh after each episode does not test whether the actor can learn that model.

Watkins and Dayan provide a clean contrasting example: their tabular Q-learning rule updates action values from experienced transitions. The convergence theorem assumes a specified Markov setting, suitable learning rates, bounded rewards, and repeated sampling of every state-action pair; samples need not form one uninterrupted trajectory. It is not a theorem that a resource-limited learner survives while exploring. [Watkins and Dayan, 1992](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/papers/cjch.pdf), §2 and theorem.

That distinction is particularly important here. An absorbing bankruptcy state can prevent further experimentation. Restarting failed episodes with fresh capital supplies an additional recovery mechanism. If such resets are used, record their source and cost; otherwise compare learning subject to the same physical solvency constraints. A guarantee of eventual value convergence conditional on endless data cannot substitute for a guarantee of continued access to that data.

Learning efficiency, viability while learning, and long-run optimality are separate tests. The present cycle need not solve all three. It should say which one its mechanism actually studies.

## Succession, transmission, and selection

At turnover, distinguish what crosses the boundary:

- physical assets and liabilities;
- permission and execution access;
- records, retained estimates, or a compiled policy;
- a rule label, horizon, or preference parameter;
- the source-selection and interpretation procedure used by the successor.

A inherited label does not automatically give the successor its predecessor's information, assets, or authority. Conversely, replacing the incumbent does not erase information still carried by public prices, the apparatus state, a clock, or another participant. The previous paid-memory models already demonstrate why retention and usable access must be distinguished.

Copying a selector from one incumbent to one successor is inheritance. Differential survival can change the composition of surviving organizations. Differential reproduction or imitation can change representation through contributions to new selectors. These are different mechanisms. Report absolute population size or number of surviving organizations alongside trait frequencies: an increasing share of a variant can coexist with severe population decline.

For a population update, define a contribution weight `w_i≥0` and a successor-type kernel `K_i(j)` for each current carrier. A generic normalized update has the form

\[
x'_j=\frac{\sum_i x_i w_i K_i(j)}{\sum_i x_i w_i},
\]

when the denominator is positive. This bookkeeping form does not explain the weights or kernels. They require a mechanism—observed payoff, reproductive output, election, imitation, training, or another stated process. It also does not specify absolute population growth; that requires its own update. If total contribution is zero, extinction cannot be hidden by normalization.

The Price-equation literature already separates selection from transmission effects. El Mouden and colleagues make that distinction for cultural traits and stress that influence is trait-specific. Neither generic social status nor organizational survival is automatically the correct contribution weight. This paper supplies conceptual distinctions, not an empirical endorsement of a turnover mechanism in the current toy process. [El Mouden, André, Morin, and Nettle, 2014](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jeb.12296), definitions and transmission discussion.

### Selection need not preserve viability

The general inference “a successful variant spreads, therefore the population becomes more viable” is invalid without a bridge between contribution and the protected function. A variant can gain influence before its deferred costs are realized; an individually favorable change can alter a shared environment; learning can transform the transmitted rule. Which possibility occurs depends on the specified mechanism.

There is direct biological prior art against an unconditional adaptation-to-persistence inference. Gyllenberg and Parvinen analyze evolutionary processes leading from a viable population to extinction and give model-specific conditions and exclusions. The publisher abstract supports this limited precedent; its detailed theorem is not imported here. [Gyllenberg and Parvinen, 2001](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092824001902538).

The current models should make their own more limited claims from their own transition rules. The biological example does not prove that every institution, economic system, or AI population follows the same mechanism.

## Discriminating controls

| Control | Hold fixed | What it discriminates |
|---|---|---|
| No future fault or harmless fault | Physical operating costs and supplied selector objective | Whether maintenance is useful only under the modeled disturbance duty |
| Free, equally timely alternative repair | Fault sequence and evaluation | Whether failure concerns one infrastructure route rather than a universal need for that carrier |
| Correct continuation value or certified terminal region | Short horizon and physical process | Horizon truncation versus limited lookahead with adequate continuation information |
| Commitment versus repeated replanning | Initial forecast, objective, and horizon | One-time investment ranking versus repeated postponement |
| Inherited rule with erased estimates, then estimates restored | Assets, authority, and fault process | Transmission of a label versus usable decision knowledge |
| Neutral copying versus payoff-weighted copying | Physical payoffs and initial type frequencies | Transmission alone versus differential influence |
| Same copying rule with longer outcome-measurement window | Physical process and inherited types | Immediate score advantage versus deferred maintenance costs |
| Safe ending or handoff | Physical costs, liabilities, and rights respected by that ending | Continuing one carrier versus fulfilling the declared duty |
| Exact proportional replication | Ratios, per-module cash, objective scaling, and observation access | A genuine scale correspondence versus an unscaled reward or fixed absolute fee |

The safe-ending control must be declared before evaluating outcomes. Supply an executable retirement, shutdown, or handoff action whose safety and outstanding obligations are checked. Reclassifying accidental collapse as a successful ending after seeing the result would not be a meaningful control. Likewise, a no-hazard case need not retain infrastructure whose only modeled purpose is hazard response.

These controls can produce null or reversed effects without weakening the underlying accounting and information constraints. They identify the domain of the selection mechanism and prevent “more maintenance” from becoming an unstated moral objective.

|---|---|---|---|
