# How continuation capacity becomes actual behavior

This cycle advances the theory from feasible responses to **the mechanisms that actually choose, learn, and transmit them**. The choices now depend on available funds, retained observations, installed apparatus, and an explicit decision rule. The rule's objective and basic update procedure remain declared assumptions.

The strongest new result is a mechanism for losing future capacity through a locally successful choice. In the repair model, a one-cycle planner's first repair succeeds and leaves more cash than the alternative, but it also makes sustainable repair unaffordable. A two-cycle planner builds the sustainable design. A short-horizon successor can then maintain that inherited design successfully. Building, choosing, inheriting, and maintaining capacity have different conditions.

The [adoption study](adoption-dynamics.md), [paid-learning study](paid-learning.md), and [selection and scale theorem](selection-and-scale.md) solve distinct declared problems under a common operational framework. Their proofs and checks do not constitute an empirical universal law or an explanation of every form of evolution.

## From possible control to an implemented process

The earlier capacity question asks whether some admissible policy can meet a declared duty. The next question fixes the actual decision mechanism and follows its consequences.

Represent its configuration as

\[
z_t=(q_t,g_t,m_t),
\qquad z_{t+1}\sim K_\sigma(\cdot\mid z_t),
\]

where `q` includes the physical process, assets, access, and cash; `g` is the current rule or program; and `m` is its real retained memory. `Kσ` contains the actual action selection, environmental law, observation delivery, learning updates, and any succession channel, in their stated order. A deterministic mechanism is a special case. A robust analysis instead admits a declared set of environmental transitions.

This adds causal content to the theory. A winning policy does not have to be inserted by the analyst at every step. A specified controller may choose a different action; a paid observation may alter its estimate; a lost register may prevent that update; a successor may inherit assets while using a different rule.

Four objects therefore remain distinct:

| Object | What the model now determines |
|---|---|
| Feasible capacity | Which duties some permitted controller can fulfill |
| Actual selection | Which action the implemented rule chooses from its information |
| Learning | How observations and paid memory change a retained estimate and later action |
| Transmission | Which assets, records, programs, and permissions reach a successor |

These mechanisms can interact through the configuration. Their existence does not imply that selection improves the protected capacity, that more information is always worth buying, or that retaining one institution is the right duty.

## A successful action can eliminate future continuation

The main experiment retains the previous eight-module repair process. Every module needs diagnosis, authorization, and execution. Diagnostic channels are shared; all production stops until repair finishes. Fault waves occur exactly eight slots apart and repairs must finish within six slots. Operating support, diagnostic upkeep, and repair stages are all paid.

At each fault boundary, the controller can buy additional channels at 30 units each or discard channels without refund. It starts with cash 240, no channels, and a cash cap of 240. These purchase and removal actions are new compared with the earlier fixed-design experiment.

The actual rule forecasts the next `h` complete cycles, chooses the payable design sequence leaving the greatest terminal cash, executes its first choice, and replans at the next boundary. It uses no infinite-viability filter. If its preferred horizon is unaffordable, it uses the longest shorter feasible horizon. Its model knowledge, objective, and computation are supplied.

At the first decision, two channels leave 140 after one cycle, three leave 134, and four leave 128. A one-cycle planner chooses two. A two-cycle planner chooses four because this leaves 136 after two cycles, exceeding the best alternatives.

| Realized outcome | One-cycle planning | Two-cycle planning |
|---|---:|---:|
| Installed channels | 2 | 4 |
| Cash after cycle 1 | 140 | 128 |
| Cash after cycle 2 | 100 | 136 |
| Cash after cycle 3 | 60 | 144 |
| Fourth fault | Complete repair unavailable | Continues |

The important boundary appears **before** the fourth fault. With `k` channels already installed, exact indefinite continuation capacity in this model is

\[
\boxed{b\ge88+30\max(4-k,0).}
\]

Four channels need 88 cash for the next repair and then earn a net eight per complete cycle. Fewer channels require purchasing the missing apparatus first. Every complete cycle using a smaller design loses support, so detours cannot finance the missing upgrade. Larger installed designs can discard excess channels and use four.

Thus `(240,0)` begins inside the viable set, but the short-horizon rule's first successful cycle ends at `(140,2)`, which needs 148. **It has lost the capacity to continue indefinitely under any admitted policy.** Changing to a more farsighted rule afterward cannot rescue that state without additional resources or a changed repair route.

The alternative ends at `(128,4)`, safely above its requirement of 88. The proof gives an invariant for all subsequent cycles; the conclusion is not extrapolated from a long simulation.

This makes the feedback in the original idea concrete: an action selected for its current result changes the conditions under which later changes can become effective. The cash balance alone obscures it. The initially preferred outcome has more cash, but the other outcome has the apparatus that makes its cash sufficient.

## Adoption and succession can favor different rules

The same short-horizon rule that fails to build four channels retains them when they are already installed. For every inherited cash level from 88 to 240, it chooses four and maps cash to `min(240,b+8)`.

A successor can therefore remain viable by inheriting the sustainable apparatus even if it does not inherit the predecessor's longer horizon. Physical assets carry part of the difference. This is a constructed result about this process; it does not establish that existing institutions deserve preservation or that inherited practices remain appropriate after circumstances change.

The financing threshold helps explain adoption. Under an ample-funding, nonbinding-cap comparison between two fixed-return designs, let the more expensive design add installation expense `A` and improve each cycle's cash return by `Δg>0`. A terminal-cash planner favors it precisely when

\[
\boxed{h\,\Delta g>A,}
\]

with the supplied lower-cost tie rule at equality. Here `A=60` and `Δg=48`, so one cycle rejects the investment and two cycles favor it. This comparison assumes the installation payment is possible. A longer forecast cannot create the missing first payment.

Two controls prevent an automatic preference for maintenance. With no faults, zero channels permitted, and a nonbinding cash cap in that control, the same rule chooses no diagnostic apparatus. With the duty ending after one completed cycle and costless harmless closure explicitly permitted, two channels fulfill the finite duty and leave the greatest cash. Indefinite continuation is one declared test among others.

## Learning changes adoption only through usable evidence

The [paid-learning model](paid-learning.md) makes the actor uncertain about a persistent regime. In the base case, the high regime has fault probability `1/2`, the low regime has probability zero, and the supplied prior assigns probability `1/5` to the high regime. Probe outcomes and the later deployment fault are independent conditional on that regime.

The controller chooses a fixed number of probes before observing them. Each costs 0.08; retaining one memory bit costs 0.02 per probe interval. Its actual register can retain whether any probe was positive, retain the count, retain only the last sample, or lose the evidence. Its deployment decision receives only the final physical register. It cannot consult the analyst's observation history.

Maintained readiness costs one and reduces a later fault's repair bill to six; the substitute repair costs fourteen. The supplied selector minimizes expected learning expense plus deployment expense and a separately declared loss if repair is unaffordable. Actual cash and that imputed loss are recorded separately.

With fifteen cash units, two probes and a retained “any positive” bit are optimal among the declared candidate protocols. They reduce the expected score from 1.4 without inquiry to 1.15. In the high regime, the actor adopts readiness with probability `3/4`; in the low regime it never does. The decision is an outcome of acquired evidence and the specified update rule.

For the admitted `N=0,…,8` probes with that register in the funded base case, the exact score is

\[
J_N=0.8+0.6\,2^{-N}+0.1N.
\]

The last term pays for obtaining and retaining the evidence. This displays a finite tradeoff between reducing uncertainty and consuming support. Erasing the bit restores the prior-based decision while leaving the inquiry bill paid. Increasing observation or memory prices can make no inquiry the selected protocol.

The memory representation matters when the regimes overlap. In a separate control, one positive observation and two positives call for different decisions. A count register then outperforms the “any positive” register despite its larger retention cost. This is selection among a supplied representation menu, not invention of an unrestricted new concept.

### An expected-score improvement can accept a loss of guarantee

At starting cash eight, the same two-probe protocol minimizes the supplied expected score but has failure probability `1/40`. The retained evidence can miss the high regime, leading to no maintenance and an unaffordable substitute repair when a fault arrives.

Yet always maintaining without probes costs at most seven and repairs every admitted deployment fault. A sure-feasible controller exists; the expected-score selector chooses a different tradeoff. The result distinguishes criteria rather than calling either calculation mistaken.

There is also a direct support limit on learning. Starting from 7.1, paying 0.2 for two probes and their register leaves 6.9, below the seven needed to maintain and repair a fault. The funded two-probe procedure has consumed the margin required for the sure guarantee. The actual score-minimizing protocol at that starting cash uses one probe instead. This retains the physical option to maintain, while its chosen action rule still accepts a 0.05 failure risk. Acquiring information and retaining the ability to act on it are separate requirements.

These are finite deployment episodes. They do not establish that a learning process finances itself indefinitely, discovers its own likelihood model, or safely explores an unknown world without resets.

## A rule must survive its own succession process

The [transmission model](selection-and-scale.md) isolates another mechanism. Each operating cycle starts with two reserve units, then owes one service unit and one succession unit. An external receipt of two arrives **after** succession has been paid.

A reserve-preserving operation produces one unit of visible output without using reserve. A consuming operation produces two output units but spends one reserve unit. Output is not a cash receipt. The first rule completes every cycle; the second reaches the succession payment without enough cash.

An initially successful rule can still fail if transmission changes it. Suppose each paid handoff independently corrupts the preserving rule into the consuming rule with probability `μ`, and corruption is irreversible in this model. Then

\[
\boxed{\Pr(\text{complete }N\text{ cycles})=(1-\mu)^{N-1}.}
\]

The first cycle is completed before its handoff can affect the next one. Any positive fixed corruption probability makes infinite survival probability zero under this particular channel law. This concerns a specified vulnerable mechanism; it does not imply that every succession process inevitably fails.

The physical plant still admits a successful controller. That existence does not give the installed corrupted program a free means to replace itself. Paid transmission, reliable transmission, and the availability of a good rule are distinct facts.

This experiment models inheritance and transmission fidelity. Population-level differential reproduction or imitation would require an additional contribution and population-update mechanism. It is not established merely because a label is copied.

## The stronger condition for transfer across scales

A capacity-preserving map says that an effective controller can be implemented at another level. Certified transfer of actual behavior requires the induced closed-loop dynamics to correspond, including learning and transmission effects relevant to the test. Internal procedures need not be literally identical when their joint observable behavior agrees.

The new theorem supplies two forms:

- For robust statements, every actual concrete transition must have a corresponding actual abstract transition, with the required information, payment, safety, and timing obligations preserved.
- For probabilistic statements, the **joint law** of the next event and state must map correctly from every relevant detailed state. Matching possible outcomes or separate one-time frequencies is insufficient.

Under the exact joint-kernel condition, corresponding initial distributions give equal observable trajectory laws. Under a uniform one-step total-variation error `ε` and initial error `δ`, the finite-horizon trajectory discrepancy is at most `min(1,δ+Nε)` after `N` steps. That approximate bound alone supplies no infinite sure guarantee.

For the actual planning rule, a useful special case is a bijection between feasible planning trees, a positive affine transformation of terminal scores, preserved tie order, and corresponding replanning updates. The adopted actions then transfer too.

The repair experiment checks a physical replication: multiply modules, cash, cap, and admissible channel counts by the same integer. Durations stay fixed, every financial quantity scales, and the terminal-cash ordering is preserved. Both the short-horizon failure and longer-horizon continuation transfer. The replicated menu is restricted to the exact scaled image; admitting extra intermediate designs would change the decision problem.

This makes the cross-scale thesis more demanding and more useful. The same feasibility constraints can apply while outcomes change. To predict the same **actual** behavior under a scale change, the selection, learning, and inheritance mechanisms must also be mapped.

The theory now contains explicit mechanisms for three formerly open links: adoption from known financial forecasts, adoption from paid uncertain evidence, and succession through a paid transmission channel. The ingredients connect to established control, learning, and transmission research. The [source audit](selection-audit.md) records the precise connections and access limits. For example, [Watkins and Dayan's learning theorem](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/papers/cjch.pdf) has explicit sampling and update assumptions; it does not supply a general guarantee that a resource-limited learner survives while gathering data. The current finite Bayesian example makes its own narrower assumptions and proves its own results.

# Funded selection among decision rules

This experiment makes the copying and financing of decision rules part of the dynamics. It extends the [fourth-cycle operating process](../cycle-4/adoption-dynamics.md) while explicitly adding population turnover, a treasury, measurement, new-plant construction, and rule transmission.

The principal result is that an early cash-ranking rule can make one program reach 100% of a population while renewal capacity declines until no successor can be funded. Evaluating later cash changes both the selected program and the renewal outcome. A calibrated forecast from the early report gives the same result as later observation: the mechanism depends on how available evidence is used, not simply on waiting longer.

All persistence results remain conditional on the specified outside grant and production inputs. The model does not establish that a population creates all its own support.

## The candidate rules and the common calendar

There are two supplied programs. `S` uses the one-cycle rolling terminal-cash planner; `L` uses the two-cycle planner. Every new organizational instance starts with the same eight-module basic plant, 240 cash, and no auxiliary diagnostic channels. The prior experiment's paid diagnostic, authorization, and execution sequence remains unchanged.

The [checker](verification/check_funded_selection.py) obtains the following profiles by executing the earlier planner and expanding its actual payment steps:

| Program | Cash after first repair cycle | Cash after second cycle | Channels at the end |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| S | 140 | 100 | 2 |
| L | 128 | 136 | 4 |

Every population epoch lasts **two complete repair cycles**, sixteen original physical slots. Under both evaluation procedures, parents operate for both cycles, offspring are created at the same endpoint, and the same funding arrives on the same schedule. An early evaluator records first-cycle cash; a late evaluator records second-cycle cash. This does not compare a one-cycle reproduction interval with a two-cycle interval.

Every parent then retires. Its remaining cash returns to the common treasury; its basic plant and auxiliary channels are dismantled without resale. This forced two-cycle turnover is a new physical mechanism. It prevents an unacknowledged transfer of installed apparatus and differs from leaving a viable L carrier operating indefinitely. Closure has no additional modeled liability beyond the listed operations and destruction of the assets.

Only a **program** is copied. A newborn receives its own fully financed plant and reserve. One cannot obtain a new functioning organization merely by copying the label S or L.

## Every birth and every measurement are financed

The birth packet costs 260:

| Component | Amount | Accounting role |
|---|---:|---|
| Newborn cash | 240 | A transfer into the child's reserve |
| Construction of the basic eight-module plant | 16 | A payment to the supplied construction process |
| Program copying and installation | 4 | A payment to the transmission process |

Construction and copying have zero additional calendar delay in this supplied model. Auxiliary channels are purchased later by the newborn's actual planner from its 240. The fixed construction price and availability of the builder are explicit assumptions.

The initial two founders, one S and one L, are established with an outside endowment of 520: 480 operating cash, 32 basic-plant construction, and eight copying/installation fees. Initial common treasury is zero. Subsequent outside support is a grant of `G=150` per active parent per two-cycle epoch; no grant arrives for an empty population. Operating production also retains the earlier model's explicit external feedstock.

At the start of an epoch, the grant arrives in the treasury. A flat audit-and-record contract costs `e=2` per parent and is prepaid before the observed outcomes. It covers recording at the declared observation time and retaining the program/report association through the common copying boundary. The early and late contracts have the same price for this controlled comparison. Program/report payload does not alter the bill or grant. An independently priced evaluation-delay model appears in [paid evaluation](paid-evaluation.md).

These treasury funds cannot be redirected to rescue or change the incumbent parent operation. Each parent executes its supplied rule using its own 240. After the second cycle, parents remit their actual remaining cash.

Let current counts be `(N_S,N_L)`, total `N`, and treasury reserve `R`. The pool available for births is

\[
F=R+(G-e)N+100N_S+136N_L.
\]

There are at most `K=4` physical sites. The number of newborns is

\[
M=\min\{K,\lfloor F/260\rfloor\}.
\]

Pay all birth packets. Carry the remainder subject to treasury cap `U=259`, discarding any overflow:

\[
R'=\min\{259,F-260M\}.
\]

Capping occurs **after** the births are funded. The cap is less than the cost of one newborn, so an empty population cannot restart from retained treasury alone. There is no unmodeled immigration or permanent external program donor.

The grant must also cover the audit at its earlier payment time: `R+GN≥eN`. Positive terminal funds would not excuse a missed audit prepayment. All base cases satisfy that guard. The no-grant control supplies four treasury units specifically to pay its first audit.

### The real cash ledger

The 240 transferred to each newborn is not destroyed expenditure. The global check includes incumbent cash, treasury, grants, operating receipts, actual operating expenses, audit bills, plant/copy fees, discarded overflow, and the cash still held by children.

For the initial mixed population, 480 incumbent cash plus the grant 300 plus actual operating receipts 480 gives 1,260. It balances exactly against 724 operating/installation expenses, four audit fees, forty new plant/copy fees, 480 child cash, and twelve remaining treasury units. Both evaluation procedures have this same ledger; only the copied program differs.

## The implemented copying rules

The first comparison copies the program of the highest measured-cash parent into every funded newborn. If several parents tie, parents among the tied group are sampled uniformly. Every copy is paid. This is an explicit score-to-copy rule, not a deduction that cash automatically causes reproductive success.

- Early raw cash is 140 for S versus 128 for L, so an initially mixed population copies S.
- Late cash is 100 for S versus 136 for L, so the same initial population copies L.

Both initially fund two children and retain twelve treasury units. Population size is a consequence of financing, not a normalized constant.

## A program can fix while its population disappears

Under early winner copying:

| Epoch | Original repair cycles elapsed | S count | L count | Treasury | S share |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1/2 |
| 1 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 12 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | 1 | 0 | 248 | 1 |
| 22 | 44 | 1 | 0 | 8 | 1 |
| 23 | 46 | 0 | 0 | 256 | Undefined |

The final 256 is real retained treasury, but it cannot pay the next 260-unit birth packet. No parent remains to receive the next per-parent grant. Extinction is not represented as a winning type with a zero denominator.

Under late winner copying, the population becomes all L in the first epoch, remains nonempty, and reaches four sites at epoch eleven. Continuing grants and the declared production mechanism finance its subsequent replacements. The claim is indefinite funded renewal under those assumptions, not independence from outside support.

### Exact renewal-capital proof

Define the bookkeeping potential

\[
\Phi=260N+R.
\]

This is the replacement packet value of the current count plus treasury, **not literal cash inventory** or a conserved substance. If spill is `s≥0`, the transition identity is

\[
\boxed{\Phi'=\Phi-12N_S+24N_L-s.}
\]

For an all-S population, every nonempty epoch decreases this finite potential by at least twelve. It must therefore become empty in finitely many epochs. This proves the conclusion beyond the displayed trajectory.

For all L, each parent contributes `136+150−2=284` to the pool, exceeding the 260 needed for one funded replacement. Therefore `M≥N` whenever `1≤N≤K`, and nonemptiness is invariant. At treasury cap 259, surplus can accumulate enough to fund additional sites until the site limit is reached. With treasury cap zero, the same population instead persists at its original count and spills its surplus; persistence and population growth are different claims.

Under this exact retirement and birth mechanism, the per-parent grant thresholds are

\[
G_{\min,L}=260+2-136=126,
\qquad
G_{\min,S}=260+2-100=162.
\]

The base grant 150 lies between them. Raising it to 162 makes pure S replacement financially sustainable. Lowering it to 125 makes even pure L exhaust finite support. These are renewal thresholds for the declared packet, audit, and cohort lifespan, not the earlier operating-viability thresholds of a continuing individual.

With no continuing grant and an initial treasury of four to prepay observation, the first epoch returns only 236, insufficient for a single new packet. Both selection procedures then produce no successor. A better score-to-copy rule cannot manufacture the missing construction and reserve resources.

## Correct interpretation can use early information

The early numerical report distinguishes the two supplied program profiles. With the known model, an evaluator can map early cash 140 to predicted two-cycle return 100, and early cash 128 to predicted return 136. Ranking that predicted return selects L while still observing at the early time.

This calibrated early procedure has exactly the same copying kernel as late observation at every one of the 3,900 population/treasury states in the finite domain. The grant, audit contract, retirement, birth time, and financing remain unchanged. The counterexample therefore concerns **raw immediate-cash evaluation versus a continuation-sensitive use of evidence**. It does not prove that later observation is inherently necessary or that short observation windows inevitably fail.

The calibration is supplied model knowledge. Learning it, verifying that it remains valid, or acting when two programs have indistinguishable early reports are different tasks. The paid-evaluator companion studies those distinctions with explicit interfaces and timing expenses.

## Softer copying and exact survival probabilities

Winner copying is not essential to the contrast. A second mechanism samples each newborn's parent independently, with probability proportional to the parent's measured cash. With `w_S,w_L` as the relevant scores,

\[
p_S=\frac{N_Sw_S}{N_Sw_S+N_Lw_L},
\qquad N'_S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(M,p_S),
\qquad N'_L=M-N'_S.
\]

The birth count `M` is already fixed by real financing; the score assigns program labels to those funded births. Scores do not create cash. This independence is a substantive joint-copying assumption, not a consequence of knowing the marginal probability of each label.

With faithful copying, a pure L population is a persistent class, and pure S is doomed by the finite-potential argument. After any finite number of epochs, current pure-L probability is therefore a lower bound on eventual survival. Adding the still-mixed probability gives an upper bound. Exact rational propagation for 24 epochs yields:

| Evaluation rule | Certified interval for eventual nonextinction probability |
|---|---:|
| Raw early cash | 0.4553133970 to 0.4553135483 |
| Late cash | 0.6490735099 to 0.6490735989 |
| Calibrated early forecast | Identical to late cash |

The remaining interval width is unresolved mixed-population probability, not Monte Carlo error. These are eventual-survival bounds derived from absorbing classes, not merely the probability of being alive after 24 epochs. Even late evaluation has a positive chance of losing L through finite-population copying and then depleting.

The results also report expected population, expected S share conditional on nonemptiness, and the ratio of expected S count to expected total. The latter two quantities need not agree. Neither should replace the absolute funded counts.

## Variation can improve a finite horizon while changing the infinite result

Now let every paid copy independently switch its program label with probability `μ`. The child S probability is

`p'_S=μ+(1−2μ)p_S`.

This is symmetric variation between the two supplied rules. It can restore L after S fixation as well as introduce S into a pure-L population.

Under late weighted copying, the exact probability of extinction by epoch thirty is lower at `μ=0.01` than at `μ=0`; the [results](verification/funded-selection-results.json) retain both finite distributions. This does not establish an infinite-horizon advantage.

For the base financing and any fixed `0<μ<1`, **eventual extinction has probability one** in this bounded model. To see why, put `m=min(μ,1−μ)>0`. Every copied child has conditional probability at least `m` of being S. There are at most four children per epoch, so an all-S batch has conditional probability at least `m^4` whenever reproduction occurs. The potential is bounded by `260·4+259=1299`. One all-S batch followed by at most 109 all-S epochs forces extinction through the negative potential increments. Hence each block of 110 epochs has, conditional on prior survival, a uniformly positive extinction probability at least `m^440`. Repeated blocks give a survival probability tending to zero.

This conservative bound can be extraordinarily small; it is not a useful forecast of how soon extinction occurs. The conclusion depends on finite storage/sites, recurring independent variation, the absence of a guaranteed rescue channel, and the specified depleting S regime. Different joint copying, protected backups, immigration, or financing change the argument. The faithful-copy boundary `μ=0` has the positive survival probabilities above.

# Paid evaluation, rule copying, and a usable successor

The same two supplied rules can produce opposite early and later rankings. A paid evaluator can therefore change which rule is copied, but correct identification alone does not guarantee that the successor can execute that rule. The evaluator may consume the reserve needed to bridge the successor's first repair. Copying a program also does not copy the channels that made its donor effective.

This is a finite evaluation-and-handoff experiment followed by an exact infinite-continuation check. It is separate from the common-calendar population model in this research cycle. There is one successor here, no endogenous evaluator financing, no population-growth theorem, and no claim that delayed evaluation is always better.

## 1. Physical process and supplied rules

The repair plant is the deterministic periodic plant used in the cycle-4 adoption study. Its basic eight-unit body is already present. An integer reserve has cap 240. An optional number of repair channels, \(k\in\{0,\ldots,8\}\), is a physical asset. Building an additional channel costs 30; discarding one is free and yields no sale proceeds. Dropping and later rebuilding pays again.

Each fault episode contains eight faults; the next episode begins eight slots later. Newly supplied diagnoses distinguish their hidden causes perfectly, and each diagnosis, authorization, and execution costs one unit per repaired item. The whole service stops earning during repair. Diagnosis can process \(k\) items per slot; authorization and execution add two pipeline slots. Thus, when \(k>0\),

\[
T(k)=\lceil8/k\rceil+2,\qquad
C(k)=24+(8+2k)T(k).
\]

A repair must finish within six slots. Every repaired healthy slot produces gross receipt 40, then pays basic operation 8 and channel upkeep \(2k\), leaving \(32-2k\). The carried reserve is capped after receipt and payment. There is no receipt during repair. Capital installation precedes repair. Since all repair payments are nonnegative and there is no intervening receipt, holding \(C(k)\) after installation is exactly the prefix-financing requirement for that episode. The cycle-4 checker separately expands this macrotransition into its diagnosis/authorization/execution slot ledger.

For current channels \(j\), choosing \(k\) costs \(30\max(k-j,0)\) before repair. The end reserve, before applying the cap at each healthy slot, is

\[
b'=b-30\max(k-j,0)-C(k)+(8-T(k))(32-2k).
\]

The actual rule **S** chooses the payable complete one-cycle plan with greatest terminal cash. Rule **L** chooses the payable complete two-cycle plan with greatest terminal cash. Both execute only the first choice and plan again next cycle. Ties use the lexicographically smallest channel sequence. If L cannot finance any two-cycle plan, it tries a one-cycle plan; either rule fails when no complete single cycle can be paid. Neither controller is supplied the infinite viability set as its objective.

The usable designs are:

| Channels | Repair duration | Repair expense | Healthy-cycle receipts after bills | Net cycle gain with existing channels |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 6 | 96 | 56 | −40 |
| 3 | 5 | 94 | 78 | −16 |
| 4 | 4 | 88 | 96 | +8 |
| 5 | 4 | 96 | 88 | −8 |
| 6 | 4 | 104 | 80 | −24 |
| 7 | 4 | 112 | 72 | −40 |
| 8 | 3 | 96 | 80 | −16 |

One channel misses the deadline; zero channels cannot repair. Each positive infinite claim below is conditional on the explicitly specified, indefinitely available healthy production input of gross 40 per slot and on the periodic fault/process contract. It is not a closed-system perpetual-growth claim.

### Capacity and actual continuation

**Plant-capacity proposition.** An infinite feasible sequence of repairs exists from \((b,j)\) exactly when

\[
b\ge 88+30\max(4-j,0).
\]

**Proof.** If the inequality holds, install four channels immediately and use them forever. Repair requires 88, and each complete cycle adds eight before the cap. Conversely, every feasible design except four has strictly negative net gain, even before any installation expense or cap loss. An infinite feasible path must therefore use four eventually. If \(j<4\), reaching four requires total positive channel purchases of at least \(30(4-j)\); all complete cycles before the first four-channel cycle have nonpositive net change. At least 88 must remain for that first repair. If \(j\ge4\), every feasible first repair itself costs at least 88. These observations give the same lower bound. ∎

For the actual supplied rules, the exact continuation regions needed here are:

| Initial auxiliary assets | S continues forever exactly when | L continues forever exactly when |
|---|---|---|
| No channels | Never, for \(0\le b\le240\) | \(b\ge208\) |
| Four channels | \(b\ge88\) | \(b\ge88\) |

These results also have short direct proofs. From a cold plant, every payable first choice available below cap 240 is among two, three, and four channels. Their one-cycle changes, including construction, are respectively −100, −106, and −112. S therefore builds two, keeps two, loses 40 per subsequent cycle, and eventually cannot pay 96. An existing two-channel plant likewise cannot be rescued by S's own one-cycle choices, regardless of its starting reserve up to 240.

When \(208\le b\le240\), L can build four and complete two cycles, ending with \(b-104\). Starting with two gives at most \(b-140\) after two cycles; starting with three gives at most \(b-122\), or \(b-128\) when switching to four. Thus L chooses four. From an existing four-channel plant, both rules keep four: it has the greatest feasible one-cycle gain, and alternative designs incur a loss and cannot improve a two-cycle result. The capacity proposition excludes all cold starting reserves below 208 and all four-channel reserves below 88. This proves the stated thresholds independently of a long simulated trace.

## 2. Trial profiles and observation

Two candidate addresses A and B contain one S program and one L program, in an unknown permutation. Both source trials start with an already-present basic plant, no auxiliary channels, and separately endowed cash 240. Their cash endowment totals 480. Their source program remains readable even if the trial plant later fails a repair. The evaluator cannot inspect the program identity before choosing a source.

| Completed checkpoint | S cash / auxiliary channels | L cash / auxiliary channels | Completed every duty through this checkpoint? |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | 140 / 2 | 128 / 4 | Both yes |
| 2 | 100 / 2 | 136 / 4 | Both yes |
| 3 | 60 / 2 | 144 / 4 | Both yes |
| 4 | 60 / 2 | 152 / 4 | S no; L yes |

S's fourth entry is its retained cash when it cannot pay a complete repair; it is not a successfully completed fourth cycle. A trial with no payable complete repair shuts down, freezes its remaining cash, and ceases further operating receipts or bills. Its failed status and readable source program remain available at the checkpoint.

The evaluator chooses its checkpoint and interpretation rule before learning the address permutation. Three supplied interpretations are checked:

* **Cash ranking:** copy the address with greater audited cash; ties choose A.
* **Pass ranking:** observe only whether each trial completed every duty through the checkpoint, then copy a passing address; ties choose A.
* **Calibrated interpretation:** compare the observed cash/status pair with a supplied, correct L profile table; copy its uniquely matching address, otherwise A.

Cash ranking at checkpoint one chooses S. At checkpoint two it chooses L. But the early cash observations already distinguish the candidates: calibrated interpretation can choose L at checkpoint one by interpreting its *lower* early cash as the known investment signature. The reversal under raw cash ranking is therefore a property of that criterion and mechanism, not an informational impossibility theorem.

By contrast, the coarse pass observation is genuinely indistinguishable through checkpoint three. Swapping the two programs leaves the ordered observation \((\mathrm{pass},\mathrm{pass})\) unchanged. No observation-consistent deterministic evaluator can guarantee identifying L under both permutations. Under the explicitly uniform permutation distribution, any randomized evaluator based on that observation identifies L with probability at most \(1/2\). At checkpoint four, pass/fail separates the sources and pass ranking identifies L. The uniform distribution is used only for reported probabilities; all sure-continuation statements quantify over both assignments.

## 3. Paid evaluation, real address memory, and transfer

The evaluator and successor share an initial reserve \(R\), separate from the 480 of source-trial cash. There is no evaluator income. Source cash is inaccessible throughout and is not a successor endowment. The base plant body of the successor is separately endowed; this experiment prices its auxiliary channels, program transfer, and working reserve. A common construction bill \(E\), if introduced before launch with no intervening income, adds \(E\) to every threshold below. The population study in this cycle uses its own explicit construction and capital charges instead.

Payment order is:

1. Pay ten for evaluator support at the end of each trial cycle up to the predetermined checkpoint \(\tau\).
2. Pay two for the audit/comparison operation.
3. If retention is selected, pay one to carry the selected address through the handoff interval.
4. Pay two to copy the program from that address.
5. If transferring donor channels, pay three for the one-to-one physical handoff.
6. Launch the successor with the remainder, capped at 240; excess is explicitly recorded as spill.

All fees are actual cash bills. They are nonnegative, and there is no interim receipt. Total affordability is therefore equivalent to every payment prefix being affordable. A reserve of 19, for example, cannot finance two waiting bills; the second checkpoint is never reached by this evaluator.

The address register has states \(\{\bot,A,B\}\). At the end of audit, the audit controller retires. The copier receives only that physical register, the public preset protocol, and its cash; it has no audit transcript, remembered cash observations, hidden action history, or free payload-dependent timing channel. Paying retention preserves A or B. Without retention the register resets to \(\bot\), and the copier's supplied default is A. Fees and timing are independent of the selected address, so residual cash does not encode it. Program-copy cost includes its delivery; the address-retention fee covers the one intervening handoff interval. Trials retire at the checkpoint, and the channel-transfer fee covers the channels' custody and transport during this interval. Successor duties begin at launch; this model does not impose a common absolute service-start deadline across different checkpoints.

Three asset contracts are distinct:

* **Program only:** copy the rule; the successor starts with zero auxiliary channels. Source channels and source cash are not copied.
* **Donor bundle:** move the selected parent's existing auxiliary channels to this one successor. The selected donor ends with zero channels and retires. Hardware is conserved, not multiplied.
* **Existing four:** the successor already owns four endowed channels, independent of the selected parent. This is a different asset start state, used as a control.

The plant's internal repair observations remain under the supplied cycle-4 diagnostic contract. The newly priced finite memory here is specifically the evaluator-to-copier address. The study does not silently retrofit every internal computer register with this one fee.

## 4. Exact financing frontiers and reversals

Let \(\rho=1\) when the address is retained and zero otherwise, and let \(d=1\) for donor-channel transfer and zero otherwise. The total evaluator bill is

\[
A(\tau,\rho,d)=10\tau+4+\rho+3d.
\]

Once the chosen source and asset contract are fixed, the exact threshold is this bill plus the actual child's required reserve. When retained observation identifies L, program-only continuation requires \(R\ge A+208\); transferring its four channels requires \(R\ge A+88\). With an already-present four-channel plant, either copied rule continues exactly when \(R\ge A+88\).

These are failures of the supplied rule, even where an alternative allowed policy has feasible continuation.

### No-hazard control

When the periodic fault is removed, both rules may choose zero auxiliary channels, receive eight healthy production receipts, and continue. The menu explicitly includes zero in this control. Receipts precede operating bills, so even a zero-reserve already-built plant can start healthy production. Both source rules reach cap 240 and their labels are indistinguishable by the tested observations. An early evaluator with \(R=15\) and a delayed evaluator with \(R=25\) each leaves zero child cash and succeeds. The second waits an extra cycle and pays ten more without improving continuation. This control changes the disturbance contract, not the rule into a welfare optimum.

## 5. Why the infinite conclusions are exact

For each of S and L under hazard/no-hazard, the checker constructs the actual deterministic successor of every state in

\[
Q=\{0,\ldots,240\}\times\{0,\ldots,8\}.
\]

There are 2,169 states per graph and 8,676 across the four graphs. It first marks states with no payable complete successor. It then repeatedly marks every state whose actual successor is marked. The remaining states form a closed invariant: every such state has a successor in the same set. Every losing state receives a positive rank that strictly decreases along its successor until a state with no payable successor is reached. Closure proves infinite continuation; the finite descending rank proves eventual failure. These are exhaustive graph certificates, not extrapolations from a selected trajectory, and concern the specified actual controller rather than an optimizer permitted to replace it.

For each evaluation protocol the checker enumerates both hidden source assignments, generates only the declared observations, executes the supplied interpretation, resets or retains the actual address register, and checks the launched state against that copied controller's invariant. The universal order is: **one preset protocol, then every hidden address assignment, then its observation-determined choice**. There is no source-identity-dependent pre-observation choice.

The 72 frontier entries cover four checkpoints, three interpretations, three asset contracts, and retention present/absent. Their reserve search through 300 is complete, not merely a finite lower-bound search: every protocol's total bill is at most 48, and reserve above \(48+240=288\) cannot change any child's capped state or selected source. Null entries therefore mean no reserve works under that protocol and cap. Fifteen selected examples additionally assert the reversals above.

The certificates are executable evidence for this finite declared model. The analytical financing, indistinguishability, and capacity arguments explain why its central numbers follow. The calculations do not establish that these fee sizes, horizons, or signal interpretations are empirically appropriate in any particular biological, social, or computational population.

# Populations, funded succession, and scale

Cycle 5 mathematical memo, 5 October 2026. This extends [actual selection and transmission](../cycle-4/selection-and-scale.md) to finite populations of physically endowed carriers. It separates differential contribution, absolute continuation, offspring dependence, and cross-scale correspondence. The results are conditional accounting and stochastic-process arguments; no new general law of evolution or mathematical priority is claimed.

## 1. The population state must include carriers and their support

At a census, write the state as

`P=( {z_i}_{i=1}^{N}, r, e )`,

where `N` is the actual carrier count, `z_i` records a carrier's plant, program, retained memory, accessible stock, age, and execution rights, `r` records any accessible shared reserve, and `e` contains the relevant common environment. A multiset suffices when identities have no further effect. When kinship, parent identity, locality, or credit relationships matter, retain those relations too.

A population transition must specify at least:

1. how carriers operate and generate observable consequences during a declared evaluation window;
2. what is measured, retained, and paid for;
3. how contribution scores affect funded allocations to successors;
4. how actual successor carriers are built, endowed, and given access;
5. the joint transmission law for their programs and records;
6. which parents retire and which assets or balances remain accessible.

A contribution weight is an input to an allocation rule. It is not itself money, physical offspring, or an endowed working process. If an observation arrives after allocation, it cannot have caused that allocation. If a parent is copied before its later failure, the earlier rule may spread despite that failure. These are temporal features of the mechanism, not implications of a generic preference for successful behavior.

After these mechanisms are supplied, a generation has an actual joint kernel

`K(P; event,P')`.

The event can include measurements, choices, fees, births, deaths, grants, and discarded balances. The state must retain any common random cause or memory needed to make this kernel a valid description. For the general statements below, state and event sets are finite or countable, every generation has a finite realized population, and the transition probabilities sum to one. An empty population is absorbing only when the declared mechanism cannot construct a new carrier from its remaining assets or external inputs.

## 2. Relative contribution is a different quantity from absolute continuation

Let `N_j` be the current number of carriers of type `j`, and `x_j=N_j/N` when `N>0`. At extinction the frequencies are undefined; assigning a surviving frequency to an empty population conceals the event of interest.

In a deterministic model with exact offspring counts

`N'_j=Σ_i N_i f_i M_ij`,

normalizing gives the familiar frequency update

`x'_j=Σ_i x_i f_i M_ij / Σ_i x_i f_i`,

provided the denominator is positive. This identity requires that its right-side count expression actually describes the mechanism. Integer rounding, inaccessible endowments, shared bottlenecks, or random offspring totals can prevent that interpretation. A deterministic fractional-mass model is another declared model, not automatically an exact finite population.

With random counts, a mean-offspring matrix can correctly describe `E[N'_j|P]` under its stated conditional transmission assumptions. That does not generally describe the expected normalized share. For example, let offspring counts be `(A,B)=(1,0)` or `(0,9)`, each with probability one-half. Then

`E[A/(A+B)]=1/2`, while `E[A]/E[A+B]=1/10`.

Neither outcome is empty. The two expressions weight differently sized realized populations differently. These outcomes can be financed by a fixed reserve sufficient for nine children; the one-child branch simply leaves unused funds. The probability distinction does not require unsupported offspring.

If the number of successor slots is fixed and positive, and each slot has type marginal `p_j`, then expected share does equal `p_j` by linearity. Independence is unnecessary for that particular mean, but it still matters for the distribution. A subsequent viability filter can make the surviving total random again.

## 3. P5.1 — Favored share can rise while all carriers disappear

Consider a deliberately small process with two types, A and B. Each live parent carries three cash units. Evaluation lasts one generation and costs one cash unit per parent. The evaluator assigns supplied contribution scores two to A and one to B. These are visible performance scores, not cash income.

After paying evaluation, parents pool their remaining cash. A child requires one unit for construction and copying plus three units of inherited operating cash. All parents retire after this allocation; no resale or outside receipt occurs. Any unallocated remainder is removed from the accessible system. Copying is faithful and every child has the same endowment and construction cost, regardless of its type.

With `N` parents, the number of funded child slots is therefore

`M=floor[2N/(1+3)]=floor(N/2)`.

Allocate these slots by largest-remainder quotas proportional to `(2N_A,N_B)`, resolving exact remainder ties in favor of A. This is the supplied finite allocation rule; contribution weights change the type distribution but do not change the available money.

Starting with 64 carriers of each type gives:

| Generation | A carriers | B carriers | A share among living carriers |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 64 | 64 | 1/2 |
| 1 | 43 | 21 | 43/64 |
| 2 | 26 | 6 | 13/16 |
| 3 | 14 | 2 | 7/8 |
| 4 | 7 | 1 | 7/8 |
| 5 | 4 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | 2 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 8 | 0 | 0 | Undefined: extinction |

The favored type takes over, but no carrier continues indefinitely. Every transition satisfies the exact ledger

`3N = evaluation fee N + construction/copy fee M + inherited cash 3M + discarded remainder`.

The initial 384 units are completely accounted for across the run. No measured score is substituted for a replenishment flow. A frequency-only account would miss the central outcome.

### General depletion lemma

Suppose a generational process has finite initial accessible stock `S₀`, no external inflow or net stock-creating conversion, nonnegative remaining stocks, and an irreversible cost of at least `c>0` per newborn. All current carriers retire by the next census; a nonempty next census therefore requires at least one new carrier. Transfers between parents, pools, and children do not create stock.

Then an empty census occurs no later than `floor(S₀/c)+1`. If the empty state is absorbing, this is permanent extinction by that bound. If retained assets can later reconstruct a carrier, the bound concerns the first interruption of active-carrier continuity; it does not locate the last possible reconstruction.

**Proof.** If the first `t` transitions all lead to nonempty censuses, at least `t` births have been funded. Their irreversible expense is at least `tc`, so `tc≤S₀`. Taking `t=floor(S₀/c)+1` contradicts this inequality. Discarded stock or additional operating costs only strengthen the obstruction. ∎

The bound is intentionally loose; the example dies in eight generations. The assumptions matter. Costless copying, arbitrarily long-lived parents, productive external inputs, or an accessible outside balance change the model. In particular, differential selection does not itself supply the omitted replenishment.

## 4. P5.2 — A constructive succession reserve condition

Consider a specified handoff with no incoming funds during construction. Suppose child `j` needs a setup/copy payment `k_j` and usable continuation reserve `r_j`. Any retained parent needs reserve `r_parent`, and a common setup stage costs `k₀`. Assume the actual assembly and transmission protocol can create the required child configurations, respects its information and authority interfaces, finishes before the parents' permitted retirement, and has no additional unpriced contention or obligation.

Then sufficient funding from an accessible common pool is

`b ≥ k₀ + Σ_j(k_j+r_j) + r_parent`.

With nonnegative payments and no intervening income, this total pays every spending prefix of a sequential implementation and leaves the specified reserves. If the listed fees and reserves are mandatory in this same handoff model, the inequality is also necessary by conservation. It is not a theorem that money alone can construct any desired carrier. Physical access, materials, duration, and the implemented program remain independent conditions; typed stocks require their own componentwise accounts or explicit conversion routes.

The reserves must refer to the actual continuation test. A child's reserve sufficient for one repair is not automatically sufficient for producing its next successor. The actual allocation must leave the reserve accessible to the child, rather than count cash simultaneously in several recipients or divert it according to an unrelated score.

### A repeated homogeneous construction

For a concrete sufficient indefinite condition, suppose each new carrier begins with reserve `R` and an actual certified operating protocol maps it to handoff cash `min(B,R+G)`, where `B` is its carried-cash cap. The certificate separately verifies every operating payment prefix from reserve `R`. Here `G` parameterizes the certified endpoint transition; merely summing receipts minus expenses does not establish that transition when intermediate spills can precede later bills. Its payment order and capping effects must be checked.

Each new child requires setup/copy expense `K` and fresh reserve `R`. If the parent produces `m≥1` children, the exact handoff funding condition is

`min(B,R+G) ≥ m(R+K)`,

equivalently

`B ≥ m(R+K)`, and `G ≥ (m−1)R+mK`.

If the actual protocol completes within the reproduction window and **every admitted joint transmission outcome contains at least one child in the same certified operating-and-reproduction class**, these conditions can be applied recursively. Starting with such a carrier, every census has a certified successor. Induction gives nonextinction and continuation along at least one certified lineage. A duty requiring several concurrent functions or a minimum population needs the corresponding stronger invariant. Producing `m` children all in that class is a stronger sufficient condition, not required for the existence of one continuing lineage.

This induction presumes the environment supplies the promised input to each continuing carrier and that simultaneous lineages do not exhaust a shared resource that the certificate treated as independent. If the promise is conditional on a population-level capacity limit, that limit belongs in the joint invariant. Parent retirement occurs only after the successor is ready. A per-copy success probability below one is not the all-outcome transmission condition.

For one child, the conditions reduce to `B≥R+K` and `G≥K`, alongside the operating and handoff certificates. For multiple children, the extra inherited endowments are real transfers that must also be funded. Multiplying contribution weights cannot replace them.

## 5. P5.3 — Offspring dependence changes extinction despite equal marginals

Give a valid parent reserve three. It prepays one operating unit, receives an explicitly external six units, and reaches handoff with eight. That funds two children, each with construction/copy expense one and reserve three. The same money and chronology apply to both mechanisms below. Invalid copies consume their funded construction and endowment and fail before the next census; they cannot donate those funds back. Valid copies can repeat the specified operating protocol.

Compare two joint transmission mechanisms, independently repeated for different valid parents and generations:

- **One protected copy:** exactly one of the two children is valid, with its position chosen fairly.
- **Independent copies:** each child is valid independently with probability one-half.

Every labeled child has marginal validity probability one-half in both mechanisms. Both produce one valid child per parent **in expectation**, and both pay for two physical births. The first mechanism has exactly one continuing carrier at every census when started from one. The second has viable count `Z_{t+1}|Z_t=n ~ Binomial(2n,1/2)`.

For independent copies,

`E[Z_t]=1` for every finite `t`, but `P(eventual extinction)=1`.

**Proof.** The conditional mean is `E[Z_{t+1}|Z_t]=Z_t`, giving mean one by induction. Let `q_t` be the probability that the lineage from one parent has no valid carrier at generation `t`. Independent sublineages give

`q₀=0`, `q_{t+1}=((1+q_t)/2)^2`.

The sequence increases and is bounded by one, so its limit `q` exists and satisfies `q=((1+q)/2)^2`. The only solution in `[0,1]` is one. Since zero is absorbing, the increasing union of finite-time extinction events is eventual extinction, with probability one. ∎

No infinite enumeration is used in this proof. The finite checker independently propagates the full viable-count distribution through seven generations, verifies the recurrence, mean one, and variance `t/2`. This is a classical critical branching-process result; the deterministic-one-child case is the essential degenerate exception, not a contradiction. See [Lyons and Peres, *Probability on Trees and Networks*, §5.1](https://rdlyons.pages.iu.edu/prbtree/). The author-hosted reference establishes classical context; the argument needed here is given in full.

The external six-unit receipt is a reliable per-valid-parent promise in this example. With a fixed shared feedstock pool, the assumed independent branching law can fail. These results do not claim that every real population with mean reproduction one goes extinct, or that marginal error rates alone identify the relevant population process. Dependence across siblings, across parents, and across generations must all be specified.

## 6. P5.4 — A full population process can transfer across scale

Let `L` and `H` be actual population processes, with state map `φ` and event map `χ`. Their states contain absolute counts, endowed configurations, common funds, clocks, controller memory, and common environmental state to the extent those affect the future. For all relevant concrete states and abstract event/next-state pairs, require

`Σ_{χ(e_L)=e_H, φ(P'_L)=P'_H} K_L(P_L;e_L,P'_L)`

`= K_H(φ(P_L);e_H,P'_H)`. **(PK)**

Assume corresponding initial distributions and corresponding tests. Then translated concrete population trajectories have the abstract joint path law. If `φ(P_L)` is empty exactly when `P_L` is empty, extinction probabilities agree; matching only normalized frequencies does not supply this condition. Cash units and test thresholds must also be translated explicitly when financial quantities are compared.

**Proof.** Conditional on every concrete past, (PK) gives the same projected next-event/state distribution as the abstract kernel. Induction gives equality of all finite cylinder probabilities. For countable state and event spaces these cylinder probabilities determine the path law. No finite population truncation is needed for this argument, but each declared kernel must be normalized and the state must contain the requisite memory. ∎

This is the previous closed-loop kernel theorem applied to population states, with its countable extension justified by the same nonnegative sums. It is not a new branching or evolutionary theorem. The extra substantive work lies in exhibiting a population-level correspondence.

A phase-by-phase sufficient certificate matches:

- evaluation windows, observations and their actual timing;
- measurement, record, construction, and transfer expenses;
- the actual funding/allocation mechanism, including rounding and caps;
- the joint program-and-endowment transmission mechanism;
- common shocks, parent retirement, and retained reserves;
- the child's subsequent interpretation of the transmitted rule and its usable information.

Every-prefix safety and bounded construction time remain necessary obligations of this sufficient implementation certificate when one generation hides multiple physical steps. An exact census kernel cannot by itself prove that no unsafe or insolvent internal state was visited. For adversarial rather than stochastic populations, use the cycle-4 actual transition relation condition uniformly over admitted environmental choices, with the same prefix and progress qualifications.

### Composition

Two population correspondences `L→M→H` satisfying (PK) compose by `φ_LH=φ_MH∘φ_LM` and `χ_LH=χ_MH∘χ_LM`. Sum the lower-level probabilities first over middle fibers and then over abstract fibers. Since all terms are nonnegative, rearranging the countable sums is valid. Initial distributions compose in the same direction. The result preserves the actual population mechanism, not merely the availability of a better reproduction policy.

## 7. Independent replication is not exact stochastic packet scaling

An exact constructive population map can group `a` corresponding carriers into a packet. Every operation, expense, reserve and contribution is replicated; corresponding packet members share the same evaluation and transmission outcome. Separate packets may still act independently. If allocation respects these packets, the detailed counts stay divisible by `a`, and dividing by `a` recovers the original joint process.

The checker verifies this kind of map for two-type populations with up to four source packets, nontrivial mortality and mutation, and packet factors two and six. It checks every one-step count kernel and the composed projection. This is a useful exact certificate, but its common-outcome assumption is substantive.

For contrast, one carrier surviving with probability one-half has extinction probability one-half after the transition. Two synchronized corresponding carriers have the same extinction probability, and their normalized count is either zero or one. Two independent carriers instead have survivor counts `0,1,2` with probabilities `1/4,1/2,1/4`; extinction probability is one-quarter. Both pairs have expected survivor count one. Independent replication improves this particular survival probability while failing the proposed exact normalized-count law.

Pooling can break a deterministic scaling claim too. In general,

`floor(aF/E) ≠ a floor(F/E)`.

Newly pooled remainders may fund additional children. To assert exact correspondence, restrict allocation to the scaled image, retain packet rules, or prove that the extra possibilities leave the actual selector unchanged. The same issue arises when a larger system gains intermediate designs, shared equipment, new communication routes, or different evaluation windows.

Changing the number of carriers is therefore neither automatically a unit conversion nor automatically a harmful or beneficial change. One must identify which budgets, dependencies, and selectors change with it. A correspondence can preserve some first moments while changing extinction, tail risk, or the probability that a protected lineage survives.

## 8. Integration and scope

The [companion population experiment](funded-selection.md) links contribution scores to the earlier short- and longer-horizon repair selectors.
